items.title: 1. Why haemodynamic monitoring matters: pressure, flow and oxygen delivery
items.priority: P2 HIGH (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 1.1 The fundamental physiological problem

- A patient can be hypotensive because the arterial system is vasodilated even though cardiac output is adequate; alternatively, a patient with normal blood pressure may have critically impaired systemic flow because intense vasoconstriction preserves pressure.
- Thus blood pressure, cardiac output, intravascular volume and tissue oxygen delivery are related, but not interchangeable.
- Selecting a monitor requires deciding which uncertainty is important enough to change treatment.
- This distinction is the organising principle for the whole set.

- **Mean arterial pressure (MAP)** is a time-averaged pressure that helps drive flow through organs.
- At physiological heart rates it is approximately DBP + one-third of pulse pressure, but invasive monitors derive MAP from the integrated arterial waveform.
- **Cardiac output (CO)** is HR × stroke volume (SV), usually 4–8 L/min in an adult at rest; **cardiac index** is CO divided by body surface area, approximately 2.5–4.0 L/min/m².
- **Systemic vascular resistance (SVR)** is (MAP − right atrial pressure)/CO × 80, reported as dyn·s·cm⁻⁵, or (MAP − RAP)/CO in Wood units.
- This derived global resistance is not a direct measurement of resistance in any particular tissue.

- Arterial oxygen content (CaO₂) is approximately **1.34 × Hb (g/dL) × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂ (mmHg)**, in mL O₂/dL.
- Oxygen delivery (DO₂) in mL/min is **CO (L/min) × CaO₂ (mL/dL) × 10**.
- A 70 kg adult with Hb 100 g/L (10 g/dL), SaO₂ 98%, PaO₂ 100 mmHg and CO 5 L/min has CaO₂ ≈ 13.4 mL/dL and DO₂ ≈ 670 mL/min.
- Increasing PaO₂ alone adds very little dissolved oxygen; correcting severe anaemia or a profoundly low CO may be more influential.
- Conversely, giving red cells or inotropes without an indication can cause harm.

- Whole-body oxygen uptake (VO₂) is DO₂ minus venous oxygen return: **VO₂ = CO × (CaO₂ − CvO₂) × 10**.
- Oxygen extraction ratio (O₂ER) = VO₂/DO₂, usually around 20–30%.
- Inadequate supply can drive up extraction and reduce mixed venous saturation, but sepsis can disrupt microcirculatory extraction so that SvO₂ is misleadingly high despite tissue hypoxia.
- An apparently reassuring macrohaemodynamic measurement cannot guarantee adequate cellular oxygenation.

- **Perfusion pressure** depends on arterial and venous/outflow pressure.
- The crude equation MAP − CVP approximates a systemic perfusion gradient; coronary perfusion is mainly diastolic aortic minus LV diastolic pressure and brain perfusion is MAP − ICP when ICP exceeds venous pressure.
- Raised right atrial or abdominal pressure may compromise renal and hepatic perfusion even with a seemingly acceptable MAP.
- Autoregulation differs between organs and is altered by chronic hypertension, sepsis and intracranial disease.

## 1.2 Build the clinical question before choosing the device

For every instability, first ask:

- (1) is this truly low perfusion or an artefact.
- (2) is adequate arterial pressure the immediate priority.
- (3) is forward flow inadequate.
- (4) is the patient likely to increase SV with additional preload.
- (5) is giving more fluid safe.
- (6) what is the response to a small targeted intervention?

- This order prevents common errors: treating a single low CVP with litres of fluid, using an unvalidated pulse contour number as the reason to give inotropes, and escalating vasopressor dose without recognising a failing right ventricle.

- The bedside evaluation begins with trend and context: surgical bleeding and fluid losses, anaesthetic depth, ventilation and PEEP, rhythm and heart rate, pulse pressure and waveform, skin temperature and capillary refill, urine output, lactate/acid–base and haemoglobin.
- Point-of-care ultrasound can identify major mechanical explanations such as tamponade, acute RV pressure loading or gross LV dysfunction.
- Monitoring should be **hypothesis-driven and decision-linked**; an additional device is justified only if its results are likely to improve management enough to outweigh procedural harm and interpretive burden.

| **Variable** | **What it actually tells you** | **A dangerous inference** |
|---|---|---|
| MAP | Arterial pressure and pressure available for organ perfusion | Normal MAP means normal CO or DO₂ |
| CVP/RAP | Pressure at the right atrium; venous congestion and downstream pressure | Low CVP always means fluid depletion; high CVP always excludes fluid responsiveness |
| CO/CI | Global forward volume flow per minute | A normal CO excludes maldistributed or microcirculatory hypoperfusion |
| SV/SV variation | Flow per beat, or respiratory variation under specified conditions | Any variation means the patient needs a fluid bolus |
| Lactate | Net production minus clearance, influenced by adrenergic stimulation and liver function | Raised lactate is synonymous with hypovolaemia |
| ScvO₂/SvO₂ | Balance of oxygen delivery, consumption and extraction | High venous saturation excludes shock |
| Echo | Cardiac chamber size/function, gross loading and potential mechanical causes | A single IVC diameter reliably defines intravascular volume |

## 1.3 Monitoring is an intervention, not a passive record

- An arterial catheter enables early recognition of rapid haemodynamic change but can also create false alarms from damping and excessive amplification.
- A PAC provides pressure and flow data in complex mixed shock but has bleeding, thrombosis and arrhythmia risks and requires substantial expertise.
- Any interpretation must include signal quality, transducer position, physiological assumptions, clinical setting and whether a reproducible change after an intervention is biologically plausible.

items.title: 2. Minimum monitoring, non-invasive blood pressure and selecting an arterial catheter
items.priority: P2 HIGH (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (3 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 2.1 The minimum standard and the higher-risk patient

- The 2025 ANZCA **PG18 Guideline on monitoring during anaesthesia** requires continuous clinical observation by an appropriately responsible anaesthetist in conjunction with monitoring devices.
- Circulation requires detection of the arterial pulse, supplemented by BP measurement, at intervals appropriate to stability and **no less frequently than 10 minutes**; this is a ceiling, not the usual interval for an unstable patient.
- For general anaesthesia, oxygen analysis, pulse oximetry, capnography and ventilation/disconnection monitoring have specific requirements, while ECG and BP monitoring must be available and used as indicated.
- An arterial monitor should be available when required.
- Alarm functions and documented trends matter as much as attaching equipment.
- For significant instability, decrease the NIBP cycle to about 1–2 minutes until continuous arterial measurement is established if indicated; many routine stable theatre patients are measured more frequently than the PG18 outer limit.

- **Non-invasive oscillometric BP** measures oscillations in cuff pressure during deflation.
- The maximal oscillation corresponds most closely to MAP, whereas systolic and diastolic values are estimated by proprietary algorithms.
- A cuff that is too small exaggerates BP; a too-large cuff may underestimate.
- The bladder size must suit limb circumference, with the cuff positioned near heart level.
- Arrhythmias, movement, vasoconstriction, obesity, extreme hypotension and compression beneath drapes reduce reliability.
- Blood pressure on a leg is not directly interchangeable with a brachial reading, and simultaneous comparisons need attention to limb position and arterial disease.

- An indwelling arterial catheter is appropriate for anticipated major haemodynamic variability, significant haemorrhage, vasoactive infusions, major cardiovascular surgery, severe cardiorespiratory disease, expected frequent blood sampling or when intermittent cuffs cannot be trusted.
- Its value is early detection, repeated blood sampling and a more precise continuous trend, not an intrinsically better prediction of which fluid or vasoactive drug the patient needs.
- An arterial line should not be placed solely because a particular procedure is 'major': choose on the interaction of patient, operation, resources and management consequences.
- In stable lower-risk patients, cuff monitoring generally suffices.

## 2.2 How the arterial pressure signal is created

- A cannula and saline-filled noncompliant tubing transmit arterial pressure to a transducer.
- A flexible diaphragm deflects across a strain gauge, converting mechanical pressure into an electrical signal.
- The displayed trace is pressure versus time; systolic upstroke follows LV ejection, peak systolic is influenced by ventricular ejection and arterial compliance, and the dicrotic notch coincides with aortic valve closure and arterial wave reflection.
- The mean pressure should be obtained by integration, not simply assuming the arithmetic mean of systolic and diastolic.

- **Zeroing** exposes the transducer to atmospheric pressure and defines zero.
- **Levelling** places the air–fluid interface at the phlebostatic axis (fourth intercostal space, mid-axillary line, approximately right atrial level) for systemic pressure.
- A transducer 10 cm **below** the correct reference over-reads by approximately 7.4 mmHg; 10 cm **above** under-reads by the same amount.
- The tubing and stopcocks must be primed, free of air, kept short and stiff, flushed with a pressure bag usually around 300 mmHg and labelled clearly to avoid accidental arterial drug injection.
- Re-level with changes in position and check the transducer's relationship to the anatomical target; in neurosurgery, cerebral perfusion may require an appropriately levelled tragus/foramen-of-Monro reference rather than the right atrial reference alone.

- A radial arterial pressure often has a higher systolic and lower diastolic pressure than proximal aortic pressure because of pulse-wave amplification; MAP is generally more similar across sites, though in severe vasoconstriction radial–femoral MAP gradients can occur.
- Catheter tip orientation, arterial spasm and damping can also explain a difference.
- Do not reflexively treat a peripheral systolic number as central aortic pressure.

## 2.3 Dynamic response: a testable source of false readings

- The entire fluid-filled measurement system acts like a second-order oscillator characterised by its **natural frequency** and **damping coefficient**.
- Normal frequency response allows accurate reproduction of a rapidly changing arterial waveform.
- If resonance is insufficiently damped, the waveform overshoots and rings; if overdamped, its amplitude is blunted.
- The waveform can change its systolic and diastolic measurements substantially while leaving integrated MAP relatively stable, provided there is no significant baseline error.

| **Signal fault** | **Typical waveform and numbers** | **Causes; what to do** |
|---|---|---|
| **Underdamped** | Sharp excessive systolic spike, pronounced oscillations after flush, falsely high SBP and low DBP; MAP often relatively preserved | Very long or elastic tubing, inadequate damping, resonance, inappropriate transducer system; inspect set, remove unnecessary extensions, compare NIBP |
| **Overdamped** | Rounded slow rise, absent dicrotic notch, falsely low SBP and high DBP | Air bubbles, fibrin/clot, narrow catheter, kink, stopcock partly closed, arterial wall contact; flush/aspirate carefully, reposition, remove bubbles, change components |
| **Baseline/zero error** | Whole waveform shifted up/down while shape remains reasonable | Mislevelling, zero drift, wrong transducer site; re-zero and re-level |
| **Physiological or sampling issue** | Fluctuating shape, intermittent loss, extreme beat-to-beat changes | AF, ectopy, coughing, vasospasm, IABP, low output; correlate ECG, NIBP and clinical state |

**Fast-flush/square-wave test:**

- Briefly flush the transducer and release: a fast rise then rapid fall to baseline with roughly one or two small oscillations is usually acceptable.
- Multiple persistent oscillations suggest underdamping; no oscillation with a sluggish return suggests overdamping.
- Interpret with clinical waveforms, not oscillation count alone.
- A damped trace in a hip-fracture patient (a previous ANZCA examination topic) should prompt systematic equipment checks before drugs are given to 'correct' a spurious systolic reading.

## 2.4 Arterial cannulation, site selection and complications

- Radial is common because it is superficial, compressible and has collateral palmar perfusion; ultrasound improves identification in oedema and shock.
- Dorsalis pedis is accessible but peripheral amplification is pronounced and is unsuitable with compromised foot perfusion.
- Femoral provides more central pressure in profound vasoconstriction and is an option in cardiac surgery or failed peripheral access, but carries bleeding, infection, mobility and limb-ischaemia risks.
- Brachial has less redundancy in distal collateral supply and is generally less attractive for routine prolonged use.
- All sites require strict asepsis, ultrasound where useful, secure fixation, regular limb assessments and prompt removal when no longer indicated.

- The modified Allen test has limited ability to predict hand ischaemia and should not be used as a guarantee of safety.
- Ultrasound Doppler and clinical vascular assessment may be appropriate in vascular disease.
- Potential complications include thrombosis/limb ischaemia, haematoma, pseudoaneurysm, infection, nerve injury, arteriovenous fistula, embolism and rare major bleeding after accidental disconnection.
- Intra-arterial drug injection can cause tissue injury; never use arterial ports for medication.
- Continuous waveforms and site checks are required during transport as well as theatre use.

## 2.5 A full examination-level comparison of blood-pressure measurement in morbid obesity

- The difficult question in severe obesity is not whether an arterial catheter is 'better', but whether the likely error and intermittency of non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP) monitoring are acceptable for this particular operation.
- Oscillometric cuffs are validated for specific arm circumferences and shapes.
- A disproportionately conical upper arm may prevent even a nominally correct cuff from distributing pressure evenly; a short cuff can overlap, and a wrist cuff held below the right atrium introduces hydrostatic over-reading.
- Before abandoning NIBP, measure the mid-upper-arm circumference, select a validated cuff whose manufacturer-stated range accommodates the limb, position the arm and cuff at heart level, compare repeated results with pulse quality and clinical context, and avoid inferring systolic or diastolic accuracy solely from a plausible mean pressure.

- NIBP's main advantages in morbid obesity are the avoidance of arterial injury and infection, simplicity, and no need for continuous line management.
- Its disadvantages are intermittent detection of abrupt hypotension, movement and electrocautery artefacts, size/shape mismatch, unreliable readings during poor perfusion and difficult access to the limb when tucked, prone or under surgical drapes.
- An appropriately validated forearm cuff at heart level may be considered when the upper arm is unsuitable, but forearm or wrist results cannot be assumed equivalent to a brachial standard and should be interpreted as site-specific trends.
- The thigh or calf may permit measurement when both arms are unavailable, but peripheral amplification and limb-position effects make absolute readings harder to interpret.

- An arterial catheter provides beat-to-beat pressure trends, repeated blood gases and a waveform for derived variables.
- It may be justified before induction when severe obesity coexists with impaired cardiopulmonary reserve, major blood loss, anticipated vasopressors, prolonged prone surgery or persistently unreliable NIBP.
- Its disadvantages are more difficult cannulation and securement in deep, oedematous tissue, thrombosis, bleeding, infection, nerve injury, spurious values from damping, and a tendency to treat artefact rather than the patient.
- Ultrasound guidance, adequate catheter length, secure fixation and regular distal perfusion assessment are essential.
- The mere diagnosis of obesity is not an absolute indication for invasive monitoring.
- This two-sided, patient-specific appraisal responds directly to the 2025.1 ANZCA Final SAQ, in which examiners required at least two advantages and two disadvantages of each option in the obese patient rather than a generic list.

## 2.6 Special vascular circumstances: previous axillary surgery and arterial-line interpretation

- ANZCA PG18's 2023 appendix, retained within the 2025 guideline, explicitly rejects routine blanket prohibition of cannulation or blood-pressure measurement in an arm following axillary lymph-node dissection if there is no lymphoedema.
- When lymphoedema is present, consider other sites where practical, balancing the risks of alternatives; it is still not an absolute ban.
- An invasive arterial line or central line inserted solely to avoid a usable arm can expose a patient to more risk than ordinary NIBP or peripheral venous access.
- Shared decision-making and institutional policies informed by actual evidence are preferable to historical wristband rules.

- If the arterial trace and cuff disagree, identify which number is reliable before escalating anaesthesia, fluids or vasopressors.
- Check level and zero, flush pressure, air bubbles and stopcocks; inspect the fast-flush response; compare arterial pulse contour and peripheral perfusion; and consider a central–peripheral pressure gradient in severe vasoconstriction.
- An overdamped system often makes systolic pressure falsely low and diastolic pressure falsely high with a relatively preserved MAP, whereas an underdamped resonant system can exaggerate systolic pressure and pulse pressure.
- A transducer height change of 10 cm changes measured pressure by about 7.4 mmHg. No monitor is self-validating simply because it displays numbers continuously.

items.title: 3. Central venous pressure and venous pressure waveforms
items.body:
## 3.1 Define the quantity before using it

- A CVP catheter senses right atrial or nearby central venous pressure relative to atmosphere; a transducer in the SVC near the RA approximates RAP.
- **CVP is a pressure, not a volume.** It reflects the interaction of venous return, RV relaxation/compliance, chamber filling, intrathoracic pressure, pericardial constraint and the pressure generated by ventilation.
- Right atrial pressure is both a downstream pressure for venous return and an indicator of right-sided congestion.
- It is not a direct measurement of LV preload and cannot identify the position on an individual Frank–Starling curve.

- Guyton's venous-return relationship makes the mechanism clearer: venous return ≈ (mean systemic filling pressure − RAP)/resistance to venous return.
- Raising RAP while mean systemic filling pressure is unchanged tends to reduce venous return, but a simultaneous fluid bolus may increase stressed venous volume and mean systemic filling pressure.
- The resulting CVP movement depends on cardiac function and vascular compliance.
- A failing RV can develop a large CVP rise with no meaningful increase in CO.
- Conversely, a vasodilated patient may have low CVP despite substantial total-body fluid excess.

- **Typical mean CVP** in a spontaneously breathing supine adult is roughly 2–6 mmHg, but 'normal' depends on reference level, PEEP, position, respiratory phase and RV function.
- Convert pressures with 1 mmHg ≈ 1.36 cmH₂O.
- Zero at the right atrial level, check catheter tip/line patency and read at end-expiration.
- A full tidal breath under positive pressure ventilation creates a rise in CVP because intrathoracic pressure rises, not because blood volume increases.
- The measured pressure is not the transmural filling pressure (intracavitary minus surrounding pleural/pericardial pressure).

## 3.2 Reading the CVP trace as physiology

- Recognise the **a wave** (atrial contraction, just after P wave), **c wave** (tricuspid bulging during early RV systole), **x descent** (atrial relaxation and downward movement of annulus), **v wave** (RA filling with closed tricuspid valve, later systole) and **y descent** (rapid atrial emptying after tricuspid opening).
- In atrial fibrillation the a wave disappears.
- Cannon a waves appear when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, as in AV dissociation/complete heart block.
- Large systolic v waves suggest tricuspid regurgitation; absence/blunting of x descent may accompany TR.
- A prominent x with reduced/absent y can accompany tamponade; a rapid y descent may occur in constrictive pericarditis (interpret with full physiology and not one sign in isolation).
- The waveforms are distorted by tachycardia, mechanical ventilation, altered compliance and catheter position.

## 3.3 Why CVP cannot determine intravascular volume or fluid responsiveness

The **2026.1 ANZCA Final SAQ** specifically asked candidates to list volume assessment methods and discuss CVP limitations (70% of marks). A full specialist answer needs four logically separate limitations, not just the slogan 'CVP is poor'.

- 1. Measurement artefacts: zeroing or levelling error; position; catheter not communicating with the RA; air/clots; valve or mechanical pressure; reading away from end-expiration. These cause inaccuracies before physiology is even considered.
- 2. Altered surrounding pressure: positive-pressure ventilation, PEEP, recruitment manoeuvres, obesity, elevated intra-abdominal pressure, pneumothorax and pericardial constraint can increase measured CVP without an increase in transmural preload.
- 3. Cardiac conditions: RV failure/MI, pulmonary hypertension, severe TR, impaired RV relaxation, tamponade, left-heart disease and altered ventricular interdependence modify the pressure–volume relationship. A high filling pressure can coexist with low effective stroke volume.
- 4. Nonlinear compliance and different loading states: pressure rises steeply in a stiff RV and only minimally in a compliant RV for the same volume. A single CVP cannot establish circulating blood volume, ventricular end-diastolic volume or responsiveness to an additional bolus.

- Therefore low CVP may increase prior suspicion of hypovolaemia in the right setting but does not independently justify fluid, while elevated CVP can help reveal venous congestion and may signal a reason to stop fluids.
- Trends, especially in concert with CO, waveform and oxygenation, are more informative than isolated numbers.
- Even trends are contaminated when PEEP, posture or RV loading changes.
- Severe venous congestion can compromise kidney filtration by increasing renal venous pressure; it is not benign.

The correct alternative is **multimodal:** clinical examination and losses, arterial waveform, echocardiography of LV/RV and lungs, a dynamically assessed SV response to passive leg raise or small fluid challenge, and tissue-perfusion signals. Static measurements such as CVP and one IVC dimension should never be accepted as a direct proxy for fluid responsiveness.

## 3.4 Clinical interpretation, not dismissal

- CVP remains useful for **venous pressure trends**, central access, central oxygen saturation sampling, identifying characteristic right atrial waveforms and contextualising organ perfusion.
- A new CVP rise with acute hypoxaemia and falling ETCO₂ in an intubated patient prompts investigation for obstructive physiology (e.g. tension pneumothorax, severe RV failure, pulmonary embolism), not simply a diagnosis of 'fluid overload'.
- A falling CVP after diuresis alongside improving kidney function and respiratory mechanics may reflect successful decongestion.
- A low CVP during massive haemorrhage is supporting evidence of reduced preload, but urgent haemostatic resuscitation rests on the entire presentation.

items.title: 4. Fluid responsiveness, fluid tolerance and the limits of dynamic indices
items.priority: P2 HIGH (3 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 4.1 Distinguish three questions that are too often collapsed

- **Fluid responsiveness** means SV/CO rises meaningfully in response to increased preload; for a bolus a rise >10–15% is a common criterion.
- It is an observation about the slope of the Frank–Starling curve, not a diagnosis of hypovolaemia or a statement that more fluid will improve outcome.
- **Fluid requirement** asks whether increasing CO is needed to correct hypoperfusion.
- **Fluid tolerance** asks whether the heart, lungs and abdominal/venous systems can accommodate more fluid without harm.
- Giving fluid is reasonable only if the expected benefit on perfusion exceeds the harm of congestion and interstitial oedema.

- A healthy, fasting patient may increase SV after a fluid bolus but does not necessarily need fluid.
- A patient with acute RV failure may also show some preload response but worsen from excessive RV dilation, septal shift and reduced LV filling.
- Conversely, a vasodilated septic patient with adequate CO but MAP 50 may need norepinephrine rather than repeated fluid boluses.
- Reassess after every trial intervention.

## 4.2 Dynamic measures: physiological basis and eligibility

- In controlled positive-pressure ventilation, inspiration raises intrathoracic pressure and alters RV preload/afterload.
- The consequent variation in LV filling and SV appears several beats later.
- Marked respiratory variation can indicate position on the steep part of the Frank–Starling curve.
- For the same reason, it can become uninterpretable with spontaneous breaths, low tidal volume, open chest, dysrhythmia or abnormal RV afterload.

- **Pulse pressure variation (PPV)** = [(PPmax − PPmin)/((PPmax + PPmin)/2)] × 100% across a respiratory cycle.
- **Stroke volume variation (SVV)** similarly uses SVmax and SVmin relative to their mean.
- In a fully controlled, regular-rhythm, closed-chest adult at conventional tidal volume, PPV >12–13% or SVV >10–13% suggests responsiveness, while low values argue against; a 'grey zone' around 9–13% is common.
- They are less dependable with low tidal volume (≈6 mL/kg predicted body weight), high respiratory frequency/low HR-to-RR ratio, PEEP effects, pulmonary hypertension, RV failure, raised intra-abdominal pressure, low compliance, open-chest procedures and arrhythmias.
- A high PPV during acute PE may reflect RV afterload variation, not the need for fluids.
- A small PPV under low tidal volume does not reliably exclude responsiveness.

| **Test** | **How to perform** | **Positive response / caveat** |
|---|---|---|
| **Passive leg raise (PLR)** | From semi-recumbent, lower trunk while raising legs ≈45°, transferring venous blood centrally; measure SV/CO in real time and return position | SV/CO rise ≈10% is commonly positive; reversible and applicable with spontaneous breathing/AF if output reliably measured; avoid with major pelvic/leg injury and interpret cautiously if intra-abdominal pressure high |
| **Small fluid challenge** | Give ≈200–250 mL balanced crystalloid over ≈5–10 min (tailor to case), measure SV before/after and evaluate respiratory/congestion signs | SV rise >10–15% supports response; irreversible extra fluid means not a benign diagnostic test in congestion |
| **Mini-fluid challenge** | Give ≈100 mL rapidly, using sufficiently precise continuous SV measurement | Smaller SV response (e.g. ≈5%) can predict standard-bolus response; susceptible to monitor noise and timing |
| **End-expiratory occlusion** | Hold ventilator at end-expiration for ≈15 s while measuring real-time CO | Rise ≈5% suggests responsiveness in selected fully mechanically ventilated patients; requires validated monitor and tolerability |
| **PPV/SVV** | Observe over multiple controlled breaths with good arterial signal | Valid only with strict mechanical/physiological prerequisites; no precise universal threshold |
| **Echo LVOT VTI** | Obtain repeatable pulsed Doppler LVOT VTI in apical five-chamber/long-axis views before and after PLR/bolus | Serial VTI change approximates SV change when LVOT geometry constant; poor alignment, arrhythmia and operator error impair precision |

- A useful **worked example:** baseline CO 4.0 L/min rises to 4.6 after PLR (15%).
- This confirms preload responsiveness, not automatic fluid need.
- If MAP 70, warm peripheries, normal lactate and diffuse B-lines, additional fluid may be unjustified.
- If MAP 54, mottling, falling urine output and no lung congestion, a cautious monitored bolus or other tailored intervention is defensible.

## 4.3 Measures of tolerance and congestion

- Echo can reveal RV enlargement, septal flattening, severe valve disease and elevated filling pressures; lung ultrasound B-lines (interstitial syndrome), pleural effusions, peripheral oedema, cumulative positive balance and venous Doppler changes may indicate reduced tolerance.
- A high or rising CVP can signal congestive risk, not necessarily a contraindication to all resuscitation.
- VExUS uses hepatic, portal and intrarenal venous Doppler with IVC to assess systemic venous congestion; it can support complex assessment but is technique dependent and should not be reduced to a single proof of volume overload.
- In the oedematous, shocked patient, the clinically meaningful question is whether the next fluid bolus will increase effective perfusion without worsening organ congestion.

## 4.4 Selecting a method of assessing preload in the real operating theatre

- A monitor should not be chosen on whether it produces a familiar number but whether it works under the patient's actual ventilation and surgical conditions.
- **During controlled laparotomy with regular rhythm and sufficiently large tidal volumes**, PPV or SVV may be interpretable if the arterial waveform is reliable.
- **During protective ventilation at 6 mL/kg, spontaneous respiratory effort, laparoscopic pneumoperitoneum, atrial fibrillation or marked RV pressure loading**, a different approach is needed: repeatable LVOT VTI during an appropriate challenge, an oesophageal Doppler where suitable, or a clinical-echo-informed small challenge.
- In severe shock, the validity of even a dynamic test changes from minute to minute as vasopressors and mechanical ventilation are adjusted.

- Do not use 'fluid responsiveness' to determine how much blood is lost.
- In major haemorrhage, surgical observation and physiology may indicate urgent blood-product resuscitation regardless of a positive or negative PPV.
- Similarly, during profound vasodilation and relative hypovolaemia the patient may be fluid responsive yet primarily need improved vascular tone.
- The teaching hierarchy is: determine the cause of inadequate perfusion → decide whether increasing flow would help → test whether preload increases flow → check that fluid is tolerated → assess the response to a defined intervention.

| **Clinical context** | **Preferred starting assessment** | **Why the alternative may mislead** |
|---|---|---|
| Healthy low-risk operation | Clinical state, standard BP/HR, quantified losses | Routine CO monitors add complexity without proven benefit |
| Complex abdominal surgery, regular controlled ventilation | Reliable arterial line; optional SV/CO trend, selective PPV/SVV | A rigid GDHT protocol is not routinely beneficial in unselected elective GI surgery |
| Atrial fibrillation and spontaneous ventilation | Bedside TTE and real-time PLR SV response when feasible | PPV/SVV assumptions fail with irregular beats and spontaneous breaths |
| Severe RV failure or pulmonary hypertension | Echo focused on RV/LV and congestion; PAC for unresolved complex physiology | High PPV and CVP may reflect RV afterload, not fluid deficit |
| Septic shock with ongoing perfusion concern | Clinical perfusion, serial lactate, CRT, dynamic SV response; echo | Normal/high CO or ScvO₂ can coexist with poor microcirculatory perfusion |
| Rapidly changing haemorrhagic shock | Arterial pressure trend, clinical bleed assessment, blood gases/haemostasis | Waiting for a sophisticated CO device delays definitive haemorrhage control |

## 4.5 When standard dynamic indices are invalid: alternatives and worked decisions

- PPV and SVV are predictive only when their ventilator–heart interaction is strong, regular and interpretable.
- A threshold around 12–13% under controlled mechanical ventilation is a commonly used starting point, not a universal treatment threshold.
- Low tidal volume, spontaneous respiratory effort, arrhythmia, an open chest, severe right-ventricular dysfunction, markedly altered chest or abdominal compliance, or intra-abdominal hypertension can invalidate the usual interpretation.
- A high PPV during severe pulmonary hypertension may reflect cyclic changes in RV afterload rather than a recruitable volume deficit; a low PPV during protective tidal-volume ventilation may be falsely reassuring.
- Instead of concluding 'not responsive', choose a test with fewer invalid assumptions.

- Passive leg raising (PLR) produces a transient reversible redistribution of venous blood from the legs and abdomen towards the chest.
- Begin semi-recumbent, lower the trunk and simultaneously elevate the legs to approximately 45 degrees, then measure actual stroke volume or cardiac output rapidly because the response is short lived.
- An increase in measured flow of around 10% can indicate preload responsiveness when signal and technique are reliable.
- Changes in blood pressure alone are less dependable.
- PLR may be impractical with pelvic injury, raised intracranial pressure or unsafe positioning; significant abdominal hypertension can make its result unreliable.
- Measure using a device with sufficient temporal resolution and then return to baseline; do not mistake the effect of the manoeuvre for a sustained improvement.

- Two alternative tests are useful when PLR is impractical.
- In a passive, mechanically ventilated patient, a brief end-expiratory occlusion (often 15 seconds) reduces cyclical impediment to venous return; a small reproducible rise in CO of approximately 5% may support responsiveness, but this requires a precise monitor and patient tolerance.
- A mini-fluid challenge, for example 100 mL rapidly administered with simultaneous flow measurement, tests the haemodynamic response to a small actual bolus; the threshold is dependent on the measurement method and protocol.
- The tidal-volume challenge transiently increases tidal volume in selected patients, and a resulting increase in PPV helps identify responders, but should not be used if greater tidal volumes would be unsafe.
- These tests are different ways to interrogate the Starling relationship, not independent proof that giving further fluid is beneficial.

- Example: a ventilated patient with ARDS has PPV 18%, lactate 4 mmol/L, escalating noradrenaline and diffuse lung B-lines.
- The high PPV could arise partly from ventilator-induced RV afterload, and the B-lines indicate limited pulmonary fluid tolerance.
- A focused echo shows a dilated RV and septal flattening.
- A fluid bolus would be hazardous even if flow rose transiently; the priority is to address RV afterload, hypoxia/acidosis, excessive intrathoracic pressure and systemic perfusion.
- Conversely, in a bleeding patient with a small LV and no congestion, a reproducible CO rise with a test may support careful replacement while haemorrhage control proceeds.
- The correct clinical decision requires responsiveness, evidence of hypoperfusion and acceptable tolerance together.

items.title: 5. Measuring and interpreting cardiac output: from first principles to advanced monitors
items.body:
## 5.1 What makes a cardiac-output monitor useful?

- The physiological concept of flow is straightforward; measuring it continuously without affecting the circulation is not.
- Each monitoring technique estimates CO by measuring some other physical property: temperature dilution, indicator dilution, pressure-wave shape, ultrasound velocity, electrical impedance or oxygen extraction.
- The estimator is then converted to flow using assumptions about distribution volume, arterial compliance, anatomy or the stability of the circulation.
- The critical appraisal is therefore **accuracy, precision, bias, trending ability, response time, invasiveness, calibration requirements, failure modes, and whether its information changes management**.
- A highly accurate measurement that takes ten minutes can be less useful for rapid surgery than a less accurate but reliable trend, while a continuously displayed but untrustworthy number is hazardous.

- The reference against which devices are often compared is intermittent pulmonary artery thermodilution, itself imperfect.
- Bland–Altman comparisons describe mean bias and 95% limits of agreement between two methods.
- Percentage error (often calculated using two standard deviations of bias divided by mean CO) is sometimes compared with a 30% criterion, but the permissibility of this number depends on precision of the reference method and clinical purpose.
- Correlation is not agreement: two devices may correlate strongly over a range of flows but systematically disagree by a clinically important amount.
- **Trend monitoring** should be assessed using concordance analysis rather than assuming that agreement at one static time point establishes detection of change.

## 5.2 Intermittent pulmonary artery thermodilution and the Fick principle

- A PAC placed in the pulmonary artery can measure CO by right-sided indicator dilution.
- Inject a known volume (commonly 10 mL) of cooler solution through the proximal RA port; a thermistor near the distal catheter senses downstream temperature change.
- The Stewart–Hamilton relationship integrates the area under the temperature-versus-time curve: a **large temperature curve area implies lower flow**, because indicator is less rapidly dispersed, and a smaller area implies higher flow.
- Obtain several technically acceptable injections at consistent respiratory phase, discard obvious outliers and average.
- The measurement is unreliable with major intracardiac shunts, significant TR (indicator recirculation), rapid temperature changes, very low or highly variable flow and inconsistent injection technique.
- When an intracardiac shunt exists, the indicator may not follow the intended passage through the right heart and pulmonary circulation.

- **Continuous thermodilution PACs** heat the blood periodically via a proximal filament and use distal thermal detection and signal processing.
- They provide an averaged flow trend over time rather than a beat-by-beat direct measurement, so there can be lag during abrupt changes.
- They may also offer RV ejection fraction or end-diastolic volume estimates depending on the device; these are load-dependent and require cautious interpretation.

- The **direct Fick principle** is CO = VO₂/(CaO₂ − CvO₂), with consistent units.
- True direct Fick requires measured oxygen consumption (metabolic cart) and accurate arterial and mixed venous samples, not an assumed VO₂.
- Using assumed oxygen consumption reduces accuracy, particularly in critical illness, fever, obesity, very high oxygen delivery or altered metabolism.
- A mixed venous sample from the PA represents venous return from the whole body; a superior vena caval sample is ScvO₂ and does not sample the lower body or coronary sinus, and the two values may diverge especially in shock.

### Worked cardiac-output calculation

With VO₂ 250 mL/min, CaO₂ 18 mL/dL and CvO₂ 13 mL/dL, the arteriovenous difference is 5 mL/dL = 50 mL/L. CO = 250/50 = **5 L/min**. If Hb falls dramatically while CO is maintained, DO₂ may decline and O₂ extraction increase; an appropriate response depends on bleeding, cerebral/coronary disease and supply-demand balance, not a number in isolation.

## 5.3 Transpulmonary thermodilution and calibrated pulse contour

- Systems such as transpulmonary thermodilution inject an indicator into a central vein and detect it downstream at a thermistor-tipped systemic arterial catheter, frequently femoral.
- The arterial dilution curve yields an intermittent CO measurement and may be combined with pulse-contour analysis to provide a faster continuously updated CO between calibrations.
- The transpulmonary passage can also produce **global end-diastolic volume (GEDV)** as a volumetric preload-related index and **extravascular lung water (EVLW)** and pulmonary vascular permeability estimates using device-specific models.
- These values may be useful in refractory shock or pulmonary oedema but are model-dependent and affected by shunts, vascular anatomy, thermal perturbation and indicator distribution.
- GEDV is a global thermodilution-derived volume, **not a direct LV end-diastolic volume**; it does not prove fluid responsiveness.

- Calibrated devices are generally most useful when there is substantial change in arterial compliance or vascular tone and serial recalibration is feasible.
- They require extra vascular access, sterile technique and trained interpretation.
- Calibration should be repeated when cardiac output or vasomotor tone changes substantially; calibration at stable baseline does not guarantee ongoing validity through severe sepsis or high-dose vasopressors.

## 5.4 Arterial pressure-wave or pulse-contour analysis

- Pulse contour estimates SV from the arterial pressure waveform.
- In simplified terms, the pressure generated by each beat is shaped by SV, arterial compliance, wave reflections, peripheral resistance and measurement site.
- A crude relation is **SV ≈ arterial pulse pressure × arterial compliance**, but real systems implement complex proprietary models.
- Calibrated systems use an independent CO estimate (e.g. thermodilution) to set the patient-specific relation; uncalibrated systems use demographic variables and characteristics of the waveform.

- **Advantages** include continuous trends, reasonable use in ventilated high-risk surgery and integration of SV/CO with PPV/SVV when assumptions hold.
- **Limitations** include inaccurate estimates with severe vasoplegia, large rapid changes in vascular resistance, aortic regurgitation, IABP/assist devices, marked arrhythmias, very poor arterial signal and peripheral amplification.
- Many models are less reliable in extreme body habitus and acute vascular stiffening.
- The device cannot remove the limitations of its arterial input: a damped transducer can generate invalid CO and SVV despite a neat monitor display.

- For an examiner's evaluation, specify what you are trying to measure and whether the technique can answer that question: a pulse-contour monitor may detect a change in SV during an intervention, but does not diagnose the **cause** of low CO.
- An echo or PAC is better for differentiating poor contractility, pulmonary hypertension, tamponade and other anatomical or mechanical problems.

## 5.5 Oesophageal Doppler, echocardiographic Doppler and other methods

- **Oesophageal Doppler monitoring** estimates velocity and systolic flow time in the descending thoracic aorta.
- The area under the systolic velocity waveform (velocity–time integral, VTI) gives distance travelled by blood per beat; multiplied by an estimated aortic cross-sectional area, it estimates stroke volume through the sampled segment.
- The system assumes a stable proportion of total CO passes through the descending aorta, and that estimated aortic diameter is appropriate.
- Probe position and angle strongly affect readings; small movement can require repositioning.
- It is relatively minimally invasive but requires oesophageal access and may be unsuitable with significant oesophageal pathology or during some procedures.

- **Echocardiography** calculates SV as **LVOT area × LVOT VTI** and CO as SV × HR.
- LVOT area = π(D/2)², so diameter error is squared: a 10% diameter error produces approximately 21% area error.
- Consistent Doppler alignment is critical; echo's great advantage is simultaneously showing cardiac anatomy and function, not merely the output number.
- In rapidly changing shock, repeated VTI with the same imaging geometry may be more useful than absolute CO.
- In aortic stenosis and regurgitation, and with dynamic obstruction, measured Doppler flow must be interpreted in relation to the pathology.

- **Thoracic bioimpedance/bioreactance** detects changes in electrical properties across the thorax associated with blood movement and derives CO from a signal model.
- These are non-invasive and may trend during PLR, but accuracy varies with motion, oedema, pleural effusions, thoracic surgery, electrocautery and rapidly changing conditions.
- Finger-cuff volume-clamp systems reconstruct a brachial pressure waveform via photoplethysmography and may estimate CO, but performance is affected by vasoconstriction, cold peripheries, motion, oedema and arrhythmias.
- Carbon dioxide rebreathing and other gas-exchange methods have restricted uses and depend on assumptions about ventilation, pulmonary shunt and gas-exchange stability; they are not a general substitute for invasive assessment of complex shock.

| **Device/method** | **Invasiveness / major advantage** | **Major weakness / appropriate role** |
|---|---|---|
| Intermittent PAC thermodilution | PA catheter; CO, PA pressure and SvO₂ with complex phenotyping | Invasive; intermittent technique; shunts/TR and signal-quality limitations |
| Continuous PAC thermodilution | PA catheter; flow trends alongside filling pressure and RV afterload | Averaging delay; invasive; may miss brief rapid changes |
| Transpulmonary thermodilution + calibrated contour | CVC plus thermistor artery; CO, GEDV and EVLW estimates | Extra access and recalibration; indicator/model assumptions; complex ICU shock |
| Uncalibrated arterial pulse contour | Arterial catheter; near-continuous CO/SV/PPV | Vascular tone, abnormal valves, arterial damping/arrhythmia can invalidate outputs |
| Oesophageal Doppler | Oesophageal probe; SV/VTI and dynamic response | Aortic-flow assumptions, position dependence, operator expertise |
| TTE/TOE Doppler | Non- or semi-invasive; structural diagnosis plus flow | Image quality, operator dependence, intermittent measurement, LVOT diameter error |
| Bioreactance / impedance | No vascular catheter; useful for repeat PLR in some patients | Limited validity in oedema, thoracic pathology or procedural artefacts |
| Finger-cuff pressure / pulse estimate | Completely noninvasive waveform | Often inadequate in severe vasoconstriction, shock, motion or arrhythmia |

## 5.6 Indications and evidence: when monitoring does not improve outcomes

- A CO monitor increases the amount of physiological data available; it does not itself improve patient outcomes.
- Any benefit depends on timely, appropriate decisions prompted by the information.
- Earlier small goal-directed therapy trials had favourable signals, but larger contemporary trials have not consistently replicated them.
- **OPTIMISE II (BMJ 2024)** randomised 2498 older elective major GI surgical patients to minimally invasive CO-guided fluids plus a fixed low-dose inotrope versus usual care.
- Thirty-day postoperative infection was **23.2% vs 22.7% (adjusted OR 1.03, P=0.81)**, without benefit, while acute cardiac events within 24 hours were increased **3.0% vs 1.7%**, mainly arrhythmia.
- The result does not prove that CO monitoring is useless in every setting; it argues against that routine combined intervention in unselected patients.

- The **2025 POQI-11 consensus** advises against routine GDHT in major elective abdominal surgery and fixed low-dose inotrope infusion, while allowing individual consideration in moderate/high-risk noncardiac surgery and selected use in CPB, post-cardiac surgery and hip fracture care with variable and often low-certainty evidence.
- The **2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign** specifically finds insufficient evidence to recommend additional minimally invasive/non-invasive CO devices routinely over usual care in septic shock, despite suggesting dynamic fluid-responsiveness measures over static assessment alone.
- The clinical question is 'what correct action will follow this measurement?', not 'what is the most sophisticated monitor available?'.

## 5.7 Matching device performance to the decisions of a specialist

- **Selection for a high-risk patient** can be made as a series of nested decisions.
- For continuous pressure in a procedure with expected rapid changes, choose a reliable arterial catheter before induction and check the dynamic response.
- If instability is unexplained, use focused echo because only imaging can establish major structural and pericardial abnormalities.
- If there is a known abnormality (e.g. severe RV failure) whose management depends on serial flow and pulmonary vascular pressures, a PAC may be justified when trained operators and interpreters are available.
- If the question is simply whether a small bolus raises SV during controlled ventilation, calibrated pulse contour or Doppler may suffice without the invasiveness of a PAC.
- For prolonged ICU shock, transpulmonary thermodilution can additionally describe global lung water and related indices; do not equate these derived values with absolute ventricular volume.

**Device comparison should be repeated when physiology changes:**

- An algorithm calibrated in a vasoconstricted patient can become misleading during vasoplegia or rapid norepinephrine escalation.
- A stable patient on a continuous system may suddenly develop AF, significant aortic regurgitation or major signal damping; PPV, SVV and estimated CO can cease to be valid even while the monitor continues displaying numbers.
- A competent clinician recognises such changes, checks the primary signal and uses an independent method when necessary.
- A calculation is only as good as its measurement inputs.

## 5.8 What the numbers really mean: precision, accuracy and calibration

- A cardiac-output device should be judged by both accuracy against an accepted reference and precision for changes over time.
- Correlation is not agreement: two methods can track together while differing markedly in absolute values.
- Bland–Altman analysis reports bias and limits of agreement; percentage error is often invoked in validation studies, but the acceptable error depends on whether the device is being used for a high-stakes individual decision or a broad trend.
- Trending ability is a separate property: a monitor may estimate absolute CO poorly yet reliably identify a substantial response to treatment, or report plausible numbers while tracking inaccurately during vasopressor-induced changes in vascular tone.

- Indicator-dilution methods are grounded in conservation of mass.
- In pulmonary thermodilution, a known temperature indicator is introduced into the central circulation, and downstream temperature change is integrated to derive flow.
- Repeat injections at a consistent respiratory phase, use appropriate injectate temperature and volume for the device, average stable measurements, and recognise error with severe tricuspid regurgitation, significant intracardiac shunting, rapid temperature change and unstable rhythm.
- Transpulmonary thermodilution additionally samples the indicator in a systemic artery, providing calibrated CO and derived volumetric variables such as global end-diastolic volume and extravascular lung water.
- These are composite derived indicators, not direct LV end-diastolic volume and not substitutes for valve/RV imaging.

- The indirect Fick method calculates CO from oxygen consumption divided by the arterial–mixed venous oxygen-content difference.
- If measured VO2 is unavailable and assumed VO2 is substituted, error can be large in sepsis, fever, sedation or cardiac disease.
- As an illustration, VO2 250 mL/min and arteriovenous oxygen-content difference 5 mL/dL give CO = 250/(5 × 10) = 5 L/min.
- If the actual VO2 is 325 but assumed to be 250, the calculated flow will be substantially underestimated.
- An examiner may expect you to explain this assumption instead of reciting the formula alone.

- Pulse-contour techniques infer stroke volume from the arterial pressure waveform via proprietary models of compliance, impedance and resistance.
- Calibrated systems use external indicator dilution to reset assumptions; uncalibrated systems estimate vascular properties statistically.
- Major changes in vasoplegia, norepinephrine dosing, severe aortic regurgitation, major arrhythmia, poor peripheral perfusion or arterial signal damping may degrade accuracy.
- Before acting on a sudden CO change, check the original arterial waveform and the patient's heart rate, pressure and other perfusion variables, then validate the trend by a separate method when necessary.

items.title: 6. Pulmonary artery catheterisation: insertion, waveforms and bedside decisions
items.priority: P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 6.1 What a PAC measures that other monitors do not

- A pulmonary artery catheter is generally a balloon-tipped flow-directed catheter inserted via a central vein, advanced through right atrium, right ventricle and into a pulmonary artery.
- The proximal port measures RAP/CVP; distal port measures PA pressure and, after short balloon inflation in a suitable region, **pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP/PCWP)**.
- The thermistor measures indicator dilution CO; a distal sample gives SvO₂.
- Together these can help separate LV-dominant failure, RV-dominant failure, severe pulmonary vascular disease and high-output distributive shock when clinical and echocardiographic assessment remains uncertain.

- A PAC is **not** indicated for every unstable patient.
- It is most defensible for selected complex cardiac surgery, advanced pulmonary hypertension/RV dysfunction, refractory mixed shock, mechanical circulatory support, transplantation or a difficult question about pulmonary vascular physiology where information will change therapy.
- Randomised ICU studies have not demonstrated a routine survival advantage from PAC placement; poor-quality treatment decisions after PAC insertion can negate any theoretical benefit.
- Consider operator expertise, thrombosis/arrhythmia risk, anticoagulation status and whether echo has already answered the clinical question.

## 6.2 Preparation and method of insertion

**Preprocedure:**

- Confirm indication, informed consent when possible, coagulation/anticoagulation assessment, vascular anatomy and access risks; ensure the intended treatment plan depends on the data.
- Prepare ultrasound, full sterile barrier, chlorhexidine antisepsis, continuous ECG, pressure transducers appropriately zeroed and flushed, catheter ports correctly labelled, balloon integrity/volume checked according to manufacturer, and reliable resuscitation equipment.
- Confirm temporary pacing/defibrillation capability when high-risk conduction disease is present.
- Choose an internal jugular/subclavian or other suitably assessed central route and insert the introducer sheath by ultrasound-guided venepuncture using Seldinger technique, confirming venous guidewire position before dilation.

- Advance the PAC within the sterile sheath with distal pressure displayed continuously.
- From a common right IJ entry, the RA waveform may appear around 15–20 cm, RV around 25–35 cm, PA around 35–45 cm and wedge around 40–55 cm; **these are rough teaching estimates, not depths to advance blindly**.
- Anatomy and access site produce substantial variation.
- Inflate the balloon only as the device directs when the catheter is ready for flow-directed advancement and allow blood flow to carry it forward; maintain waveform observation and never force against resistance.
- Do not pull a PAC back with its balloon inflated.
- If sustained ventricular ectopy or heart block develops, stop advancement, withdraw to a safe position and treat the arrhythmia.
- Avoid overinflation or prolonged wedge and watch for pulmonary artery rupture, especially in fragile pulmonary vasculature or anticoagulated patients.

- When a wedge tracing is obtained, **deflate the balloon promptly**; return to PA waveform must be verified.
- Verify appropriate tip location and absence of pneumothorax after insertion with imaging/ultrasound as indicated; evaluate pressure tracings and catheter length, secure tubing, and obtain a baseline CO and mixed venous saturation.
- The balloon should not be left inflated and the distal lumen should not be used for routine infusion when wedged.
- Balloon-induced vascular injury can be catastrophic; use the minimum inflation necessary and do not wedge repeatedly without a reason.

## 6.3 Characteristic right-heart and pulmonary waveforms

- Normal reference ranges vary with ventilation and pathology.
- A common adult teaching range is **RAP 2–6 mmHg; RV systolic 15–30 and diastolic 2–8 mmHg; PA systolic 15–30, diastolic 8–15, mean ≈10–20 mmHg; PAOP ≈6–12 mmHg**.
- Correctly level and zero, assess waveform morphology and measure at end-expiration.
- RV pressure has systolic pulses but very low diastolic pressure; PA pressure rises with systole but retains a higher diastolic baseline with an arterial dicrotic notch from pulmonic-valve closure.
- During occlusion, the tracing becomes a low-pressure atrial-type waveform with a/v waves and no PA systolic pulses.

**Pressure progression:**

- RA (a/v waves, low pressure) → RV (tall systolic, diastolic near zero) → PA (similar RV systolic but higher diastolic + dicrotic notch) → wedge (lower-pressure delayed atrial waveform).
- Reappearance of a PA waveform on balloon deflation confirms the device has not remained inadvertently occlusive.
- A large wedge v wave can occur with severe mitral regurgitation or reduced LA compliance and means mean PAOP may overestimate LV end-diastolic pressure.

## 6.4 What a wedge pressure measures—and what it does not

- With a balloon wedged in **West zone 3** (pulmonary arterial and venous pressures greater than alveolar pressure), the static column distal to the balloon communicates with pulmonary venous pressure and indirectly LA pressure.
- PAOP may approximate LA pressure and, absent important mitral/pulmonary venous disease, be used to estimate LV end-diastolic pressure.
- It still does **not measure LV preload volume** or LV end-diastolic pressure exactly.
- This inference fails in mitral stenosis, significant MR with large v waves, pulmonary venous obstruction, significant PEEP/high intrathoracic pressure, non-zone-3 catheter location and other altered compliance/ventricular-interaction states.

- PAOP measured at end-expiration on positive-pressure ventilation includes an extramural pressure component.
- A rising wedge on escalating PEEP may not indicate the same rise in LV transmural filling pressure.
- PCWP may be lower than PA diastolic in normal circumstances; when high PVR or pulmonary vascular disease separates the PA and pulmonary veins, PA diastolic cannot be assumed equal to wedge.
- If a wedge tracing looks wrong, do not force balloon inflation to obtain the 'expected' number.

## 6.5 Derived values and clinically useful patterns

- **Transpulmonary gradient (TPG)** = mean PAP − PAOP.
- **Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR)** = (mPAP − PAOP)/CO in Wood units (multiply by 80 for dyn·s·cm⁻⁵).
- In contemporary haemodynamics, PVR **>2 WU** is abnormal in pulmonary hypertension classification, with invasive haemodynamic definitions interpreted alongside mPAP, PAOP and clinical phenotype.
- A rise in PVR can reflect PE, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, ARDS, high ventilatory pressures or chronic pulmonary vascular disease.
- **Cardiac power output** = MAP × CO / 451 in watts; low power indicates impaired systemic hydraulic performance but does not independently prescribe a particular treatment.
- **Stroke volume** is CO/HR, and **SVR** requires consistent MAP, RAP and CO measurements.
- **RV stroke work index** and other derived metrics become error-prone when primary measurements are imprecise.

| **Pattern** | **RAP/CVP** | **PA pressure / PAOP** | **CO and SvO₂** | **Interpret and respond** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hypovolaemic/haemorrhagic | Often low | PAOP often low | Low CO and low SvO₂ | Stop bleeding, replace blood/appropriate fluid, avoid extrapolating from one pressure |
| LV cardiogenic failure | Normal/high | PAOP high; PA often high secondarily | Low CO, low SvO₂ | Echo/ECG, treat ischaemia/valve lesion, consider inotrope/afterload, manage congestion |
| RV infarction/failure | High | PA pressure variable; PAOP may be normal/low | Low CO, low SvO₂ | Echo RV, correct hypoxia/acidosis, avoid excessive RV preload; use appropriate perfusion support |
| Precapillary pulmonary hypertension/PE | Often high | PA pressure high, PVR high; PAOP often ≤15 | CO low when severe; SvO₂ low | RV afterload reduction and cause-specific therapy; avoid reflex large fluid boluses |
| Distributive vasoplegia | Often low/variable | Often low/variable | CO commonly high initially, but may be low; SvO₂ may be high | Source control, vasopressor, individualised fluids and myocardial assessment |
| Tamponade/constriction | Elevated; waveforms change | Filling pressures may approximate/equalise | Low CO | Urgent echo, cause-specific decompression; do not rely on numeric 'equalisation' alone |

### Worked PAC interpretation

- A patient has MAP 60 mmHg, RAP 14 mmHg, mPAP 46 mmHg, PAOP 12 mmHg and thermodilution CO 3.2 L/min.
- **PVR = (46−12)/3.2 = 10.6 WU**.
- The elevated RAP, high PA pressure, low-ish PAOP and low CO favour severe RV afterload disease rather than pure LV filling-pressure overload.
- Echo should assess RV dilation, septal shape and valvular disease.
- Giving repeated 500 mL boluses solely to raise CO may further distend the RV; focus on oxygenation, acid–base, pulmonary vascular resistance, RV perfusion and definitive aetiology.
- Record how values and perfusion change after each intervention.

## 6.6 PAC complications and prevention

- Complications arise from **access** (arterial puncture, pneumothorax, haematoma, infection, thrombosis, air embolus), **advancement** (PVCs, VT/VF, transient or complete heart block, knotting), **residence** (thrombosis, infection, valve injury, endocarditis), and **wedging** (pulmonary infarction, haemorrhage/rupture).
- Advanced age, anticoagulation, pulmonary hypertension and repeated balloon manipulation may increase the severity of pulmonary vascular injury.
- An air-inflated balloon must be routinely checked per manufacturer; do not inject solutions not intended for that lumen.
- Remove the PAC when the clinical question is resolved and reassess if a new pressure value is inconsistent with the patient's physiology.

## 6.7 Interpreting a real wedge tracing, pulmonary vascular resistance and discordant data

- A wedge trace is valid only when the catheter is truly occlusive and the sampled pulmonary vascular segment allows pressure continuity between the PA tip and left atrium.
- Pulmonary West zone 3 conditions (pulmonary arterial pressure greater than venous pressure, both exceeding alveolar pressure) are most favourable.
- In high PEEP, regional overdistension or hypovolaemia, alveolar pressure can dominate the local vasculature and a putative wedge value may reflect intrathoracic/alveolar pressure rather than left atrial filling.
- Measure consistently at end-expiration and record the PEEP and reference height.
- Check that the tracing becomes atrial-type during transient inflation, returns promptly to a PA trace on deflation, and that the occluded sample is appropriate only when needed and safely obtained.

- PAOP estimates left atrial pressure, not LV end-diastolic volume.
- In mitral stenosis, pulmonary venous obstruction, substantial mitral regurgitation (large v waves), abnormal LV compliance or high intrathoracic pressure, the relationship between mean PAOP and LV end-diastolic pressure becomes unreliable.
- Even LV end-diastolic pressure is an imperfect surrogate for preload volume because the diastolic pressure-volume curve shifts with hypertrophy, ischaemia and pericardial constraint.
- If PAOP is 24 mmHg yet TTE shows severe mitral regurgitation and massive v waves, do not automatically conclude severe intravascular fluid overload or treat a pressure without understanding its mechanism.

- Calculate PVR = 80 × (mean PA pressure − PAOP)/CO in dyn·s·cm⁻⁵, or (mean PA pressure − PAOP)/CO in Wood units.
- A patient with mPAP 42 mmHg, PAOP 12 mmHg and CO 3 L/min has PVR 10 Wood units (800 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵), indicating a marked precapillary pressure gradient.
- The same mPAP with PAOP 30 and CO 6 gives PVR only 2 Wood units, suggesting a fundamentally different haemodynamic mechanism.
- Mean PA pressure and wedge values alone do not distinguish those states; CO and clinical context are essential.
- The contemporaneous haemodynamic definition of pulmonary hypertension and its classification require confirmation in an appropriate specialist context; the purpose here is safe bedside interpretation.

- SVR = 80 × (MAP − RAP)/CO (dyn·s·cm⁻⁵).
- Suppose MAP 62 mmHg, RAP 14 and CO 3.0: SVR is approximately 1280, so the patient is not simply vasodilated; poor flow and elevated right-sided pressure may dominate.
- If MAP is 62, RAP 4 and CO 8.0, SVR is approximately 580, compatible with prominent vasodilation.
- In either case avoid interpreting SVR as a measured vascular property independent of flow: it is derived from multiple measurements and can be misleading when those inputs are inaccurate.
- Serial haemodynamic changes and echo phenotype often matter more than a single reference-range comparison.

- During PAC advancement, the sudden emergence of a wide-complex ventricular ectopic run when the catheter reaches the RV should trigger immediate pause and reassessment.
- In left bundle-branch block, transient right bundle-branch irritation can produce complete heart block; a pacing/defibrillation plan is prudent before passage in patients with important conduction disease.
- A falsely 'wedged' catheter left obstructive can cause infarction or fatal PA rupture.
- Never leave the balloon inflated, never force advancement, and have a clear endpoint beyond which the expected diagnostic value does not justify repeated attempts.

items.title: 7. Focused cardiac echocardiography for haemodynamic instability
items.body:
## 7.1 When to reach for echo

- Ultrasound allows the anaesthetist to distinguish problems that may appear identical as a low MAP: vasoplegia, LV failure, RV failure, obstructive shock, severe valve pathology and pericardial effusion.
- **The main immediate questions** are: Is the heart filling?
- Are LV and RV contracting effectively?
- Is there a major valve or outflow problem?
- Is the pericardium obstructing filling?
- Is the pulmonary circulation loading the RV?
- A focused scan is an extension of clinical assessment, **not a complete formal echocardiogram**, and should not delay time-critical treatment in a collapsing patient.

- In the **2025.2 ANZCA Final SAQ**, candidates were asked to evaluate TTE specifically in a haemodynamically unstable patient under general anaesthesia.
- Examiners highlighted errors in substituting TOE, drifting into general preoperative echo uses, or listing uses without limitations.
- A strong answer acknowledges that TTE can rapidly diagnose the likely type of shock, be repeated to assess response to treatment, avoid invasive complications and simultaneously screen pleural/lung findings; equally, surgical drapes, prone/lateral position, pneumoperitoneum, obesity, ventilation, limited windows, operator training and the need to avoid interrupting surgery limit its intraoperative utility.
- If usable transthoracic windows are unavailable and clinically appropriate, TOE may offer continuous images—but the original TTE-specific clinical question must still be answered as asked.

## 7.2 Standard windows and anatomy

- A useful focused sequence covers **parasternal long axis (PLAX), parasternal short axis (PSAX), apical four chamber (A4C), subcostal four chamber and subcostal IVC**, with apical five-chamber LVOT VTI when feasible.
- Patient position and surgical access may modify the order.
- Acquire multiple windows rather than assigning a definitive diagnosis from a single poor image.
- Assess the whole patient: lung sliding and B-lines, pleural effusions and the abdomen may materially change the shock differential.

| **View** | **Essential structures and what to look for** | **Major pitfalls** |
|---|---|---|
| PLAX | LV chamber size and systolic thickening, RV outflow, LA, aortic/mitral valves, pericardial fluid; regional wall abnormality | Off-axis imaging can make LV seem small or overestimate thickness |
| PSAX at papillary muscles | Circumferential LV function; RV pressure/volume overload creates a D-shaped LV | D-shaping is not uniquely PE; severe chronic pulmonary hypertension also causes it |
| A4C | Relative RV/LV size, global function, atria, septum and AV valves | Foreshortening underestimates cavity dimensions; eyeballing EF is imprecise |
| Apical five chamber | LVOT pulsed Doppler VTI; Doppler through aortic valve with correct alignment | Doppler sample too proximal/distal, aortic stenosis, wrong insonation angle |
| Subcostal 4C | Effusion, RV/LV function, helpful under ventilation or poor parasternal windows | Pericardial/pleural distinction may be difficult, especially isolated images |
| IVC / hepatic veins | Respiratory variation, venous congestion context, RA pressure clues | Obesity, PEEP, high IAP, TR and RV failure invalidate single-cutoff volume interpretation |

## 7.3 Interpreting LV function, RV function and obstruction

**LV systolic function:**

- A grossly reduced EF with small SV suggests pump failure, while a seemingly 'hyperdynamic' LV with an almost obliterated cavity may indicate low preload or profound vasodilation, not automatically absolute hypovolaemia.
- **Ejection fraction (EF) = (EDV−ESV)/EDV** and is afterload dependent: severe vasoconstriction can lower measured EF even with unchanged intrinsic contractility.
- Regional wall-motion abnormalities raise concern for ischaemia/infarction, though pacing, cardiomyopathy, conduction disturbance and stress cardiomyopathy also cause abnormal motion.

**RV:**

- Compare RV and LV size in A4C; RV enlargement, reduced free-wall shortening, septal flattening and significant TR suggest RV pressure/volume stress.
- **TAPSE <17 mm** and **RV fractional area change <35%** are conventional indicators of reduced RV longitudinal or global systolic function, but both depend on image quality, loading and prior surgery; neither should be used as the sole RV measure.
- The tricuspid regurgitant peak velocity estimates RV–RA gradient by **4 × velocity²**; estimated RV systolic pressure adds RAP only in the absence of significant RV outflow obstruction.
- Poor Doppler envelope, severe TR and uncertain RAP can make calculated pressures unreliable.
- Acute PE often causes RV dilation but absence of RV strain does not exclude PE.

**LVOT obstruction:**

- In an underfilled, hypercontractile LV during anaesthesia, dynamic obstruction and systolic anterior mitral valve motion can cause sudden hypotension with a high-velocity late-peaking LVOT jet.
- Treatment may differ radically from generic 'increase inotrope': reduce exacerbating inotropy, restore carefully selected preload, increase afterload (often phenylephrine or another appropriate vasoconstrictor), and slow heart rate if appropriate.
- Identify structural hypertrophic disease and avoid mislabelled causes of shock.

**Tamponade:**

- Look for circumferential effusion, RA or RV diastolic collapse, a plethoric IVC (limitations under ventilation), exaggerated respiratory Doppler variation and clinical obstructive shock.
- Small but rapidly accumulating blood may cause severe tamponade, while chronic large effusions may be tolerated.
- Postcardiac surgery, a loculated clot can obstruct a chamber without a circumferential black-fluid rim.
- The need for pericardial drainage arises from haemodynamic effect, not effusion depth alone.

## 7.4 Echo phenotype: translate the image into a treatment decision

| **Main finding** | **Leading mechanism** | **Clinical actions** |
|---|---|---|
| Small, vigorous LV; RV not dilated; low SV | Low effective preload or vasodilation | Quantify losses, dynamic test where feasible; cautious fluid if needed, vasopressor for vasodilation |
| Poor global LV contraction; larger LV; B-lines | LV pump failure ± fluid congestion | ECG/troponin/ischaemia evaluation, adjust afterload and inotropy, avoid blind fluids |
| Markedly dilated RV and D-shaped LV; low SV | Acute/chronic RV pressure overload, PE, hypoxia or high ventilator pressure | Correct hypoxia/acidosis, review ventilation and RV perfusion, search for PE/other cause |
| Effusion with chamber collapse or localised postoperative clot | Obstructive pericardial physiology | Time-critical decompression with appropriate team, avoid precipitous loss of preload |
| Severe valve lesion/new regurgitation | Mechanical cardiac lesion | Confirm full anatomy if needed, choose lesion-specific haemodynamics, obtain surgical/cardiology input |
| New regional wall-motion abnormality | Acute ischaemia or other segmental dysfunction | ECG, coronary/haemodynamic assessment, cause-specific management |

## 7.5 Dynamic echo and the assessment of fluid responsiveness

- With a stable LVOT diameter and imaging plane, **percentage change in VTI approximates percentage change in SV**.
- During PLR, a reproducible ≥10% increase is commonly used to suggest fluid responsiveness.
- At a heart rate 90 bpm, LVOT diameter 2.0 cm (area 3.14 cm²) and VTI 18 cm yield SV ≈56.5 mL and CO ≈5.1 L/min.
- After PLR, VTI 21 cm yields SV ≈66 mL and an increase of 16.7%.
- This is a response to preload, not proof that continuing fluid will improve outcome.
- In AF, average several representative beats; with severe tachycardia, frequent ectopy or Doppler misalignment, small measured changes can be artefactual.

- **IVC assessment** can add evidence of venous pressure and fluid tolerance but is frequently oversimplified.
- In a spontaneous-breathing patient, small/collapsible IVC can be compatible with low RAP; in a mechanically ventilated patient, raised thoracic pressure can dilate IVC and change its variation.
- Measurements are distorted by TR, RV failure, abdominal pressure, lung compliance and patient effort.
- A single 'collapsibility' percentage cannot replace a real-time SV response or comprehensive shock assessment.

## 7.6 TTE versus TOE: evaluating their value and safety

- TTE is non-invasive, repeatable, rapid and able to survey heart plus lungs, but image quality may be compromised during a surgical procedure by positioning, drapes, pneumoperitoneum and mechanical ventilation.
- TOE provides closer, often superior posterior cardiac and valve views and can remain in situ during cardiac operations, but requires insertion into the oesophagus, appropriate anaesthesia/sedation and specialist expertise; it carries risks of dental/pharyngeal/oesophageal injury, bleeding and rare perforation.
- Significant oesophageal pathology (e.g. obstruction or perforation) can be a major contraindication, while prior surgery, severe varices, active bleeding or dysphagia require careful individual assessment.
- TOE does not replace the need to understand TTE, particularly when the question specifically asks about **intraoperative TTE**.

- Choose the minimum effective test that answers the immediate diagnostic question; a severely unstable patient may benefit from a 60-second limited scan rather than a prolonged study delaying surgery or resuscitation.
- When quantitative echo is performed, document image quality, loading and rhythm, and distinguish **observed** findings from inference.
- Training, governance, documentation and referral for comprehensive echo are parts of safe focused practice.

## 7.7 ANZCA 2025 credentialling: focused POCUS is not comprehensive echocardiography

- The College differentiates **focused point-of-care cardiac ultrasound**, which answers a narrow bedside question and is covered by **PG47 (2025)**, from basic or comprehensive TOE and comprehensive TTE, which are covered by **PG46 (2025)**.
- In that guideline, echocardiography is used for formal studies and reporting; a rapid POCUS examination has a narrower scope and does not certify exclusion of detailed valvular, congenital or coronary disease.
- For a trainee, knowing the canonical views and typical patterns is an examination learning requirement, **not evidence of independent procedural competence**.
- Safe clinical performance requires structured supervised training, portfolio/assessment, continuing competency, appropriate archiving and reporting, and an agreed escalation pathway when images are non-diagnostic or implications are important.
- The BJA Education review by Cheng and Arntfield (2024) emphasises training, standard views, shock interpretation and quality assurance.

- A systematic intraoperative focused sequence begins with a **specific question**, such as whether unexplained hypotension reflects poor LV pump function, RV pressure loading or pericardial obstruction.
- Obtain the best accessible two to four views quickly without abandoning primary anaesthetic responsibilities.
- Report the image-quality limitations, repeat the study after treatment if it will change management, and seek comprehensive TTE/TOE if uncertainty persists.
- This is safer and more defensible than producing a spurious EF number from an oblique image or claiming a negative POCUS excludes pulmonary embolism or tamponade.

**TTE versus TOE at induction:**

- TTE is quick and non-invasive, often suitable for the first survey, but may have poor windows under sterile draping, lateral/prone positioning, obesity or pneumoperitoneum.
- TOE can continue monitoring during surgery and better assess posterior valves/thoracic aorta, yet requires appropriate indications and is semi-invasive.
- It is inappropriate to insert TOE merely because TTE was requested if a useful TTE could answer the immediate question and risk-benefit favours it.
- A formal report or an appropriately recorded focused result must be accessible to the treating team.
- In unstable patients, a second skilled clinician may be required to scan while the primary anaesthetist continues resuscitation.

## 7.8 A practical focused TTE sequence and its limitations under general anaesthesia

- In an unstable anaesthetised patient, start with the clinical problem: new severe hypotension at induction, unexpected hypoxaemia, rising CVP, arrhythmia or loss of cardiac output.
- Stabilise oxygenation, ventilation and circulation while scanning; do not suspend life-saving treatment to obtain perfect windows.
- Parasternal long-axis provides an initial assessment of LV cavity size and contraction, left atrium and pericardial space.
- Parasternal short-axis at mid-papillary level shows global LV wall thickening, regional differences and septal shape; a flattened septum with an enlarged RV supports right-sided pressure or volume loading.
