- Apical four-chamber compares chamber sizes and identifies gross biventricular dysfunction, while subcostal views are particularly useful during CPR or when transthoracic windows are limited.
- The IVC is supportive contextual evidence, not a stand-alone fluid prescription.

- Quantification should be appropriate to image quality.
- LVOT VTI is a flow-distance measurement in cm; paired with LVOT area it yields stroke volume.
- A change in VTI measured from the same window and Doppler angle can be more robust than claiming an exact EF during shock.
- Look for a small vigorously contracting LV (low effective filling or vasoplegia), global LV depression (cardiogenic component), acute RV dilatation and septal distortion (pulmonary pressure loading), a large or haemodynamically significant pericardial effusion, and an underfilled hyperdynamic LV with systolic anterior mitral motion (dynamic LVOT obstruction).
- Distinguish positive findings from non-exclusion: a normal limited bedside scan cannot rule out pulmonary embolism, myocardial ischaemia or important valve pathology.

- Under general anaesthesia, obesity, surgical drapes, pneumoperitoneum and lateral or prone positioning may preclude apical or parasternal views.
- Thus the strengths of TTE are speed, non-invasiveness, repeated dynamic reassessment and the ability to integrate lung imaging; the liabilities are interrupted surgery, dependence on operator expertise, limited acoustic windows and measurement errors with poor alignment.
- TOE may be an alternative when appropriately indicated and performed by a trained operator, but requires consideration of oesophageal risk and additional expertise.
- In the ANZCA 2025.2 SAQ, the word 'evaluate' requires a judgement: does TTE provide enough actionable diagnostic information, at acceptable cost and delay, in this specific unstable patient?
- This is more demanding than simply listing what echocardiography can show.

- Document the focused question, windows obtained, major findings, uncertainty and management consequence.
- For instance, a patient develops hypotension after induction, and a quick PLAX/PSAX examination shows vigorous LV shortening, no effusion and a non-dilated RV.
- Hypovolaemia and vasodilation remain possible; neither can be distinguished by EF alone.
- If volume loss is unlikely, an appropriate vasoconstrictor with reassessment may be more rational than empiric fluid.
- A second examination after treatment demonstrating improved filling and VTI supplies direct evidence that the intervention changed circulation, while remaining distinct from proof of organ perfusion.

items.title: 8. Vascular access: selecting, inserting and maintaining the appropriate catheter
items.priority: P3 MODERATE (6 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (2 parent LOs)
items.los: IT_SQ 1.1; BT_RT 1.35; AT_GS 1.11; AT_GS 1.12; BT_GS 1.71; AR_ME 3.2; AT_GS 1.14; AT_GS 1.13
items.body:
## 8.1 In the shocked patient, access is a resuscitation decision

- Access is not defined by 'central versus peripheral' but by **what must be infused, at what rate, for how long, and with what hazards**.
- A patient actively exsanguinating needs rapid delivery of blood components; **two short, large-bore peripheral cannulae (usually 14–16 G if readily feasible)** often achieve better gravity/pressure-driven flow than a long multilumen central catheter.
- If access is impossible, use ultrasound-guided peripheral access, a short large-bore introducer/rapid infusion catheter or intraosseous access while planning definitive access.
- Do not let multiple prolonged peripheral attempts delay emergency blood products, TXA when indicated, surgery or source control.

- For a tube, the Hagen–Poiseuille relation under ideal laminar flow is **Q = πΔPr⁴/(8ηL):** flow rises steeply with internal radius, increases with driving pressure and decreases with length and fluid viscosity.
- Real blood through catheter hubs, connectors and rapid infusers is non-Newtonian/turbulent at high flows, so this is an illustrative principle, not a precise clinical rate prediction.
- A short wide catheter usually has substantially higher flow than a long catheter of nominally similar gauge.
- Blood warming, avoiding obstructive extension sets, pressure bags and properly functioning rapid-infusion devices may matter as much as catheter calibre.
- A three-lumen 7 Fr CVC divides its cross-section among narrow lumens and is not equivalent to a large-bore introducer for haemorrhage.

- **Intraosseous (IO)** access can be placed in seconds in emergency settings (proximal tibia, humerus or other approved site), provides access to central venous return for fluids and most resuscitation medications, and can be used briefly while venous access is secured.
- Flow requires pressure infusion rather than gravity alone; a humeral IO may provide higher flow than tibial depending on site and device.
- Confirm correct placement and flush vigorously, stabilise and reassess for extravasation and compartment syndrome.
- Contraindications include fracture of the chosen bone, local infection, prosthesis or recent IO attempt at that site (device-specific).
- IO access is a rescue bridge, not ideal long-term access.

## 8.2 Improve first-pass peripheral cannulation and reduce discomfort

- The best cannula is the smallest and least invasive device that reliably meets treatment requirements; repeated traumatic attempts carry pain, infiltration, delay and eventual exhaustion of superficial veins.
- Assess previous difficult access, obesity, oedema, dehydration, IV drug use, arm surgery and planned use (including contrast and long-term therapy).
- Warm the limb and use dependent positioning, appropriate tourniquet pressure, good lighting, transillumination/near infrared if helpful and ultrasound for deep veins.
- Select a straight segment away from flexion creases or obvious valves and avoid inflamed, infected, thrombosed or injured areas.
- Apply topical local anaesthetic when time allows; intradermal small-volume lidocaine or appropriate local anaesthetic can reduce insertion pain, but injection itself hurts and benefits depend on patient preference and urgency.
- Aseptic non-touch technique and chlorhexidine skin preparation help reduce infection.

- For **ultrasound-guided peripheral IV**, select a vein with suitable diameter/depth and sufficient straight length; compressibility and absence of thrombus distinguish it from artery.
- The image must follow the actual needle tip to avoid posterior-wall puncture.
- Short-axis/out-of-plane is easily learned but needle shaft can be mistaken for the tip; deliberately move the probe to track the tip.
- Long-axis/in-plane shows the shaft but requires alignment.
- A longer cannula is often essential in a deep vein: a short cannula with only a few millimetres remaining intravascular will fail with limb movement.
- Confirm easy saline flushing, absence of swelling, secure with sterile transparent dressing and reassess regularly.

- An **ultrasound-guided long peripheral or midline catheter** may be useful for access over several days when therapy is peripheral-compatible.
- A midline generally terminates in a proximal arm vein rather than the central veins and **must not be assumed suitable for all vesicants, high-osmolality nutrition or prolonged concentrated vasopressors**.
- Device-specific policies govern dwell time and therapy suitability.

## 8.3 Site-specific central venous access: anatomy and trade-offs

- The main central routes are **internal jugular (IJ), subclavian/axillary and femoral**; external jugular access is sometimes possible but wire passage and reliable tip placement are less predictable.
- Choose according to urgency, operator familiarity and ultrasound anatomy, haemostasis, infection/thrombosis risk, patient positioning, surgical field, renal disease and future access requirements.
- The 2026 WHO CVC infection guideline broadly favours jugular or subclavian over femoral for infection prevention, and may favour subclavian over jugular when feasible, but the recommendation is conditional and must be weighed against mechanical risks.
- In an actively bleeding shocked patient or one with an inaccessible chest/neck, femoral access may be the safest rapid option despite its disadvantages.
- A subclavian catheter risks venous stenosis and should generally be avoided in advanced CKD or patients likely to need dialysis access.

| **Route** | **Anatomical/clinical strengths** | **Important disadvantages or special situations** |
|---|---|---|
| **Right IJ** | Superficial ultrasound windows; compressible; generally direct route to SVC/RA; useful for dialysis/PAC | Carotid puncture, neck haematoma/airway compromise, infection, malposition; head position and thrombosis matter |
| **Left IJ** | Alternative when right inaccessible | Longer angled course via left brachiocephalic vein; higher risk of tip malposition, vessel contact or perforation if wire/dilator mishandled |
| **Subclavian / infraclavicular axillary** | More comfortable for longer use; sometimes lower infection risk; accessible when neck cannot be used | Noncompressible deep bleeding, pneumothorax, arterial injury, venous stenosis; less attractive in coagulopathy/CKD |
| **Femoral** | Fast in emergencies, away from airway; compressible; practical during CPR; ultrasound accessible | Infection/thrombosis, line contamination, mobility limitations; retroperitoneal bleed if punctured too high |
| **External jugular** | Superficial, sometimes rapid temporary route | Sharp angles/valves impede wire and reliable central placement; not always suitable for critical infusions |

- In ultrasound-guided IJV insertion, never assume vessel arrangement: the carotid may lie posterior rather than purely medial to the vein, particularly with head rotation.
- **The 2019 ANZCA Blue Book chapter “Preventing vascular damage during central venous catheter insertion via the internal jugular vein”** emphasises imaging the actual needle tip and confirming guidewire location before dilation; an in-plane or short-axis image showing needle shaft inside a vein is not proof that its unseen tip has not entered the carotid behind it.
- A large dilator advanced into an artery converts a potentially compressible needle puncture into a major vascular emergency.
- If a dilator or large-bore catheter has entered an artery, **leave it in place and obtain urgent vascular/interventional specialist advice**; blind removal can cause stroke or fatal bleeding.

## 8.4 Ultrasound-guided CVC insertion: a complete safe technique

**Before needle puncture:**

- Verify indication and intended device, coagulation/anticoagulation, vessel anatomy and thrombosis, allergies and informed consent where feasible.
- Use a dedicated assistant, full aseptic barrier (cap/mask/sterile gown and gloves/full-body drape), sterile ultrasound cover and gel, skin antisepsis allowing drying, local anaesthetic, and continuous ECG/SpO₂/BP monitoring as indicated.
- Position for comfort and safety (head-down only if tolerated; avoid it with raised ICP or cardiorespiratory intolerance).
- Ultrasound identifies compressible vein and relative artery, then visualises the moving needle tip.

**During insertion:**

- Use a shallow controlled puncture, aspirate venous blood, and independently verify venous position before dilation.
- Dark blood/low pulsatility are unreliable in hypoxaemic shock.
- Confirm the guidewire **within the vein** in transverse and longitudinal views, ideally also tracing it proximally; pressure waveform/transduction, blood gas, ultrasound or fluoroscopy can confirm when uncertain.
- Advance dilator only over a verified wire with controlled depth to avoid deep perforation.
- Never force a wire or dilator.
- Maintain hold of the guidewire at all times, withdraw if ectopy occurs, and inspect/remove guidewire completely before catheter use.

**After insertion:**

- Aspirate and flush each port, secure, dress, record depth/site/time and confirm an appropriate tip position in the lower SVC/cavoatrial junction for a standard upper-body CVC using validated intracavitary ECG, X-ray or ultrasound as locally available.
- Screen for pneumothorax/haemothorax with lung ultrasound or radiograph when indicated.
- Do not use a catheter with uncertain vessel location or malposition for irritant drugs.
- Inspect for bleeding/haematoma, catheter-related thrombosis, line sepsis and air embolism; reassess daily whether removal is possible.
- Use the minimum number of lumens, disinfect hubs, maintain intact clean dressings and minimise breaks in a closed system.

**Complication pathways:**

- If suspected air embolus from open hub, immediately occlude source, give 100% oxygen, stabilise circulation and consider hyperbaric referral in clinically important arterial/cerebral involvement.
- If catheter-associated bloodstream infection is suspected, assess severity, obtain appropriate paired cultures, give antibiotics if indicated and determine whether removal is required rather than routine line retention.
- CVC insertion complications include guidewire loss, dysrhythmia, myocardial perforation/tamponade, thrombus, arterial injury, nerve injury, pneumothorax, haematoma and venous stenosis.
- Document incident details and follow-up.

## 8.5 PICC insertion: when three weeks of access changes the choice

- A **peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC)** is inserted through a suitable upper-arm peripheral vein (commonly basilic, alternatively brachial/cephalic) but its **tip terminates centrally** at the lower SVC/cavoatrial junction.
- PICCs may be useful for weeks to months of antibiotics, some chemotherapies, long-term access or selected parenteral nutrition; the exact indication depends on catheter compatibility and service expertise.
- They avoid direct neck/chest puncture and therefore reduce insertion-related pneumothorax and major arterial injury, often allow bedside insertion with ultrasound, and may be more comfortable for prolonged care.
- However, small arm veins containing a large catheter predispose to upper-limb deep venous thrombosis; malposition, arm oedema, infection, phlebitis, occlusion, breakage and migration also occur.
- PICCs can compromise future dialysis fistula veins, so consult renal access teams before insertion in advanced CKD.

**Technique:**

- Ultrasound-map both arms, choose a vein large relative to the catheter (commonly aim for catheter-to-vein diameter ratio ≤45% where feasible), avoid thrombosed/poorly perfused limbs, prepare under sterile maximal-barrier conditions and anaesthetise skin.
- Puncture with ultrasound using a micropuncture needle, pass guidewire, dilate to peel-away introducer, advance the measured catheter length to central position, flush and secure without sutures where possible.
- Confirm tip location by approved intracavitary ECG or imaging, check for catheter kink or arm-vein thrombosis, and document safe use.
- Use the smallest lumen count and calibre suited to therapy, because larger multilumen PICCs increase thrombosis and infection burden.
- Secure and maintain with a formal catheter-care bundle, review need daily and remove promptly when no longer indicated.

### PICC versus conventional CVC: exam-relevant evaluation

- A **2015.2 ANZCA Final SAQ** asked for advantages/disadvantages of PICC over a percutaneous central venous catheter and ways to minimise PICC risk.
- A complete answer must address **duration, therapy compatibility, insertion complication, DVT/occlusion, infection, tip position and maintenance**.
- PICCs usually have lower insertion risk for pneumothorax and direct arterial injury but often higher upper-limb thrombosis risk, especially in cancer, critical illness and large-diameter/multilumen lines.
- Infection comparisons vary markedly by clinical population, device, days in place and maintenance quality; it is incorrect to claim PICCs are either invariably safer or invariably more infective.
- A conventional IJ CVC is more appropriate for short-term critical infusions, rapid haemodynamic rescue or PAC introduction; a large-bore introducer is preferable for massive rapid blood delivery.
- A tunneled catheter or implanted port may be superior for some prolonged intermittent therapies.
- For PICC complication prevention: ultrasound vein selection and catheter sizing, strict asepsis, precise tip confirmation, securement and dressing, patency protocol, avoidance of unnecessary lumens and early removal are more defensible than reliance on an antibiotic-lock product alone.

## 8.6 Guidelines and context

- The **WHO 2024 peripheral-catheter** and **2026 centrally inserted CVC** guidance emphasise hand hygiene, education, maximal sterile barriers, ultrasound/appropriate site selection, surveillance and catheter-maintenance bundles.
- A catheter that was inserted perfectly but left unnecessarily in place still exposes the patient to avoidable thrombosis and infection.
- Centre-specific infection surveillance and competency matter; the most effective catheter is one that performs its task safely and is promptly removed.

## 8.7 PICC insertion and management: teach the entire procedural pathway

- For prolonged IV therapy, compare device options before puncture.
- A PICC is a long central catheter introduced through an arm vein, usually basilic or brachial, with the tip in the lower SVC at the cavoatrial junction; it is not a long peripheral catheter or midline.
- The basilic vein is often favourable because of its diameter and course.
- Use duplex ultrasound to assess vein diameter, depth, compressibility and thrombosis, preserve potential dialysis-fistula veins in advanced CKD, and select the smallest calibre and fewest lumens that meet the treatment need.
- A larger catheter relative to vein diameter increases upper-limb thrombosis risk.
- Contemporary safe-access guidance recommends keeping catheter cross-sectional occupancy low, with one-third of the vein area a conservative target; published PICC studies also use diameter-ratio thresholds, which are not directly identical to area ratios.

Explain the procedure step by step:

- Consent and indication check.
- Equipment and maximal aseptic preparation.
- Ultrasound-guided micropuncture of the selected vein.
- Guidewire passage with continuous control.
- Small incision and insertion of introducer or peel-away sheath according to device.
- Measure catheter insertion length.
- Advance the catheter while minimising malposition into internal jugular or contralateral brachiocephalic veins.
- Confirm central tip location (intracavitary ECG, fluoroscopy or imaging as appropriate).
- Verify each lumen aspirates and flushes.
- Document external length, secure with a suitable stabilisation device and apply sterile dressing.

- Remove the peel-away sheath and wire completely.
- Many PICCs are inserted by dedicated vascular-access teams; procedural competence still requires supervised training.

- The reason to document tip location is clinical: a non-central tip may promote thrombosis, malfunction and vessel injury, while too-deep right atrial positioning may provoke arrhythmia or rarely perforation.
- Tip-confirmation methods have limitations with abnormal rhythm, venous anatomy or altered pacing; use alternate imaging when the usual method cannot establish placement.
- Insertion complications include arterial/nerve injury, bleeding, malposition, pneumothorax (rare compared with centrally placed CVC), air embolism, arrhythmia and difficult threading.
- Later complications include catheter-associated thrombosis, occlusion, dislodgement, local cellulitis and bloodstream infection.
- Never force a PICC that will not flush; evaluate mechanical causes and thrombosis and seek specialist review.

- For a three-week antibiotic course, a PICC can avoid repeated cannulation and is comparatively safe from pneumothorax and major arterial injury, but the longer intravascular length and smaller arm veins make thrombosis and occlusion especially relevant.
- A short conventional CVC may be faster in shock and may offer better high-flow or vasoactive access, but it has greater neck/chest insertion hazards and is less suitable for outpatient management.
- A midline may be less invasive for suitable peripheral-compatible therapies, but its tip is not central and its compatibility must be assessed.
- The 2015.2 Final SAQ expects not only the PICC-versus-CVC comparison but also ultrasound sizing, aseptic insertion, accurate tip confirmation, minimum necessary lumens, care bundle and prompt removal.

- Dressing and maintenance are as important as insertion: strict hand hygiene and access-port disinfection, an intact clean dry dressing, regular site/limb checks, flushing according to device and drug-compatibility policies, prompt investigation of fever/line tenderness/unilateral arm swelling, and daily review of whether the line remains necessary.
- A newly symptomatic swollen arm warrants assessment for catheter-associated thrombosis.
- Whether a functioning catheter may remain in place during anticoagulation is individual and depends on infection, positioning, ongoing need and local vascular protocols; suspected infected or malfunctioning devices require a different pathway.

## 8.8 Central and peripheral line hazards: prevention, recognition and rescue

- The most consequential CVC insertion complication is dilation of an unrecognised artery.
- Venous blood can appear bright red in high oxygenation or dark when shocked; non-pulsatile return does not reliably prove venous placement.
- Visualise the wire in the target vein with ultrasound before dilation, checking enough of its course to exclude posterior transfixion.
- When the diagnosis is uncertain, pressure waveform or manometry and blood-gas analysis provide independent confirmation.
- The ANZCA 2019 Blue Book discusses combining methods rather than relying on colour.
- If a large dilator or catheter has entered an artery, especially ≥6 Fr, leave it in place, resuscitate as necessary and call vascular/interventional specialists; withdrawal with pressure alone may cause uncontrolled haemorrhage or stroke.
- Distinguish this from a small needle puncture, for which compression and observation may suffice based on site and anticoagulation.

- Air embolism occurs when an open line or venous introducer is above central venous pressure, especially with spontaneous inspiratory effort or poor connections.
- Immediately clamp/occlude the source, flood the field with saline where appropriate, administer high-concentration oxygen, support haemodynamics and arrange specialist help; prevention includes secure closed connectors, suitable positioning, careful exchanges and positive-pressure or Valsalva technique when clinically appropriate.
- Suspect pneumothorax when there is unexplained hypoxia, increased airway pressure or hypotension after jugular/subclavian access; ultrasound or radiography may confirm, but do not delay treatment of suspected tension physiology for an image.
- Sudden arrhythmia may indicate guidewire/catheter passage into the right heart; withdraw to appropriate position and confirm tip location.

- Catheter-related bloodstream infection is prevented by using an indication-appropriate site, hand hygiene, full sterile barriers, chlorhexidine-alcohol skin antisepsis when suitable, allowing drying, sterile ultrasound covers, standardised insertion bundles, hub disinfection, dressings, maintenance education and timely removal.
- WHO 2026 covers the complete CVC lifecycle, not insertion alone.
- A line should not be routinely replaced simply because a fixed number of days has passed if it remains clinically necessary and uninfected; assess ongoing indication and site condition.
- New fever in a patient with a central line is not automatically CLABSI—consider sources and obtain appropriate peripheral/line blood cultures before antibiotics where safe, then treat and remove or retain according to infection severity and organism-specific guidance.

- Peripheral noradrenaline can be justified while an unstable patient awaits central access, provided the catheter is well positioned in a visible large proximal limb vein, concentration and dose are protocolled, the site is frequently inspected and a second access is available.
- The 2025 Association of Anaesthetists guideline provides a short-duration, low-concentration pathway; these are not unconditional permissions for indefinite high-dose infusions.
- Stop infusion immediately if extravasation is suspected, maintain access for aspiration where appropriate, follow the local tissue-injury protocol and involve the relevant team.
- Avoid equating 'can use peripherally' with 'all peripheral devices and doses are equally safe'.

## 8.9 Rapid infusion: the 2017 Final SAQ physiology translated into a practical circuit

- In life-threatening haemorrhage, the infusion circuit is a series of resistances.
- The principal determinants of achievable flow are pressure gradient, fluid viscosity, catheter internal radius and length, plus the resistance of connectors, clamps, filters, extension tubing, blood warmer and rapid infuser.
- Hagen–Poiseuille's fourth-power radius relationship applies to laminar Newtonian flow in a rigid tube; at high blood-flow rates turbulence, non-Newtonian viscosity and device-specific components invalidate simple numerical extrapolation.
- Nevertheless, the governing practical lesson remains: a short wide-bore peripheral cannula, large-bore introducer or rapid-infusion catheter is often more useful for high-flow blood than a long, narrow-lumen standard CVC.

- A worked physics comparison illustrates why nominal cannula gauge is important.
- If internal radius increases by 25% with all other idealised factors fixed, calculated laminar flow rises by 1.25^4 ≈ 2.44-fold; doubling length halves flow.
- These are relative comparisons, not clinically guaranteed ml/min values.
- Actual flow must be assessed from the product's manufacturer testing with fluids and pressure conditions relevant to the intended transfusion.
- During major haemorrhage use a properly configured rapid infuser/warming system and account for viscosity, clot/filter obstruction, pressure limits, device shear/haemolysis risk and extravasation.
- Do not delay definitive haemostasis while trying to optimise cannula dimensions beyond what the patient permits.

Safety extends beyond speed:

- Confirm venous placement and secure the device before pressure delivery.
- Prevent air entrainment.
- Use compatible components and appropriate blood warming.
- Monitor haemolysis, hypothermia, ionised calcium, coagulation and overload.
- Separate incompatible infusions.

- Intraosseous access is a short-term rescue when venous access cannot be obtained, but higher flow generally needs a pressure system and careful surveillance for extravasation/compartment syndrome.
- This is the complete 'why' behind choosing two large peripheral cannulae for haemorrhage rather than simply advising 'get central access'.

items.title: 9. Perioperative fluid prescription: composition, requirements and safety
items.priority: P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (3 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 9.1 Separate maintenance, deficit, blood loss and resuscitation

- Perioperative prescribing should start with **what problem a fluid is intended to solve**.
- A patient may need water and electrolytes for maintenance while fasting, replacement of measured gastrointestinal or renal losses, blood components for haemorrhage, or a small volume challenge for inadequate flow.
- These indications require different products and rates.
- There is little physiological justification for replacing a hypothetical 'third-space loss' with large standardised crystalloid volumes.
- After surgery, stress-related ADH release and a reduced ability to excrete water increase hyponatraemia risk, particularly with hypotonic fluids.
- For most adult perioperative resuscitation, a balanced isotonic crystalloid is a sensible first-line choice; long-term maintenance needs are a different calculation.

- A low-risk, stable adult with normal kidneys undergoing minor surgery usually requires **little more than replacement of actual deficits/losses plus modest maintenance**, not a multi-litre infusion solely because of a fasting interval.
- Before prescribing, ask if the patient has drunk clear fluid recently according to local fasting guidance, whether they receive oral fluids soon after surgery, what is lost from the operative field, whether fever/vomiting or diuresis is present, and whether cardiac/renal/hepatic disease reduces their ability to handle salt and water.

## 9.2 Fluid types and their physiology

- **Balanced crystalloids** (e.g. Hartmann's/lactated Ringer's, Plasma-Lyte) provide sodium/chloride closer to extracellular fluid than 0.9% saline and have buffer anions metabolised to bicarbonate-equivalent.
- Formulations differ significantly in sodium, potassium, calcium and osmolality; choose the actual product after checking its composition, compatibility and local availability.
- The presence of small potassium concentrations in some balanced fluids does not imply they are automatically contraindicated in renal failure; large 0.9% saline loads can cause hyperchloraemic acidosis, which may worsen potassium movement out of cells.
- Use clinical context and local guidance rather than reflexively declaring every potassium-containing fluid unsafe.

- **0.9% saline** contains 154 mmol/L each of sodium and chloride and has a strong-ion difference close to zero, so large volumes can cause hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, reduced renal blood flow in some settings and sodium/chloride loading.
- It may have a role with marked chloride-depletion metabolic alkalosis or particular neurological/compatibility considerations.
- **Dextrose-containing fluids** provide free water after glucose metabolism and are generally inappropriate as the sole resuscitation fluid for shock; they may be used for maintenance/glucose supply based on patient needs.
- **Albumin** expands plasma volume differently from crystalloids and is considered selectively, not as routine replacement for fasting; avoid starch solutions in the critically ill because of kidney injury concerns.
- Avoid gelatin for septic shock in line with recent sepsis guidance.

| **Product/class** | **Main physiologic use** | **Important caution** |
|---|---|---|
| Balanced isotonic crystalloid | Initial volume replacement/resuscitation in many perioperative and critical-care settings | Still causes oedema if overused; check actual potassium/calcium and compatibility |
| 0.9% sodium chloride | Chloride-depletion, specific compatibility or sodium/chloride replacement indications | Hyperchloraemic acidosis and chloride loading with large volumes |
| 5% dextrose / hypotonic maintenance | Free water and glucose when specifically needed | Dangerous as sole shock fluid; dysnatraemia risk with ADH activity |
| Albumin solution | Selected intravascular volume expansion with specific indications | Cost and context-dependent outcomes; not substitute for bleeding blood components |
| Blood products | Restore oxygen carriage/coagulation in haemorrhage | Transfusion reactions, volume, calcium, temperature, coagulopathy; activate blood protocols appropriately |

## 9.3 Worked maintenance and replacement prescription

- For an uncomplicated healthy 70 kg adult, common adult maintenance planning ranges are approximately **25–30 mL/kg/day water**, **≈1 mmol/kg/day sodium/potassium/chloride**, and **50–100 g glucose/day** to limit starvation ketosis, with considerable variation for elderly, frail or renally impaired patients.
- At 70 kg this is around 1.75–2.1 L/day or 73–88 mL/h, before counting oral intake, medications and measured losses.
- This is **not an automatic theatre infusion rate**; in an ambulatory case where oral intake resumes soon after surgery, total IV requirement may be much lower.
- Monitor weight, cumulative balance, electrolytes, renal function, glucose and clinical signs when prescribing beyond a brief procedure.

**Example 1 (low-risk case):**

- A 60 kg healthy patient fasting for a morning laparoscopic procedure, haemodynamically stable, small blood loss, expected to drink in recovery.
- Give only enough balanced crystalloid to maintain IV patency, replace any real deficit or loss, and treat hypotension based on its mechanism; do not invent a fixed 6-hour fasting deficit requiring litres of fluid.
- Encourage oral intake early when safe.

**Example 2 (GI loss):**

- Patient loses 1200 mL/day of gastric fluid through an NG tube and has hypochloraemic alkalosis.
- Estimate and replace measured loss with an appropriate chloride-containing fluid and potassium as needed after checking electrolytes, renal function and ECG, **in addition to** tailored maintenance.
- Fluids can contain the same water but supply radically different electrolyte and acid–base effects.

**Example 3 (active haemorrhage):**

- Tachycardia, falling ETCO₂ and MAP during laparotomy with estimated rapid 1500 mL blood loss.
- Check haemoglobin, coagulation, temperature, calcium and bleeding source; activate haemorrhage protocol and deliver warmed blood products as appropriate.
- A large crystalloid bolus does not correct oxygen-carrying capacity or consumptive coagulopathy and worsens dilution and oedema.

## 9.4 Avoid 'liberal versus restrictive' slogans

- The **RELIEF trial** in major abdominal surgery showed that an excessively restrictive fluid strategy increased postoperative acute kidney injury compared with a more liberal regimen; conversely, positive fluid balance and pulmonary/intestinal oedema are associated with complications.
- The lesson is not to chase a universal positive balance but to individualise a patient-specific baseline, replace measured losses and determine whether targeted resuscitation is needed.
- **2024 POQI fluid consensus** supports physiologically appropriate, individualised fluids throughout the perioperative course; the risks of both under-resuscitation and overload depend on comorbidity and procedure.
- Prescribe through recovery rather than leaving patients to accumulate days of 'maintenance' after they can eat and drink.

## 9.5 Fluid composition, effective losses and full adult prescribing decisions

- A fluid prescription begins with a deficit or ongoing requirement, not with a habit.
- Estimate maintenance water and electrolytes only when the patient cannot meet them enterally, then add measured gastrointestinal, urinary, fistula, drain or surgical losses, and treat true hypoperfusion separately.
- Healthy adults commonly require about 25–30 mL/kg/day of maintenance water, but the elderly, frail and cardiac/renal-impaired may need less; consider sodium and potassium delivery and glucose instead of treating every bag as physiologically interchangeable.
- A normal day-case patient expected to drink promptly after surgery often needs little IV maintenance fluid.
- An unstable patient with capillary leak may need early intravascular resuscitation but accumulates extravascular oedema from excessive prolonged infusions.

- Composition matters.
- Normal saline contains 154 mmol/L sodium and chloride, so several litres deliver a substantial chloride load that can lower strong-ion difference and generate hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.
- Balanced crystalloid recipes vary: Hartmann's typically contains sodium around 131 mmol/L, chloride about 111 mmol/L, potassium around 5 mmol/L, calcium around 2 mmol/L and lactate buffer; Plasma-Lyte typically contains sodium around 140, chloride around 98, potassium around 5 and acetate/gluconate buffers without calcium.
- Formulations vary by region, so verify the local product label before relying on these illustrative numbers.
- Dextrose solutions predominantly become electrolyte-free water after metabolism and do not reliably restore circulating volume in shock.
- Colloids do not correct a lack of oxygen-carrying capacity in haemorrhage.

- Consider a 75 kg patient fasting overnight for a two-hour laparoscopic operation with minimal predicted loss.
- If oral fluids will resume in PACU, do not 'replace' a calculated 1–2 L fasting deficit purely from time since last solid food; instead titrate small IV volumes to access requirements and actual losses, and treat induction hypotension based on its mechanism.
- Now consider the same patient with a postoperative NG output of 1.5 L/day and a rising bicarbonate: measure the loss, check chloride, potassium, magnesium and creatinine, and replace gastric water and chloride deficits with an appropriate chloride-rich strategy alongside carefully tailored maintenance.
- A patient with measured haemorrhage requires haemostatic resuscitation and source control, not equal millilitres of crystalloid for each millilitre of blood loss.

- For a ventilated patient with RV failure and severe venous congestion, normal MAP after norepinephrine does not justify maintenance infusion at an automatic rate.
- Check whether fluid is needed at all, whether the RV can accept it, and whether congestion (CVP trends, hepatic/portal venous Doppler, renal function, oedema and oxygenation) is threatening organ perfusion.
- In a low-risk patient, by contrast, short-duration balanced crystalloid without advanced monitoring is usually sufficient.
- Document the daily net balance, cumulative exposure, body weight, objective losses, biochemical trends and stop/review criteria.
- The prescription should evolve across the perioperative phases rather than continuing unchanged for days.

items.title: 10. Goal-directed haemodynamic therapy: when it is useful, when it is not
items.priority: P2 HIGH (3 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (3 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.los: AT_GS 1.21; BT_GS 1.77; SS_IC 1.28; BT_PO 1.5d; SS_IC 1.29; SS_IC 1.19; AT_GS 1.15
items.body:
## 10.1 From a plausible physiological strategy to an evidence-based decision

- Goal-directed haemodynamic therapy (GDHT) is not simply giving extra crystalloid until SV stops increasing.
- It means a **declared monitor + physiological target + chosen intervention + reassessment protocol**, often using flow measurements and MAP alongside tissue-perfusion assessment.
- Classic algorithms sought 'supranormal' cardiac output/DO₂ because survivors of high-risk surgery had higher values; however, the association did not prove that forcing all patients to those values would improve outcomes.
- Increased inotrope dose may increase tachyarrhythmia and myocardial oxygen demand, while repeated boluses on the flat Starling curve increase venous congestion.
- The monitored number should never substitute for understanding why the patient is unstable.

- The modern approach optimises **arterial pressure, cardiac function and oxygen delivery**, then integrates tissue perfusion and fluid tolerance.
- Fluid should be given to a patient with a credible flow/preload problem, not to everyone whose monitor can demonstrate a small SV response.
- Norepinephrine can correct inadequate vascular tone when SV is adequate; an inotrope may be considered when there is evidence of low forward flow from systolic dysfunction, but requires indication and monitoring for harms.
- Treat bleeding, sepsis and mechanical pathology definitively rather than relying on increasingly elaborate haemodynamic numbers.

## 10.2 A practical goal-directed decision sequence

- **Step 1 — establish the underlying diagnosis and a pressure floor.** Confirm measurement quality and correct promptly reversible problems such as excessive anaesthetic depth, bleeding, tamponade, severe arrhythmia or ventilator-induced reduction in venous return.
- Establish a plausible MAP target (often ≥65 mmHg in uncomplicated adults during major surgery, higher when clinically justified), individualised for chronic hypertension, coronary/cerebral disease and procedure.
- The 2026 Association of Anaesthetists/British and Irish Hypertension Society guideline discusses a common higher-risk intraoperative target of **MAP >70 mmHg and/or SBP >100 mmHg**; this is a context-specific recommendation, not a universal mandate.
- Treat sustained hypotension promptly and avoid reflex large boluses for anaesthetic vasodilation.

**Step 2 — decide whether forward flow is inadequate:**

- Use clinical perfusion, lactate/CRT, CO if indicated and echo.
- Low MAP with a normal/high CO often implies low SVR; low CO despite adequate perfusion pressure requires evaluation of preload, contractility, afterload and rhythm.
- Echo can reveal tamponade, severe valve lesion or RV dysfunction, which changes the algorithm fundamentally.

- **Step 3 — if considering fluid, perform a valid dynamic assessment and check tolerance.** A PLR-induced or bolus-induced >10–15% SV increase supports responsiveness; it does not establish safety.
- Use a small monitored bolus when a clinical perfusion problem and acceptable lung/RV/venous tolerance coexist.
- Document the net change in flow, BP, oxygenation, pulmonary congestion and losses.
- Stop when benefit plateaus or harms emerge.

**Step 4 — add or adjust vasoactive drugs for mechanism:**

- With vasodilatory hypotension, titrate an appropriate vasopressor to effective organ perfusion.
- With low CO from cardiogenic dysfunction, correct ischaemia, arrhythmia, hypoxaemia and metabolic disturbances; consider lesion-specific inotropy rather than fixed empiric infusion.
- In RV failure, avoid escalating pulmonary vascular resistance with hypoxia/acidosis and excessive airway pressures, and correct systemic hypotension threatening RV coronary perfusion.
- When tissue hypoperfusion persists despite apparently normal global measures, reassess microcirculation, abdominal pressure, anaemia and other causes rather than chasing ever-higher CO.

**Step 5 — reassess in recovery and critical care.** Perioperative trajectories continue after theatre. Delayed fluid overload, AKI, postoperative bleeding and cardiac events can occur after the monitoring device is removed. Handover physiological rationale and unresolved risks, not just the amount infused and the last MAP.

## 10.3 Evidence audit: OPTIMISE II, POQI 2025 and the limits of routine protocols

- Many older teaching notes present GDHT as a universal standard for complex abdominal surgery.
- That is no longer justified.
- **OPTIMISE II** tested a defined protocol involving CO-guided fluids plus low-dose inotrope in older major elective GI patients and found **no reduction in infections (23.2% vs 22.7%)** and a rise in very early acute cardiac events, especially arrhythmias.
- The **2025 POQI-11 international consensus** therefore recommends against routine GDHT for major elective abdominal surgery and against fixed low-dose inotrope infusions.
- It permits individualised consideration in other moderate/high-risk procedures and suggests selected use in CPB, post-cardiac surgery and hip fracture cases, with evidence strength varying by setting.

- This creates a useful distinction: **dynamic fluid-responsiveness testing is a diagnostic technique**, whereas **routine GDHT protocol implementation is a therapeutic package with a different evidence base**.
- A useful PPV measurement or echo does not prove that a uniform algorithm improves outcomes.
- Both the 2024 POQI fluid consensus and 2026 sepsis guidance support individualising fluid decisions, while cautioning against inferring that one monitor or target guarantees improved survival.

## 10.4 Sepsis and shock: apply current, not superseded, algorithms

- In sepsis, loss of vascular tone, altered venous capacitance, inflammatory endothelial permeability and variable myocardial dysfunction make both pressure and flow highly dynamic.
- The **2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign** conditionally suggests at least **30 mL/kg crystalloid within the first 3 hours** for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, with frequent assessment and attention to under/over-resuscitation.
- In unstable shock, early peripheral norepinephrine can be appropriate rather than waiting for a central line, particularly when accompanied by initial fluid resuscitation.
- The guideline strongly recommends an initial MAP target **65 mmHg** for most adults with septic shock; for adults ≥65 years it conditionally suggests **60–65 mmHg**, emphasising individualisation.
- These population recommendations are not a substitute for coronary, cerebral or renal perfusion considerations in particular patients.

- After initial resuscitation, further boluses should be **dynamic-measure guided** when possible (PLR plus a genuine flow measurement, or a carefully performed bolus challenge) and weighed against fluid accumulation.
- Serial lactate is useful, but clinicians should not repeatedly give fluid until lactate normalises: lactate rises with catecholamines, seizures, liver dysfunction and impaired clearance.
- Add capillary refill and skin perfusion, mentation, urine output, bedside echo and respiratory assessment.
- SSC 2026 finds **insufficient evidence** to recommend routine extra minimally invasive/non-invasive CO devices compared with usual care for septic shock; ultrasound can still be clinically decisive for diagnosing myocardial or obstructive components.
- Fluid responsiveness ≠ fluid requirement remains the essential distinction.

## 10.5 When to abandon a protocol

- A protocol should be interrupted if the assumptions that validate its monitoring fail (rapid vasopressor-related compliance changes, arrhythmia, open chest, intraoperative pneumoperitoneum or severe RV pressure loading), the treatment creates harm (new B-lines, worsening oxygenation, rising CVP and falling CO), or a more urgent causal diagnosis appears.
- Record the reason and perform targeted reassessment.
- A sophisticated algorithm followed blindly is inferior to a reasoned decision made from simpler reliable information.

## 10.6 Applying and critically evaluating goal-directed therapy in real patients

- A useful goal-directed intervention has five elements: a relevant clinical problem, a valid measurement, a prespecified therapeutic option, a reassessment interval and a safety limit.
- Example: after induction for major abdominal surgery, MAP is 54 mmHg, heart rate 82/min, arterial waveform reliable and LVOT VTI 14 cm.
- Before giving fluid, ask whether there is evidence of low-flow hypoperfusion, vasodilation, haemorrhage or cardiac obstruction.
- A reproducible VTI increase to 16 cm after a small test indicates an approximately 14% rise in flow from altered preload, but if oxygenation is worsening with new lung B-lines, more fluid may be intolerable.
- If perfusion is adequate and profound anaesthetic vasodilation is likely, an appropriately selected vasopressor may be the better treatment even though the patient is fluid responsive.

- A second example illustrates why algorithmic haemodynamic targets need an organ context.
- A patient with sepsis has MAP 68 mmHg on norepinephrine, CO 7 L/min, warm skin, lactate 5 mmol/L and urinary output 0.3 mL/kg/h.
- Pushing CO higher with fluid or inotrope is not automatically beneficial.
- Review lactate trajectory and beta-adrenergic effects, septic source control, capillary refill, renal obstruction, venous congestion and cardiac function.
- Serial lactate and capillary refill are useful adjuncts in the 2026 SSC; it suggests dynamic tests rather than static indices alone when selecting further fluid.
- It finds insufficient evidence for routine minimally invasive or non-invasive CO monitors in every septic-shock patient.
- The target is improved patient physiology, not a mandatory CO number.

- Evidence should change how the intervention is offered.
- OPTIMISE II did not reduce infection after routine CO-guided fluid plus fixed low-dose inotrope in major elective gastrointestinal surgery, and early cardiac complications increased.
- The 2025 POQI-11 group therefore recommends against routine GDHT protocols in major elective abdominal surgery and against fixed low-dose inotropes as a protocol component.
- This does not prohibit an individualised response to significant haemorrhage, cardiac dysfunction or uncertain fluid responsiveness.
- Earlier positive trials may differ from contemporary studies in baseline care, risk, algorithms, outcomes and co-interventions.
- Disentangle 'the monitor can measure CO' from 'a particular protocol improves clinical outcomes'.

Make a treatment table mentally:

- If pressure is low and flow normal/high, consider relative vasodilation and vasopressor need.
- If flow and pressure are low with an empty, recruitable ventricle and good tolerance, targeted fluid may be indicated.
- If flow is low with poor LV contraction and elevated filling pressures, consider cardiogenic mechanisms and selected inotrope/afterload management.
- If the RV is dilated under high pulmonary pressure, reduce PVR and preserve coronary perfusion rather than blindly filling.

- A repeated flow measure, perfusion endpoints and complications should close the loop after every intervention.

items.title: 11. Indicators of tissue oxygenation and adequacy of resuscitation
items.body:
## 11.1 Tissue oxygenation is not measured by MAP or CO alone

- The central purpose of circulatory resuscitation is to provide cellular oxygen and nutrients while removing metabolites, not to produce normal-looking values.
- Global DO₂ depends on CO, haemoglobin and arterial saturation.
- Local oxygen supply additionally depends on regional blood flow, capillary density, microcirculatory distribution, diffusion distance and mitochondrial ability to use oxygen.
- In haemorrhage, oxygen delivery may fall mainly because Hb and CO decrease; in septic shock, an apparently adequate CO or high venous O₂ saturation may coexist with regional shunting and poor extraction.
- To evaluate the patient's response, combine pressure, flow, biochemical, peripheral and organ-specific measures rather than chasing a single target.

- **Signs of poor perfusion** include altered mental state, cold or mottled extremities, slow capillary refill, reduced urine output, rising lactate, increasing base deficit, low ScvO₂/SvO₂ in the right context, ST changes, falling ETCO₂ at unchanged ventilation and deteriorating renal/liver function.
- None is fully sensitive or specific.
- In particular, low urine output can be due to neurohormonal stress, postoperative antidiuretic hormone release, obstruction and kidney injury without new intravascular volume deficit.

## 11.2 Lactate: production, clearance and limitations

- Lactate is generated continuously from pyruvate via lactate dehydrogenase and serves as a fuel and substrate for gluconeogenesis.
- A rise occurs when generation exceeds clearance (principally liver and kidneys).
- **Type A hyperlactataemia** is associated with inadequate tissue oxygen supply (e.g. shock, severe hypoxaemia), but lactate can also rise from **beta₂-adrenergic stimulation** (endogenous or exogenous catecholamines), seizures, high work of breathing, impaired hepatic clearance, thiamine deficiency, metformin toxicity and some mitochondrial/medication effects.
- Thus lactate ≥2 mmol/L is a warning sign that requires explanation; a single reading does not diagnose hypovolaemia, sepsis or necessarily anaerobic metabolism.

- **Serial lactate** can help determine whether the patient's overall trajectory is improving.
- Calculate percentage reduction = (initial − later)/initial × 100. A fall from 6.0 to 4.2 mmol/L is 30% reduction, but the clinical meaning depends on time elapsed, source control and changing adrenergic therapy.
- Serial sampling without judging urine output, skin perfusion, dynamic tests and other organ measures encourages 'lactate chasing' with unnecessary fluid.
- The 2026 SSC suggests serial lactate assessment, while explicitly advising against continued fluid administration solely to normalise lactate after initial resuscitation.

## 11.3 Base deficit, acid–base changes and renal perfusion

- **Base excess** estimates the metabolic component of acid–base status at standardised PCO₂ and temperature; a negative base excess is a **base deficit**.
- An increasing deficit during trauma can reflect accumulating unmeasured anions from poor perfusion, but can also arise from hyperchloraemic acidosis after large saline loads, renal dysfunction, ketoacidosis or toxins.
- Temperature, albumin, ventilation and timing influence interpretation.
- A worsening base deficit in a bleeding trauma patient can support concern for occult hypoperfusion even when MAP is maintained by catecholamines, but it is not a substitute for haemorrhage assessment and correction.

- **Urine output** is an integrated kidney/haemodynamic measure and a marker of volume and renal functional response over time; it is not instantaneous and can be distorted by diuretics, CKD, stress hormones, urinary obstruction, vasopressin and non-oliguric AKI.
- Persistent <0.5 mL/kg/h is a common warning threshold for AKI assessment, not a trigger for an automatic crystalloid bolus.
- Review bladder catheter patency, MAP/CO, venous congestion, nephrotoxins and renal injury before deciding on treatment.

## 11.4 Mixed and central venous oxygen saturation

- Mixed venous oxygen saturation (**SvO₂**) from pulmonary arterial blood reflects the net amount of oxygen returning after systemic extraction, with coronary sinus blood included.
- A common resting range is approximately **65–75%**; low values may indicate low CO, anaemia, hypoxaemia or increased VO₂ (fever/shivering), while very high values may occur with increased CO, impaired tissue extraction or severe shunting.
- Central venous saturation (**ScvO₂**) is usually obtained from SVC blood, omitting inferior body venous return and coronary sinus blood; the difference from SvO₂ varies and becomes especially unreliable in shock.
- **They are not interchangeable measurements** and neither is a direct tissue oxygen sensor.

- Derived extraction can help interpret the change.
- If arterial oxygen saturation is 98% and SvO₂ 60% with similar haemoglobin binding, extraction is approximately (98−60)/98 = 39%, above the usual resting fraction; the patient may be compensating for reduced delivery or increased metabolism.
- A rising SvO₂ after a fluid challenge can indicate improved global delivery if VO₂ and oxygenation are stable, but can also reflect impaired extraction; confirm with CO, lactate, capillary refill and organ function.

**Worked example:**

- Patient in septic shock has MAP 70 on noradrenaline, CO 7 L/min, ScvO₂ 82%, lactate 5 mmol/L and mottled knees.
- The high CO and ScvO₂ do **not** exclude serious shock.
- Maldistributed microcirculatory flow, altered oxygen extraction and catecholamine effects may coexist.
- Evaluate infection source, capillary refill/skin, lactate trend, cardiac function, microvascular factors and need for ongoing resuscitation rather than administering inotropes because lactate remains high.

## 11.5 Capillary refill, temperature gradients and organ-specific signals

- **Capillary refill time (CRT)** is a cheap adjunct to perfusion assessment.
- Apply consistent pressure to a fingertip/patella for a few seconds, release and measure return of colour; prolonged refill (commonly >3 s in adults, depending on temperature and method) supports impaired peripheral perfusion, but ambient temperature, vasoconstriction, oedema and observer variability confound it.
- Peripheral-to-central temperature difference and skin mottling are additional clinical clues.

- The **ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trial (JAMA 2019)** compared CRT-targeted versus lactate-targeted resuscitation in 424 early septic-shock patients.
- Twenty-eight-day mortality was 34.9% versus 43.4%, but the primary difference did **not reach statistical significance** (P=.06); CRT-guided therapy was associated with less organ dysfunction at 72 hours and lower early fluid exposure.
- It supports the plausibility and practicality of assessing peripheral perfusion, but should not be cited as definitive proof that CRT targets reduce mortality.
- SSC 2026 suggests CRT as an adjunct to other measures.

- **Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS)** estimates regional tissue oxygen saturation (cerebral or peripheral), integrating arterial and venous components.
- It may be valuable in selected cardiac, vascular or neuro procedures but measures local tissue rather than whole-body oxygenation.
- Sensor position, extracranial contamination, skin pigmentation, haemoglobin and regional blood flow affect interpretation; protocols vary and there is no universal saturation value ensuring adequate organ perfusion.
- End-tidal CO₂ during CPR or sudden shock provides information about pulmonary blood flow and effective circulation if ventilation and metabolism are otherwise stable, but abrupt changes can also be caused by equipment or ventilation changes.

## 11.6 A structured resuscitation dashboard

| **Domain** | **Examples** | **Interpretation and response** |
|---|---|---|
| Pressure | MAP, diastolic pressure, CVP, pulse contour | Confirm signal, set context-specific perfusion target; identify vasodilation vs flow failure |
| Flow/pump | CO, CI, LVOT VTI, RV/LV echo | Identify low forward output or mechanical problem; decide whether SV change is meaningful |
| Preload response | PLR and SV/VTI change, valid PPV/SVV | Assess if further fluid can raise SV, then separately assess need and safety |
| Oxygen delivery | Hb, SaO₂/PaO₂, CO, SvO₂/ScvO₂ | Identify anaemia, hypoxaemia, low flow or increased extraction |
| Tissue/organ | CRT, temperature/mottling, lactate, base deficit, urine output | Track recovery; explain abnormalities rather than treating one isolated number |
| Congestion/tolerance | Lung B-lines, RV dilation, rising CVP, venous Doppler, net balance | Prevent additional fluid-induced pulmonary/renal/hepatic congestion |

## 11.7 The venous–arterial carbon dioxide gap and organ perfusion: an additional, limited adjunct

- The central venous–arterial PCO2 difference [P(cv–a)CO2 = PcvCO2 − PaCO2] can rise when global blood flow is inadequate relative to CO2 production.
- In simple terms, CO2 returning from tissue is less effectively washed out at low flow; a gap greater than roughly 6 mmHg is often used as a warning of potentially inadequate flow, although the threshold and meaning depend on context.
- The relationship is not equivalent to tissue hypoxia: CO2 content and PCO2 are nonlinearly related, severe anaemia and acid–base state influence the result, and microcirculatory shunting can produce abnormal CO2 handling even with adequate measured CO.

- Interpret venous CO2 with arterial gas, global CO and venous oxygen saturation.
- Low ScvO2 plus a high CO2 gap may support concern for inadequate DO2 or flow, whereas high ScvO2 in septic shock does not exclude maldistributed capillary perfusion.
- The CO2 gap can be enlarged by changes in ventilation, impaired microcirculation or sampled central-vein territory, and an isolated number should not mandate fluids or inotropes.
- A proposed P(cv–a)CO2 / C(a–cv)O2 ratio has been studied as a surrogate for anaerobic metabolism, but evidence, sampling variability and physiological assumptions limit its routine use as a treatment target.
- It is supplementary information, never a substitute for causative diagnosis and serial patient assessment.

- Capillary refill time should be measured with consistent pressure and site, ambient temperature and timing.
- Prolongation can reflect cutaneous vasoconstriction, cold environment and catecholamine effect, but a trend may be valuable alongside urine output, lactate and mental state.
- Use several independent signals to decide whether an intervention achieved sustained improvement.
- The ANZCA Final expects evaluation: for each measure explain what it reflects physiologically, how it is acquired, when it becomes unreliable and what action it can and cannot justify.

items.title: 12. Integrating monitoring into common perioperative and intensive-care presentations
items.priority: P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (3 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 12.1 The induction hypotension algorithm

- After induction, a patient becomes hypotensive.
- Do not reflexively order a large bolus.
- Confirm the pressure signal, ECG and pulse; consider anaphylaxis, bleeding, anaesthetic-induced vasodilation/myocardial depression, loss of venous return from positive-pressure ventilation, and pre-existing cardiac pathology.
- In a relatively well-perfused patient with an apparently normal pulse pressure but low MAP, vasodilation may be predominant; appropriately titrated vasopressor and reducing excessive anaesthetic depth may be more effective than litres of fluid.
- In a patient with a small LV and low VTI after haemorrhage, flow restoration and blood replacement may be needed.
- In a patient with sudden RV dilation and a falling ETCO₂, investigate PE, air embolism, high airway pressure and other obstructive causes.
- A careful response to a defined intervention teaches more than a static number.

## 12.2 Complex major surgery

- For a patient with impaired cardiac reserve undergoing prolonged abdominal surgery, choose an arterial catheter before induction when rapid BP changes or vasoactive requirements are likely.
- Consider bedside echo/CO trending if the data will affect decisions.
- Set personalised goals based on vascular disease and possible organ perfusion deficits; avoid sustained MAP below a tolerable range.
- Prescribe fluid based on losses and a valid dynamic response, with attention to fluid tolerance and venous congestion.
- If SV fails to rise after a bolus, stop administering fluid merely because urine output remains low.
- **OPTIMISE II and POQI 2025** do not justify a standing plan to use a fixed low-dose inotrope in every major abdominal patient.
- Reassess ongoing therapy in PACU/ICU.

## 12.3 Mixed cardiogenic and distributive shock

- A septic patient with septic cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension may have a high CVP, low CO and vasodilated circulation simultaneously.
- A high CVP does not prove adequate LV preload, and a low MAP does not identify whether venous return, LV contractility or systemic vascular tone predominates.
- Echo should distinguish RV enlargement, LV systolic dysfunction and dynamic obstruction; consider PAC if major uncertainty persists despite echo and tailored therapy.
- Fluid might transiently raise SV yet increase lung water and renal venous pressure.
- Decide stepwise whether to improve MAP with a pressor, support contractility, reduce RV afterload or remove congestion.
- Serial lactate/CRT and oxygen delivery responses provide more reliable endpoints than trying to normalise CVP.

## 12.4 Haemodynamic monitoring in obesity

- In morbid obesity, the NIBP cuff may not fit the upper arm; a correctly sized upper-arm cuff or appropriately validated alternative is essential.
- An undersized cuff falsely elevates pressure.
- The decision about an invasive arterial catheter should be based on expected instability, tissue perfusion risk and reliability of non-invasive readings—not obesity alone.
- Arterial ultrasound may be useful when landmarks are difficult.
- Non-invasive CO monitors may have limited validated performance in extreme body habitus.
- Echocardiographic windows can be poor, while PEEP and increased intra-abdominal pressure distort CVP and IVC interpretation.
- This covers the interpretation expected from the **2025.1 Final examination topic comparing invasive and non-invasive BP options in morbid obesity**.

## 12.5 Pulmonary hypertension and right-ventricular failure

- The RV normally pumps into a low-resistance, high-compliance pulmonary circuit.
- Hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidemia and excessive pulmonary inflation raise PVR and can cause acute RV dilation and septal shift, reducing LV filling.
- Echo characterises RV dimensions and performance; a PAC may quantify PA pressure, PAOP, PVR and mixed venous oxygen balance in highly selected cases.
- Avoid excessive crystalloid simply to achieve a 'normal' CVP.
- Maintain systemic pressure sufficient for RV coronary perfusion, avoid precipitants of pulmonary vasoconstriction and seek cause-specific therapies.
- A worsening CVP plus falling cardiac index during escalating PEEP is a clue to impaired RV outflow, not evidence that the patient requires still more volume.

## 12.6 Monitoring complications are themselves critical events

- Unexpected fall in arterial pressure with preserved pulse quality may be an equipment problem; an absent CVP waveform after catheter manipulation may be disconnection or malposition; new tachyarrhythmia during PAC advancement is likely mechanical irritation.
- When a device causes arterial injury or thrombosis, resuscitation and urgent procedural/specialist management override the original monitoring purpose.
- A central line in a dialysis patient may compromise future access.
- Before transferring care, include device type and site, known complications, last flush/zero checks, catheter depth, current infusions, and what the team considers a true haemodynamic deterioration.
- Monitoring safety is continuous, not completed at insertion.

items.title: 13. Worked integrated cases for ANZCA Final reasoning
items.los: Integrates the outcomes in this set
items.body:
## Case 1 — The 'low CVP' after laparotomy

An anaesthetised 76-year-old with severe coronary disease has MAP 59, HR 88, CVP 3 mmHg, Hb 116 g/L, normal oxygenation and urine output 20 mL/h. The surgeon reports no significant bleeding, but the patient is receiving a volatile anaesthetic and remifentanil.

**Interpretation:**

- CVP 3 does not demonstrate fluid deficit.
- A low measured value may occur with anaesthetic venodilation; poor organ perfusion cannot be inferred from urine output in the first hour.
- Verify transducer position and end-expiratory measurement, look for evidence of reduced CO and dynamic fluid response, review anaesthetic dose and perfusion pressure.
- With plausible vasodilatory hypotension, a titrated vasopressor may be preferable to repeated crystalloid.
- If the patient has a low LVOT VTI with demonstrable PLR response and no congestion, a small monitored fluid bolus is reasonable.
- **Examiner point:** the 2026.1 CVP question required the physiology and measurement confounders, not simply a list of 'more reliable monitors'.

## Case 2 — A damped radial arterial trace in a hip-fracture patient

The radial monitor shows 80/65 mmHg with a flattened upstroke, but a correctly sized arm cuff reads 115/70. The patient is warm, awake and not bleeding.

**Interpretation:**

- A systolic-diastolic waveform pulse pressure of 15 mmHg that contradicts clinical status and cuff measurement suggests damping, not necessarily a true low SV.
- Perform a fast-flush test and inspect for bubbles, clot, kink, stopcock obstruction, catheter tip against wall, line length and pressure bag.
- Zero and level correctly.
- The mean value may be relatively preserved in simple damping, but both readings must be reconsidered if levelling is wrong.
- Replace faulty equipment before escalating vasoactive drugs.
- This is the practical substance behind the historically examined arterial-line accuracy question.

## Case 3 — Low BP with a dilated right ventricle

During major orthopaedic surgery, ETCO₂ abruptly drops from 35 to 18 mmHg, MAP drops to 48 and oxygen saturation falls. PLAX/A4C TTE shows an acutely enlarged RV and a small LV; the arterial-line signal is well formed.

**Interpretation:**

- An acute obstruction to pulmonary flow or rise in PVR is urgent; consider PE, air/fat embolism, tension pneumothorax, severe hypoxia or ventilatory pressure effects.
- The high right-sided pressure does not mean adequate systemic flow.
- Call for help, deliver oxygen, manage airway/ventilation, assess for pleural/lung causes and take appropriate cause-specific action.
- Maintain systemic perfusion and consider urgent senior echo/cardiology involvement.
- A large indiscriminate fluid bolus may worsen RV dilation and LV compression.
- The next useful monitor is the one that resolves the cause, not another uncalibrated CO display.

## Case 4 — Transplant candidate with conflicting PAC data

A 49-year-old with suspected pulmonary hypertension has CVP 15 mmHg, PA 70/30 (mPAP 43), PAOP 10 and thermodilution CO 3.0 L/min.

**Calculation:**

- TPG = 43−10 = 33 mmHg. PVR = 33/3.0 = **11 WU**.
- Severe RV afterload disease is likely.
- Check wedge validity and oxygen/ventilator settings, assess echo for RV dilation, TR and left-heart disease.
- A wedge value is not an exact measure of LV volume.
- The physiology directs treatment toward RV protection and pulmonary vascular evaluation; routine 'volume loading to normalise CVP' is unsafe.

## Case 5 — A PICC for three weeks of antibiotics

A 62-year-old with osteomyelitis requires three weeks of IV antimicrobial treatment, is ambulatory, has no advanced CKD and needs one compatible drug.

**Evaluation:**

- Compared with repeated short peripheral IVs, a single-lumen PICC may be convenient and reduce repeated cannulation.
- Compared with neck/chest CVC, it avoids most insertion pneumothoraces and large central arterial punctures, but its main concerns are upper-arm DVT, migration, infection and catheter occlusion.
- Confirm indication, ultrasound vein size and no thrombosis; select minimum catheter diameter/lumens, apply sterile insertion bundle, confirm cavoatrial tip position, secure and maintain with trained care.
- Ask whether an oral antimicrobial option or ultrasound-guided long peripheral alternative is suitable.
- Remove as soon as treatment ends.
- In advanced CKD, protect future dialysis access and consult nephrology.

## Case 6 — Fluid responsive but not fluid tolerant

A mechanically ventilated septic patient has MAP 68 on norepinephrine, PLR SV rise 14%, CVP 17, diffuse lung B-lines and a dilated RV. Lactate is 3.2 mmol/L, down from 5.4.

**Interpretation:**

- The patient is preload responsive by flow criterion yet demonstrates impaired fluid tolerance; do not equate 'responsive' with 'give fluid'.
- Evaluate oxygen delivery, RV function, capillary refill, urine output and other causes of residual lactate.
- If flow augmentation is essential, a carefully monitored small intervention could be considered with immediate reassessment, but persistent bolus therapy risks worsening lungs and RV.
- Continue definitive septic management and mechanism-specific vasoactive support.
- This is the central conceptual distinction of modern goal-directed therapy.

## Case 7 — Intraoperative TTE: answer the question that was asked

During emergency abdominal surgery, a patient becomes profoundly hypotensive despite reasonable anaesthetic depth and an initial vasopressor bolus. The question asks specifically: **evaluate intraoperative transthoracic echocardiography (TTE)**.

**Reasoned evaluation:**

- TTE can rapidly test LV function and filling, RV size/strain, pericardial effusion and gross valves, distinguish categories of shock, and assess whether a PLR/targeted fluid or vasoactive intervention changes SV.
- It does not require an oesophageal probe and can be repeated.
- However, sterile drapes, surgical positioning, insufflation, obesity, ventilation and available expertise may prevent adequate windows.
- Inability to image one chamber is not a negative study.
- If the question allows it, TOE may be an alternative when TTE is unusable but must not displace the requested evaluation of TTE.
- Escalate to comprehensive imaging when uncertainty matters.
- These are the exact emphases of the 2025.2 examiner's report.

## Case 8 — A septic patient with persistent lactate 5 mmol/L

After antibiotics and surgical source control, a septic patient has MAP 72 with norepinephrine, CO 7.2 L/min, ScvO₂ 84%, CRT 2 seconds, improving urine output and normal oxygenation; lactate remains 5, although it was 8 earlier.

**Interpretation:**

- Global oxygen delivery and clinical perfusion appear to be improving, and hyperlactataemia may reflect adrenergic metabolism and impaired clearance as well as prior hypoperfusion.
- Do not give repeated fluids or fixed inotrope merely to 'normalise lactate'.
- Follow lactate trend, glucose, liver function, temperature, acid–base and ongoing source control; assess for residual regional ischaemia when clinically suspected.
- Use echo/monitoring to answer a new question rather than escalating treatment solely on one lab result.

## Case 9 — Pulmonary artery catheter advancement causes complete heart block

During PAC insertion in a patient with existing left bundle branch block, passage through the RV is followed by profound bradycardia and complete AV block.

**Interpretation:**

- Mechanical trauma to the right bundle can cause transient RBBB; in pre-existing LBBB this may produce complete heart block.
- Stop advancement, withdraw appropriately, ensure oxygenation/perfusion and institute pacing as indicated by haemodynamic stability.
- This high-risk patient should have immediate pacing capability planned before insertion.
- Routine PAC placement without a clear question and preparation exposes patients to avoidable procedural complications.

## Case 10 — Low-risk laparoscopic procedure with a fasting patient

A healthy 55 kg adult undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy, is stable, with minor operative blood loss, and plans to drink within 1–2 hours after recovery. They have fasted from solid food overnight but were permitted clear liquids under local fasting policy.

**Prescription:**

- A calculated daily water-maintenance range of ≈1.4–1.65 L/day is **not** a deficit that must be replaced in theatre; fluid requirement for this short procedure is modest unless actual losses or signs of impaired perfusion arise.
- Give sufficient balanced crystalloid for IV access, intraoperative needs and measured losses; evaluate any BP reduction according to mechanism (e.g. anaesthetic vasodilation or pneumoperitoneum) rather than treating automatically with a litre of saline.
- Avoid unnecessary maintenance once safe oral intake resumes, with timely discharge documentation.

items.title: 14. Numbers to know cold
items.body:
Reference values that come up repeatedly across this set.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| CO, CI, SVI | 4–8 L/min; 2.5–4.0 L/min/m²; 33–47 mL/m² |
| SVR, PVR | 800–1200; about 20–130 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ |
| CVP | 0–8 mmHg |
| PA pressure, PAOP | 15–30 / 4–12 (mean 9–18); PAOP 6–12 mmHg |
| SvO₂, ScvO₂ | about 65–75%; ScvO₂ above 70% (historic target) |
| Lactate | below 2 mmol/L |
| PPV, SVV thresholds | about 13%; about 10–13% (grey zone 9–13%) |
| Fluid responsiveness | SV rise of about 10–15% after challenge or passive leg raise |
| LVOT VTI | about 18–22 cm |
| TAPSE, S′ | below about 16 mm, below about 10 cm/s abnormal |
| IVC | 2.1 cm and 50% collapse as cut-offs |
| Percentage error for new CO monitors | about 30% |
| Transducer | natural frequency above about 40 Hz; damping coefficient about 0.64–0.7 |
| PAC balloon volume | 1.5 mL air |
| Arterial pressure bag | 300 mmHg; flush about 3 mL/h |

items.title: State the Fick principle and how it is used to measure cardiac output.
items.q: State the Fick principle and how it is used to measure cardiac output.
items.a:
- Cardiac output = oxygen consumption / (arterial minus venous oxygen content).
- Needs a mixed venous sample from the pulmonary artery.
- Direct Fick is the reference method but is rarely practical; assumed VO2 gives an indirect Fick estimate with additional error.
- Partial CO2 rebreathing is a separate Fick-based technique; indirect oxygen-Fick means using estimated rather than measured VO2.


> **Closing point:** Flow equals uptake divided by the arteriovenous difference.

items.title: How does pulmonary artery thermodilution work and what are its errors?
items.q: How does pulmonary artery thermodilution work and what are its errors?
items.a:
- Cold bolus injected in the RA; temperature change measured at the PA thermistor.
- Area under the curve is inversely proportional to flow (Stewart-Hamilton).
- Low output gives a large, slow curve; high output a small, fast curve.
- Errors: tricuspid regurgitation, intracardiac shunt, irregular injection, respiratory cycle timing, rapid IV fluid.


> **Closing point:** Average three injections that agree within 10%.

items.title: Compare transpulmonary thermodilution and PAC thermodilution.
items.q: Compare transpulmonary thermodilution and PAC thermodilution.
items.a:
- Injection via CVC, detection by a femoral or axillary arterial thermistor (PiCCO, EV1000).
- Gives CO, global end-diastolic volume, extravascular lung water and SVV.
- Needs calibration; less invasive than a PAC.
- Errors: shunt, aortic aneurysm, regurgitant valves, ECMO.


> **Closing point:** Calibrated systems drift less than uncalibrated ones.

items.title: How does pulse contour analysis estimate cardiac output and when is it unreliable?
items.q: How does pulse contour analysis estimate cardiac output and when is it unreliable?
items.a:
- Stroke volume derived from arterial waveform area and arterial compliance.
- Calibrated (PiCCO, LiDCO) or uncalibrated (FloTrac, Vigileo).
- Unreliable with: damping, arrhythmias, aortic regurgitation, IABP, rapid change in vascular tone.
- Track the trend rather than the absolute value.


> **Closing point:** Changes in vascular tone invalidate the compliance estimate.

items.title: How does oesophageal Doppler measure flow and what are its limits?
items.q: How does oesophageal Doppler measure flow and what are its limits?
items.a:
- Probe in the distal oesophagus measures velocity in the descending aorta.
- Flow time corrected (FTc) and peak velocity are influenced by filling, afterload, rate and contractility; neither is a pure measure of one property.
- Assumes about 70% of cardiac output goes to the descending aorta.
- Limits: operator dependence, probe position, awake patient intolerance, oesophageal pathology.


> **Closing point:** Position the probe for the best aortic signal.

items.title: How does bioreactance or bioimpedance measure cardiac output?
items.q: How does bioreactance or bioimpedance measure cardiac output?
items.a:
- Electrodes on the chest measure thoracic impedance (or phase shift).
- Changes with each stroke relate to aortic blood volume.
- Fully non-invasive.
- Limits: diathermy, arrhythmia, lung water, movement, obesity.


> **Closing point:** Convenience does not establish accuracy or reliable trending in an unstable patient.

items.title: What is a percentage error of 30% and why does it matter?
items.q: What is a percentage error of 30% and why does it matter?
items.a:
- Critchley and Critchley criterion for a new CO monitor against a reference method.
- The historical 30% criterion assumed particular reference/test precision; neither 20% nor 30% is a universal property.
- Many minimally invasive monitors fail in extremes of vascular tone.
- Trending ability needs a separate polar plot analysis.


> **Closing point:** Agreement of trend can be better than agreement of absolute value.

items.title: Which PAC measurements are directly measured and which are derived?
items.q: Which PAC measurements are directly measured and which are derived?
items.a:
- Measured: RA, PA and wedge pressures, thermodilution CO, SvO2, temperature.
- Derived: SVR, PVR, stroke volume, indexed variables.
- SVR = (MAP − CVP) × 80 / CO.
- PVR = (mPAP − PAOP) × 80 / CO.


> **Closing point:** Derived values multiply the error in the measured ones.

items.title: Why does CVP fail as a guide to volume status?
items.q: Why does CVP fail as a guide to volume status?
items.a:
