- Reflects RA pressure, not volume.
- Confounded by compliance, intrathoracic pressure, PEEP, valve disease, RV function and tricuspid disease.
- Zero level and transducer position change the value.
- Weak relationship to fluid responsiveness (area under the curve about 0.56 in meta-analysis).


> **Closing point:** A CVP number cannot predict a response; even a CVP change alone cannot establish a flow response.

items.title: Describe the physiology of pulse pressure and stroke volume variation.
items.q: Describe the physiology of pulse pressure and stroke volume variation.
items.a:
- Positive pressure inspiration reduces RV preload and can transiently increase LV filling by pulmonary blood displacement and reduce LV afterload; RV afterload may rise.
- The fall in venous return shows in LV stroke volume a few beats later.
- A preload-dependent ventricle shows greater variation.
- Thresholds: PPV above 13% and SVV above 10 to 12% predict a response.


> **Closing point:** Heart-lung interaction acts as a built-in fluid challenge.

items.title: List the conditions needed for PPV and SVV to be valid.
items.q: List the conditions needed for PPV and SVV to be valid.
items.a:
- Controlled ventilation without spontaneous effort.
- Classical validation used around 8 mL/kg predicted body weight; a brief supervised tidal-volume challenge may help. Do not abandon lung-protective ventilation merely to use PPV.
- Sinus rhythm.
- Closed chest, normal intra-abdominal pressure.
- Normal RV function and compliance.


> **Closing point:** Choose another test whenever validity conditions fail.

items.title: How do you perform a passive leg raise and interpret it?
items.q: How do you perform a passive leg raise and interpret it?
items.a:
- Semi-recumbent to supine with legs raised 45 degrees for 1 minute.
- Moves about 300 mL from the legs and abdomen.
- A rise in stroke volume or cardiac output of 10% or more predicts a response.
- Valid in spontaneous breathing and arrhythmia; measure flow, not blood pressure.


> **Closing point:** It is a reversible fluid challenge.

items.title: What is the end-expiratory occlusion test?
items.q: What is the end-expiratory occlusion test?
items.a:
- Hold expiration for 15 seconds in a ventilated patient.
- Venous return rises without inspiratory impedance.
- A small CO/SV rise around 5% may predict response if the monitor is sufficiently precise; pressure alone is not an equivalent flow endpoint.
- Needs an uninterrupted hold and a rapid precise flow measure; spontaneous inspiratory efforts can invalidate it.


> **Closing point:** A fluid challenge without giving fluid.

items.title: What is the mini fluid challenge?
items.q: What is the mini fluid challenge?
items.a:
- 100 mL over 1 minute.
- A rise in stroke volume or velocity-time integral of 6 to 10% predicts a response.
- Needs a precise flow monitor.
- Reduces the risk of overload compared with a full bolus.


> **Closing point:** Small volume, precise measurement.

items.title: Define fluid responsiveness and distinguish it from hypovolaemia.
items.q: Define fluid responsiveness and distinguish it from hypovolaemia.
items.a:
- Increase in stroke volume of 10 to 15% after a fluid bolus.
- About half of ICU patients and many intraoperative patients respond.
- Responsiveness shows the Starling curve position, not need.
- Consider fluid for hypoperfusion plus responsiveness **and acceptable tolerance**.


> **Closing point:** Responsiveness is a physiological possibility, not an indication.

items.title: How do you assess IVC and what are its limitations?
items.q: How do you assess IVC and what are its limitations?
items.a:
- Measured subcostally, 2 cm from the RA.
- In spontaneous breathing, IVC diameter plus inspiratory change can help estimate RA pressure; strong inspiratory effort can mislead.
- Ventilated-patient distensibility thresholds depend on the formula and strict conditions; IVC variation is not a reliable universal response test.
- Limits: raised intra-abdominal pressure, RV failure, PEEP, arrhythmia.


> **Closing point:** A plethoric IVC suggests a full RA, not a full circulation.

items.title: Give a reproducible structure for a focused cardiac ultrasound assessment.
items.q: Give a reproducible structure for a focused cardiac ultrasound assessment.
items.a:
- LV: size, global/regional function and possible LVOT obstruction.
- RV: size, function and septal position.
- Valves and pericardium: major lesions and tamponade physiology.
- Filling/flow: integrated congestion assessment and measured VTI/SV response.
- Add lung and vascular views for the clinical question.


> **Closing point:** Use a consistent sequence within PG47 scope; no single teaching acronym is an ANZCA-mandated diagnostic algorithm.

Source: Blue Book 2015

items.title: Which TTE views are used in a focused exam?
items.q: Which TTE views are used in a focused exam?
items.a:
- Parasternal long axis.
- Parasternal short axis (papillary muscle level).
- Apical four-chamber.
- Subcostal four-chamber and IVC.
- Add lung views in the shocked patient.


> **Closing point:** Subcostal view works when other windows are poor.

items.title: How do you estimate stroke volume with echo?
items.q: How do you estimate stroke volume with echo?
items.a:
- SV = LVOT area × LVOT velocity-time integral.
- LVOT area = π × (diameter/2)².
- Measure the VTI with pulsed-wave Doppler at the LVOT in the apical five-chamber view.
- Cardiac output = SV × heart rate.
- Error comes from diameter measurement (squared).


> **Closing point:** A change around 10–15% may be useful if acquisition and measurement precision support it.

items.title: What does an underfilled hyperdynamic LV with a small cavity suggest?
items.q: What does an underfilled hyperdynamic LV with a small cavity suggest?
items.a:
- Hypovolaemia or vasodilation.
- Systolic cavity obliteration (kissing papillary muscles).
- Normal or high EF.
- Consider LVOT obstruction.


> **Closing point:** Look at the whole picture, not the EF alone.

items.title: Which findings suggest acute right ventricular strain on echo?
items.q: Which findings suggest acute right ventricular strain on echo?
items.a:
- RV larger than LV (ratio above 1).
- Septal flattening (D-shaped LV) in systole or diastole.
- McConnell sign: RV free-wall hypokinesia with apical sparing; not specific for PE.
- Raised TR velocity, dilated IVC, TAPSE ≤17 mm or S′ ≤9.5 cm/s supports abnormal longitudinal RV function in ASE 2025; integrate other findings.


> **Closing point:** Think pulmonary embolism, RV infarct or acute lung injury.

items.title: What are the echo signs of tamponade?
items.q: What are the echo signs of tamponade?
items.a:
- Pericardial effusion with RA systolic or RV diastolic collapse.
- Plethoric IVC.
- Respiratory variation in mitral and tricuspid inflow.
- Clinical diagnosis: Beck triad, pulsus paradoxus.


> **Closing point:** Ventilation, PH and loculated postoperative collections can obscure classic signs; integrate haemodynamics.

items.title: What is the RUSH or POCUS approach to undifferentiated shock?
items.q: What is the RUSH or POCUS approach to undifferentiated shock?
items.a:
- Pump: LV and RV function, pericardium.
- Tank: IVC, lungs, abdomen (free fluid), pleura.
- Pipes: aorta (aneurysm, dissection), DVT.
- Classifies shock: hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive.


> **Closing point:** Pump, tank, pipes.

items.title: Which Doppler formulae do you need to know?
items.q: Which Doppler formulae do you need to know?
items.a:
- Bernoulli: pressure gradient = 4 × V².
- Continuity: A1 × V1 = A2 × V2.
- Aortic valve area from LVOT area and velocity ratio.
- RVSP = 4 × TR velocity² + estimated RA pressure; equals PASP only without pulmonary/RVOT obstruction.


> **Closing point:** Velocity squared times four.

items.title: What are the main limitations of transthoracic echo in anaesthesia?
items.q: What are the main limitations of transthoracic echo in anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Poor windows (obesity, lung disease, ventilated patients, surgical field).
- Operator dependence and training requirement.
- Snapshot rather than continuous.
- Prone/lateral positioning can restrict windows; usable views may still be obtained by a skilled operator.


> **Closing point:** Escalate to TOE when TTE is inadequate.

items.title: When is TOE preferred for haemodynamic monitoring?
items.q: When is TOE preferred for haemodynamic monitoring?
items.a:
- Unstable patient with inadequate TTE windows.
- Repeated imaging of ventricular function, filling/congestion and flow in selected major surgery; not a direct preload-volume measurement.
- Transgastric mid short-axis view monitors ischaemia and filling.
- Perforation/obstructing oesophageal disease/active major GI bleeding are major contraindications; varices, previous surgery and cervical disease require individual assessment.


> **Closing point:** An indwelling TOE probe allows repeated imaging, but interpretation remains intermittent and operator-dependent.

items.title: What makes an arterial pressure system accurate?
items.q: What makes an arterial pressure system accurate?
items.a:
- Adequate natural frequency and damping must be considered together; commonly >20–25 Hz with appropriate damping is desirable, rather than a universal heart-rate multiple.
- Damping coefficient about 0.6 to 0.7.
- Short, stiff tubing without air bubbles.
- Transducer levelled to the right atrium and zeroed to atmosphere.


> **Closing point:** Optimal damping is a compromise between speed and overshoot.

items.title: Under-damped versus over-damped: what do you see?
items.q: Under-damped versus over-damped: what do you see?
items.a:
- Under-damped: overshoot, high systolic, low diastolic, narrow notch.
- Over-damped: low systolic, high diastolic, flattened trace, loss of notch.
- MAP is often less affected, but severe distortion, obstruction or levelling errors can still make it wrong.
- Causes of over-damping: air bubbles, clots, kinks, loose connections.


> **Closing point:** Investigate and correct a poor trace; do not assume its MAP is valid.

items.title: Describe the fast flush test.
items.q: Describe the fast flush test.
items.a:
- Flush briefly and watch the trace.
- Count oscillations after the flush and measure the amplitude ratio.
- One or two oscillations: optimal.
- Many oscillations: under-damped. None: over-damped.


> **Closing point:** Fast flush gives natural frequency and damping.

items.title: What are the complications of radial artery cannulation?
items.q: What are the complications of radial artery cannulation?
items.a:
- Haematoma and bleeding.
- Thrombosis and distal ischaemia (rare).
- Infection.
- Vasospasm and inaccurate readings.
- Nerve injury and arterial injection of drugs.


> **Closing point:** Most radial lines are removed without sequelae.

items.title: What are the problems of non-invasive BP in morbid obesity?
items.q: What are the problems of non-invasive BP in morbid obesity?
items.a:
- Cuff too small gives falsely high readings; too large falsely low.
- Conical arms prevent a good fit.
- Oscillometric devices have errors in obesity.
- Options: forearm or wrist cuff, appropriately sized cuff, invasive arterial line.


> **Closing point:** Cuff bladder should cover 80% of arm circumference.

items.title: Why does peripheral systolic pressure exceed central?
items.q: Why does peripheral systolic pressure exceed central?
items.a:
- Wave reflection and tapering of arteries.
- Systolic higher and diastolic lower distally.
- Mean pressure slightly lower.
- Effect lessens in elderly and with vasodilation.


> **Closing point:** Mean and diastolic pressures vary little.

items.title: Give the formula for oxygen delivery and its normal value.
items.q: Give the formula for oxygen delivery and its normal value.
items.a:
- DO2 = CO × CaO2 × 10 when CO is L/min and CaO2 is mL/dL.
- CaO2 = Hb × 1.34 × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2, with Hb g/dL, saturation as a fraction and PaO2 mmHg; convert NZ g/L/kPa values first.
- Normal about 1000 mL/min (500 to 600 mL/min/m²).
- Consumption about 250 mL/min; extraction ratio 25%.


> **Closing point:** Delivery depends on flow, haemoglobin and saturation.

items.title: What does a high ScvO2 or SvO2 mean?
items.q: What does a high ScvO2 or SvO2 mean?
items.a:
- Reduced extraction (sepsis, mitochondrial dysfunction).
- Shunting or arteriovenous shunt.
- Wedged PA catheter.
- Hypothermia, cyanide, or high oxygen delivery.


> **Closing point:** Normal does not exclude tissue hypoxia.

items.title: List causes of raised lactate.
items.q: List causes of raised lactate.
items.a:
- Type A: tissue hypoxia (shock, regional ischaemia, hypoxaemia, severe anaemia).
- Type B: adrenaline or beta-agonists, liver failure, metformin, thiamine deficiency, malignancy.
- Seizures and exercise.
- Serial change informs assessment; treat the cause, not lactate normalisation with repeated fluid.


> **Closing point:** Interpret lactate with the clinical context.

items.title: What patients benefit from goal-directed therapy?
items.q: What patients benefit from goal-directed therapy?
items.a:
- Consider flow monitoring for selected patients with significant risk, persistent instability or uncertain haemodynamics.
- Match it to the operation, physiology and an actionable treatment question.
- Older pooled benefits are not proof of benefit in every high-risk patient.
- Avoid routine fluid loading or inotrope solely to reach a monitor target.


> **Closing point:** Target the patients who are most at risk.

items.title: What did the OPTIMISE trials show?
items.q: What did the OPTIMISE trials show?
items.a:
- OPTIMISE (2014): cardiac-output-guided protocol, not significant on primary outcome; meta-analysis suggests fewer complications.
- OPTIMISE II (2024): infection 23.2% versus 22.7%; early cardiac events 3.0% versus 1.7% with the tested CO-guided fluid plus routine-inotrope protocol.
- This neutral/harm signal is protocol-specific and does not establish that every flow-monitoring strategy is ineffective.
- Mortality benefit not shown.


> **Closing point:** Verify trial numbers before quoting.

Source: BJA Educ

items.title: What are the capillary refill time findings in sepsis resuscitation?
items.q: What are the capillary refill time findings in sepsis resuscitation?
items.a:
- Normal is under 3 seconds (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK target).
- ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2019: mortality difference was not statistically significant in a superiority trial; it did not prove non-inferiority.
- ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025): personalised CRT-based protocol improved a hierarchical composite (win ratio 1.16), mainly through shorter vital support; not a stand-alone mortality benefit.
- Faster, cheaper and bedside.
- Mottling score adds information.


> **Closing point:** Clinical perfusion indicators are useful targets.

Source: BJA Educ

items.title: What are the principles of fluids in sepsis?
items.q: What are the principles of fluids in sepsis?
items.a:
- Balanced crystalloid first.
- Assess hypoperfusion, responsiveness and tolerance separately; CRT is a perfusion marker, not a responsiveness test.
- Positive balance and high CVP link to harm.
- Noradrenaline for persistent vasoplegia; concurrent fluid/vasopressors may be needed in unstable shock.
- After stabilisation, stop unnecessary inputs and consider monitored diuresis for harmful overload; avoid routine ultrafiltration without an indication.


> **Closing point:** Fluid is a drug with a dose.

Source: BJA Educ 2026

items.title: What determines flow through a cannula?
items.q: What determines flow through a cannula?
items.a:
- Hagen-Poiseuille: flow proportional to radius to the fourth power.
- Inversely proportional to length and viscosity.
- Pressure bag increases the driving pressure.
- Short, wide catheter: highest flow.


> **Closing point:** Halving the radius cuts flow sixteen-fold.

items.title: Give typical flow rates for 14G, 16G and 18G cannulas.
items.q: Give typical flow rates for 14G, 16G and 18G cannulas.
items.a:
- 14G: about 270 mL/min.
- 16G: about 180 mL/min.
- 18G: about 90 mL/min.
- Rapid infusers can exceed 500 mL/min.


> **Closing point:** The colour-coded rates are for water, not blood.

items.title: What are the contraindications to intraosseous access?
items.q: What are the contraindications to intraosseous access?
items.a:
- Fracture or recent IO in that bone.
- Infection at the site.
- Prosthetic joint or surgery at the site.
- Bone disease such as osteogenesis imperfecta requires device/site-specific assessment; use the manufacturer contraindications rather than treating every osteoporosis diagnosis as an absolute ban.


> **Closing point:** Choose another bone if one is not suitable.

items.title: What are the complications of intraosseous access?
items.q: What are the complications of intraosseous access?
items.a:
- Extravasation and compartment syndrome.
- Infection and osteomyelitis.
- Fat embolism and growth plate damage (rare).
- Fracture and failure to position.


> **Closing point:** Replace with suitable definitive access as soon as practical; respect the IO device/local maximum dwell time (often 24 h).

items.title: Which strategies improve peripheral cannulation success?
items.q: Which strategies improve peripheral cannulation success?
items.a:
- Warm the limb, dependent position, tourniquet, hydration.
- Ultrasound guidance.
- Appropriate site and size.
- Experienced operator after two attempts.


> **Closing point:** Plan for the difficult patient.

items.title: How do balanced solutions differ from 0.9% saline?
items.q: How do balanced solutions differ from 0.9% saline?
items.a:
- Saline: sodium 154, chloride 154 mmol/L; strong ion difference zero.
- Balanced solutions have chloride 98 to 110 and a buffer (lactate, acetate, gluconate).
- Large saline volumes cause hyperchloraemic acidosis and possible AKI.
- SMART found a small reduction in a composite kidney outcome; PLUS found no significant 90-day mortality difference. They do not show identical results.


> **Closing point:** Choose balanced crystalloid unless a specific reason exists.

items.title: What is the role of restrictive versus liberal perioperative fluid?
items.q: What is the role of restrictive versus liberal perioperative fluid?
items.a:
- Restrictive and liberal both have harm.
- RELIEF (2018): restrictive regimen did not improve disability-free survival and raised AKI.
- Aim for adequate perfusion without congestion; zero arithmetic balance is not a universal target.
- Use vasopressors rather than fluid for anaesthetic vasodilation.


> **Closing point:** The extremes are worse than the middle.

items.title: What are the harms of synthetic starches?
items.q: What are the harms of synthetic starches?
items.a:
- Increased AKI and renal replacement therapy.
- 6S found increased mortality and RRT in severe sepsis; CHEST found increased RRT without a significant mortality difference.
- Coagulopathy.
- Regulators restrict their use.


> **Closing point:** Avoid hydroxyethyl starch in critically ill patients.

items.title: What are the complication rates by central venous site?
items.q: What are the complication rates by central venous site?
items.a:
- IJ: compressible and accessible to ultrasound; arterial injury/haematoma and pneumothorax remain possible.
- Subclavian/axillary: comfortable with infection/thrombosis advantages in some trials, but bleeding, pleural injury and future dialysis access matter.
- Femoral: useful and compressible; consider retroperitoneal bleeding, thrombosis, hip flexion and site care.
- Rates depend on population, ultrasound, operator, attempts and duration; historical percentages are not universal contemporary risks.


> **Closing point:** Select the site for this patient; there is no universal ranking of total complications.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: How do you prevent vascular injury during IJ cannulation?
items.q: How do you prevent vascular injury during IJ cannulation?
items.a:
- Real-time ultrasound; follow the tip in a competent short-/long-axis or oblique technique.
- Trendelenburg with head rotation below 45 degrees.
- Confirm the wire in the vein by ultrasound before dilating.
- Transduce pressure or check a blood gas before dilation.


> **Closing point:** Check before you dilate.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: How do you manage an inadvertent carotid arterial catheter?
items.q: How do you manage an inadvertent carotid arterial catheter?
items.a:
- Small needle: remove and press for 5 to 10 minutes.
- Large-bore dilator or catheter: do not simply pull.
- Obtain imaging and vascular or endovascular surgery advice.
- Plan for stroke and haemorrhage risk.


> **Closing point:** Large-bore arterial injury needs a plan before removal.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: What are the PAC waveforms and normal values?
items.q: What are the PAC waveforms and normal values?
items.a:
- RA: mean 2 to 8 mmHg.
- RV: 15 to 30 / 0 to 8 mmHg.
- PA: 15 to 30 / 4 to 12 mmHg (mean about 15).
- Wedge: 6 to 12 mmHg.


> **Closing point:** RV diastolic pressure falls; PA diastolic steps up.

items.title: What are the complications of a PA catheter?
items.q: What are the complications of a PA catheter?
items.a:
- Arrhythmia (RBBB, complete heart block with LBBB).
- PA rupture, pulmonary infarction.
- Knotting, valve damage.
- Infection and thrombosis.


> **Closing point:** Never leave the balloon inflated or the catheter wedged.

items.title: Where is the central venous catheter tip best placed?
items.q: Where is the central venous catheter tip best placed?
items.a:
- At the atriocaval junction (lower SVC / upper RA).
- Check on chest X-ray, ECG guidance or fluoroscopy.
- Too deep risks arrhythmia, perforation and tamponade.
- Too shallow or malpositioned can cause dysfunction/thrombosis; assess device and anatomy.


> **Closing point:** Confirm position through the applicable pathway; a saline bubble/swirl test does not precisely localise the tip.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: 1. Methods of estimating cardiac output in the critically ill
items.q: Evaluate the methods available for estimating cardiac output in a critically ill patient.
items.a:
## Principles

| Method | Principle | Strength | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fick** | CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2) | Reference standard in theory | Needs a true mixed venous sample and measured oxygen consumption; assumed VO2 adds error. Match content/flow units |
| **Thermodilution** (PAC, transpulmonary) | Stewart-Hamilton: area under the temperature-time curve is inversely related to CO | Widely used standard | Errors with tricuspid regurgitation, shunt, arrhythmia, injectate temperature and volume, respiratory variation |
| **Indicator dilution** (lithium, dye) | Dilution curve | Calibration for pulse contour | Needs a drug and sampling; interference (muscle relaxants for lithium) |
| **Pulse contour** | Arterial waveform area proportional to stroke volume | Continuous, minimally invasive | Depends on compliance and damping; arrhythmia and IABP |
| **Doppler** (oesophageal, echo) | CO = VTI x cross-sectional area x heart rate | Non-invasive, bedside | Beam angle error; aortic area assumed; operator skill |
| **Bioimpedance and bioreactance** | Thoracic electrical signal | Non-invasive | Oedema, arrhythmia and diathermy |
| **Partial CO2 rebreathing** | Fick principle using CO2 | Non-invasive | Needs controlled ventilation and accurate gas exchange; shunt/dead-space/VQ abnormalities confound estimates |
| **Clinical** | Perfusion signs, lactate, ScvO2 | No equipment | Poor accuracy |

## Judging a monitor

Compare with a reference by **Bland-Altman analysis**; a **30% percentage-error criterion is historical**, not a universal pass mark. Absolute agreement and **tracking change** answer different questions; assess bias, limits of agreement, reference precision and whether a measured change exceeds noise.

## Choosing

Consider invasiveness, patient factors (arrhythmia, valve disease, shock, open chest), required update rate, available skills, and whether the question is diagnostic (echo, PAC) or a trend (pulse contour). Combine methods and judge them against clinical perfusion.

## Evidence

No monitor guarantees outcome benefit. A reliable measurement must lead to appropriate treatment; a protocol can also be neutral or harmful if its intervention is inappropriate.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes Fick and thermodilution with the formula
- Describes at least four further methods
- Gives a strength and a limitation for each
- Mentions percentage error and tracking ability
- Gives criteria for choosing
- Links measurements to appropriate treatment without assuming every protocol improves outcomes

items.title: 2. Continuous cardiac output monitors and pulse contour analysis
items.q: Evaluate the role of continuous cardiac output monitoring devices, including pulse contour analysis, in the perioperative period.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** Older goal-directed-therapy teaching must be interpreted alongside OPTIMISE II (2024) and current shock guidance; see the source key.

## Why monitor flow

Blood pressure is a poor surrogate for flow: it can look normal while cardiac output is inadequate (vasoconstriction) or fall while flow is preserved (vasodilation). Cardiac output (CO) monitoring lets you guide fluid, inotrope and vasopressor therapy in high-risk surgery, shock and complex cardiac or hepatic cases.

## Device types

| Type | Examples | Principle | Main limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pulse contour, **calibrated** | PiCCO, LiDCO | Arterial waveform area plus calibration by transpulmonary thermodilution or lithium dilution | Needs arterial and central or lithium access; recalibrate with changing vascular tone |
| Pulse contour, **uncalibrated** | FloTrac, MostCare | Device-specific waveform model; MostCare/PRAM does not simply use demographic calibration | Less accurate when vascular tone changes (vasoplegia, vasopressors) |
| **Oesophageal Doppler** | CardioQ | Descending aortic velocity and flow time | Operator and probe position; often poorly tolerated awake |
| **Bioimpedance and bioreactance** | NICOM | Thoracic electrical signals | Reduced accuracy with oedema, arrhythmia, diathermy |
| **Finger-cuff volume clamp** | ClearSight | Continuous pressure and algorithm | Poor perfusion, oedema, vasopressors |
| **Echocardiography** | TTE, TOE | LVOT VTI and area | Intermittent; operator dependent |
| **PA catheter** | Thermodilution | Common comparator in trials, with its own measurement error | Invasive, risks |

## Evaluation

**Advantages:** selected devices can track flow/response in real time with less invasiveness than a PAC; some provide **dynamic indices** (SVV/PPV) and can support a treatment protocol. Clinical benefit depends on patient selection, measurement reliability and the treatment chosen, not simply fitting a monitor.

**Limitations:** accuracy of agreement with thermodilution is limited (historical interchangeability criterion around 30%, dependent on reference precision and context); arrhythmia, aortic regurgitation, IABP, damped traces, vasoconstriction and changes in vascular compliance disturb pulse contour; monitors measure trends, not absolute truth; benefits depend on a **protocol** and acting on the data.

## Preop

Use a minimally invasive device for high-risk surgery with expected fluid shifts, add echo for diagnosis, and consider a PAC for selected right-heart/PH or complex shock questions.

## Intraop

Validate the waveform/calibration and the conditions for any dynamic index. Treat the cause of low flow/pressure and remeasure response; combine the device with clinical examination and echo when needed.

## Postop

Continue only while measurements can change care; reassess perfusion, congestion and need for invasive devices, and document a handover/removal plan.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains why flow, not pressure, matters
- Classifies devices and states the principle of each
- Distinguishes calibrated from uncalibrated pulse contour
- Lists limitations of accuracy and validity conditions
- Mentions dynamic indices and goal-directed protocols
- Notes uncertain mortality benefit
- Gives a rationale for choosing a device

items.title: 3. Central venous pressure: evaluate its place in perioperative fluid management
items.q: Discuss the limitations of central venous pressure (CVP) for assessing intravascular volume and fluid responsiveness. In what circumstances is CVP still clinically useful?
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would begin by defining what CVP actually measures, then separate three reasons it is a poor “volume-status” test: measurement error, physiological confounding and the weak relationship between static pressure and preload responsiveness. I would finish by explaining the limited but genuine information CVP still provides when interpreted as a waveform, trend and congestion/right-heart variable.

## 1. What CVP is

CVP is an estimate of right atrial pressure when the catheter tip, transducer level and pressure system are appropriate. It reflects the interaction of venous return, right-ventricular function, venous capacitance, intrathoracic/pericardial pressure, pulmonary vascular load and intra-abdominal pressure. It is therefore a pressure at one point in the circulation, not a direct measurement of circulating blood volume.

## 2. Measurement limitations
- Incorrect leveling or zeroing causes a systematic pressure error; the transducer must be referenced to the right atrium and re-leveled after substantial position change.
- Air bubbles, clot, compliant tubing, partial catheter occlusion or inappropriate respiratory timing can distort the waveform/value.
- Positive-pressure ventilation and PEEP alter measured right-atrial pressure; the airway pressure component does not necessarily represent an increase in transmural filling pressure.
- One isolated measurement is especially weak. A consistently measured trend linked to a specific intervention is more informative.

## 3. Physiological confounders unrelated to blood volume

| Cause of high/low CVP | Why it confounds “volume status” |
|---|---|
| RV failure / pulmonary hypertension / PE | High right-sided pressure may coexist with low LV filling and poor output; more fluid can worsen RV dilation and congestion. |
| Tricuspid regurgitation | Large systolic v waves and elevated mean pressure may reflect regurgitation rather than useful preload. |
| Tamponade / constriction | Pericardial constraint raises right-sided pressure despite impaired filling/flow. |
| High PEEP / high intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure | External pressure raises measured CVP independent of circulating volume. |
| Venodilation / altered venous capacitance | CVP may be low despite reasonable total blood volume. |

## 4. Why CVP poorly predicts fluid responsiveness

Fluid responsiveness depends on the slope of the ventricular Frank–Starling relationship, not simply on a filling pressure. The same CVP can occur on the steep or flat part of that curve depending on RV/LV function, vascular tone and external pressures. Therefore a “low CVP” should not be used as a fluid trigger and a “high CVP” does not by itself exclude preload responsiveness.

## 5. What CVP is still useful for
- Right-sided filling-pressure context and recognition of venous congestion, particularly when combined with echo and organ-congestion findings.
- Waveform interpretation: a/v waves, AV dissociation, tricuspid regurgitation and selected pericardial physiology.
- Trend during a controlled intervention when the measurement conditions are unchanged.
- A component of a broader haemodynamic assessment in RV failure, pulmonary hypertension and complex shock — not the sole decision-maker.

items.title: 4. Predicting fluid responsiveness: methods and limits
items.q: Compare the methods available to predict whether a haemodynamically unstable patient will respond to fluid, with their limitations.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Assessing dynamic fluid-responsiveness" (BJA Educ 2018): only about 50% of patients with shock are fluid responsive; dynamic measures based on heart-lung interactions are the cornerstone; an actual or reversible preload challenge can test response; the response definition and monitor precision matter.

## Why it matters

Fluid is a drug: giving it to non-responders risks oedema, raised venous pressure and organ dysfunction. **Fluid responsiveness** means stroke volume rises by about 10 to 15% after a bolus.

## Static measures (poor)

CVP, PAOP, end-diastolic volumes and IVC diameter do not reliably predict response. Extreme values may change probability but are not a stand-alone fluid indication.

## Dynamic measures

| Method | Principle | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| **Pulse pressure variation (PPV) and stroke volume variation (SVV)** | Heart-lung interaction: above 12 to 13% suggests responsiveness | Needs controlled ventilation and accurate gas exchange; shunt/dead-space/VQ abnormalities confound estimates with sufficient tidal volume (classically around 8 mL/kg predicted body weight); do not prescribe injurious ventilation to validate a test, sinus rhythm, closed chest; unreliable with spontaneous breathing, low tidal volume, arrhythmia, RV failure, high abdominal pressure or low HR/RR ratio (roughly <3.6) |
| **Passive leg raise** with CO measurement | Autotransfusion of about 300 mL, reversible | Needs a direct flow measurement (not BP); pain or intra-abdominal hypertension limits |
| **End-expiratory occlusion test** | 15-second hold increases preload | Mechanically ventilated, able to tolerate a brief expiratory hold without interruption; sufficiently precise rapid flow monitor |
| **Mini fluid challenge** (100 to 250 mL) | Small bolus with flow measurement | Needs a precise monitor |
| **Echocardiography** | LVOT VTI variation, IVC distensibility, LV cavity | Operator and window; IVC unreliable in many conditions |
| **Pleth variability index** | Finger waveform variation | Vasoconstriction, poor perfusion |

## Practical approach

Use a dynamic test with a **flow-based** endpoint (stroke volume, VTI, CO), ensure the test's conditions are met, and combine with clinical context, lactate and perfusion. Responsiveness is not an indication by itself: give fluid for a plausible perfusion benefit only when tolerance is acceptable; stop for absent response, resolved need or congestion.

## Self-marking checklist

- States that static indices (CVP, PAOP) predict poorly
- Explains fluid responsiveness and the rise in stroke volume
- Describes PPV and SVV with threshold and validity conditions
- Describes passive leg raise and states a flow measure is needed
- Mentions fluid challenge, end-expiratory occlusion and echo
- Gives limitations for each
- Gives a practical combined approach

items.title: 5. Interpreting pulmonary artery catheter data in shock
items.q: Discuss how you would interpret the data from a pulmonary artery catheter in a patient with shock of uncertain cause.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Pulmonary artery catheterisation" (BJA Educ 2024): the PAC is valuable "in the right patient, setting and heart"; recent RCTs showed no outcome benefit.

## Data available

Right atrial (RA), right ventricular, pulmonary artery (PA) pressures, **pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP)**, cardiac output and index, SvO2, and derived SVR and PVR.

| Normal values | |
|---|---|
| RA | 2 to 8 mmHg |
| PA | 15 to 30 / 4 to 12 (mean 9 to 18) |
| PAOP | 6 to 12 |
| CI | 2.5 to 4.0 L/min/m2 |
| SVR | 800 to 1200 dyn.s/cm5 |
| PVR | Approximately 0.5–2 Wood units (40–160 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵); >2 WU is elevated in current precapillary PH definitions |
| SvO2 | 65 to 75% |

## Profiles in shock

| Shock | CO | PAOP / RA | SVR | SvO2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hypovolaemic | Low | Low | High | Low |
| Cardiogenic (LV) | Low | High PAOP | High | Low |
| RV failure or PE | Low | High RA, low or normal PAOP | High | Low |
| Distributive (septic) | High or normal | Low or normal | Low | High or normal |
| Tamponade | Low | Often converging raised diastolic pressures; not invariably equal | High | Low |

## Pitfalls

- **PAOP** is a poor index of volume: affected by PEEP, mitral disease, ventricular compliance, pulmonary hypertension and wedge position (zone 3).
- Respiratory variation (read at end-expiration), damping, transducer level and tricuspid regurgitation (thermodilution error).
- Interpret credible absolute values **and trends/responses**; neither trend tracking nor a plausible number excuses an invalid measurement.

## Use in practice

Titrate fluid, inotropes, vasopressors and pulmonary vasodilators; separate left from right ventricular failure; diagnose and classify pulmonary hypertension (right heart catheterisation is required).

## Self-marking checklist

- Lists the measured and derived parameters
- Gives normal values for key variables
- Interprets profiles for at least 4 shock types
- States pitfalls of PAOP and thermodilution
- Emphasises trend and response to therapy
- Gives clinical uses including pulmonary hypertension

items.title: 6. Pulmonary artery catheter: evaluate its role in anaesthesia
items.q: Evaluate the use of a pulmonary artery catheter (PAC) in perioperative anaesthetic practice. Include what it measures, when it may be useful, how the information changes management, limitations and important complications.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would evaluate the PAC rather than list parameters. I would explain the unique information it provides, identify patients in whom that information is actionable, show how the measurements change therapy, then balance this against invasiveness, measurement assumptions, serious complications and less invasive alternatives.

## 1. What the PAC adds

| Variable | Clinical use |
|---|---|
| RA/CVP | Right-sided pressure and congestion context; waveform. |
| PA pressure | Pulmonary vascular/RV afterload; response to pulmonary vasodilators and ventilatory changes. |
| PAOP/PAWP | Estimate of left-atrial pressure only when assumptions are valid; can help separate left-sided filling-pressure elevation from isolated pulmonary vascular/RV problems. |
| Thermodilution CO/CI | Quantifies flow and response to fluid, vasoactive and inotropic therapy. |
| SvO₂ | Global balance of O₂ delivery and consumption; interpreted with Hb, SaO₂, CO and metabolic demand. |
| Derived SVR/PVR | Describes systemic/pulmonary vascular load; useful when linked to pressure and CO rather than treated as stand-alone targets. |

## 2. Situations where I can justify it
- Severe pulmonary hypertension or complex RV failure where PA pressure, PVR, CO and SvO₂ will guide vasopressor, inotrope and pulmonary vasodilator therapy.
- Selected complex cardiac surgery and mechanical circulatory-support settings.
- Refractory or mixed shock in which initial echo/less invasive monitoring has not resolved the mechanism and continuous invasive data will alter management.
- Cases requiring repeated pulmonary haemodynamic measurements over time when intermittent echo is insufficient.

## 3. How the information changes treatment

For example, low systemic pressure with low CO and high PA pressure/RV failure suggests a very different treatment from low pressure with high CO/low SVR. In RV failure I may prioritise systemic perfusion pressure, reduce pulmonary vascular resistance, optimise ventilation and use inotropy rather than giving repeated fluid. A low SvO₂ may prompt me to examine CO, Hb, SaO₂ and metabolic demand instead of chasing one target. PAOP and echo together can help clarify whether pulmonary oedema is related to high left-sided filling pressure or another mechanism.

## 4. Limitations and safety
- PAOP and CVP are pressures, not blood-volume measurements, and are affected by PEEP, ventricular compliance, valve disease and catheter position.
- Thermodilution has errors with tricuspid regurgitation, intracardiac shunts and inconsistent injection/respiratory timing.
- Insertion/use can cause arrhythmias, right bundle-branch block, infection/thrombosis, knotting, valvular injury, pulmonary infarction and rare catastrophic pulmonary artery rupture.
- Routine PAC use has not shown a universal survival benefit. Benefit depends on appropriate selection, correct interpretation and a treatment strategy that can respond to the data.
- TTE/TOE and less invasive CO systems answer many questions with lower procedural risk, although they may be intermittent or less comprehensive for pulmonary haemodynamics.

## 5. PAOP and derived-variable pitfalls

| Variable | Potential trap | How I would protect against it |
|---|---|---|
| PAOP/PAWP | PEEP, West-zone position, mitral disease, pulmonary venous disease and altered LV compliance can make it a poor surrogate for LV preload. | Measure carefully at a consistent respiratory phase and interpret with echo/clinical context rather than treating it as “LV volume”. |
| SVR/PVR | They are calculated from pressure gradients and CO, so measurement error is compounded. | Use them to describe physiology and trends, not as isolated treatment targets. |
| SvO₂ | Low value has multiple causes; normal/high values can occur in distributive shock. | Interpret with Hb, SaO₂, CO and metabolic demand. |
| Thermodilution CO | Tricuspid regurgitation, shunts and inconsistent injection/respiratory timing alter measurements. | Repeat consistent measurements and compare with clinical/echo data. |

## 6. Overall judgement

I would not insert a PAC to obtain more numbers. I would use it when its unique combination of continuous pulmonary pressures, flow and mixed venous oxygenation is likely to resolve an important uncertainty and change therapy more reliably than a less invasive alternative.

**Examiner lens:** The 2023.2 report explicitly warned that “evaluate” requires more than a list. Better answers linked CO, pulmonary pressures, SvO₂/PAOP and derived variables to fluid, vasopressor, inotrope and pulmonary-vasodilator decisions, acknowledged pulmonary artery rupture/arrhythmias, compared less invasive alternatives and recognised the lack of routine survival benefit.

items.title: 7. Choosing monitoring to guide fluids in major abdominal surgery
items.q: Discuss the appropriate choice of monitoring devices to guide fluid management in a patient having major abdominal surgery.
items.a:
## Principle

Choose monitoring according to **patient risk, surgery and expected fluid shifts**, the question being asked, and the skills available. More monitoring is not always better.

## Preop

### Tiered approach

| Level | Patient and surgery | Monitoring |
|---|---|---|
| **Basic** | Low-risk, minor surgery | Appropriate PG18 monitoring plus clinical perfusion/fluid assessment; urinary catheterisation is not mandatory for every case |
| **Intermediate** | Moderate surgery | Arterial line for beat-to-beat pressure, lactate and gases, pleth variability, capnography, urine output |
| **Advanced** | High-risk patient or major surgery (major abdominal, vascular, hepatobiliary), anticipated large shifts or cardiorespiratory disease | Consider CO monitoring with an actionable question; SVV/PPV only if valid, echo for diagnosis, and central access when the therapy/access need warrants it |
| **Specialised** | Selected severe PH/RV failure, transplantation or complex shock | Consider PAC and/or TOE according to the unanswered question, risks and skills |

## Intraop

### Relevant parameters

- **Flow:** stroke volume, CO, response to a fluid challenge.
- **Dynamic indices:** SVV and PPV (with their conditions of validity).
- **Perfusion:** lactate, base deficit, ScvO2, urine output, capillary refill.
- **Static values** (CVP) may identify congestion/pressure change but neither a value nor trend alone predicts fluid response.

## Limitations to consider

Patient (arrhythmia, spontaneous breathing, obesity), surgery (open abdomen, laparoscopy, positioning), device (calibration, accuracy), and the time to act on results.

## Evidence

Older pooled studies suggested fewer complications or shorter stay, but trial populations/protocols differ and modern neutral trials prevent a universal benefit claim. OPTIMISE II (2024) tested CO-guided fluid plus routine low-dose inotrope: infections 23.2% versus 22.7%, adjusted OR 1.03 (95% CI 0.84–1.25); early cardiac events 3.0% versus 1.7%. Reserve fluids/inotropes for an identified need; monitoring alone is not a treatment.

## Postop

Continue selected monitoring only while it can alter care; reassess perfusion, congestion, oral intake and device removal. Provide a response-focused handover rather than a list of monitor values.

## Self-marking checklist

- States that monitoring is chosen by risk and surgery
- Gives a tiered approach from basic to advanced
- Lists flow, dynamic and perfusion parameters
- Explains CVP as a pressure/congestion adjunct, not a volume or response predictor
- Lists limitations affecting device choice
- Mentions evidence for goal-directed protocols

items.title: 8. A basic haemodynamic echo assessment (TTE and TOE)
items.q: Outline a basic haemodynamic assessment using transthoracic or transoesophageal echocardiography.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2015, "Goal-directed transthoracic echocardiography" (Dennis): a goal-directed scan is a short, point-of-care study by a trained operator that identifies major abnormalities and guides treatment; a negative limited study does not exclude every cause. PG46 and PG47 (2025) now distinguish echo/POCUS training and scope.

## Aim

A brief, repeatable examination answering: **is it the LV, the RV, volume, valves or the pericardium?**

## A reproducible clinical sequence

Assess LV, RV, valves, pericardium, filling/congestion and flow, integrated with lung/vascular imaging and the clinical examination. This is a teaching sequence, not an ANZCA-mandated acronym.

## Views and what to look for

| Window or view | Findings |
|---|---|
| **Parasternal long axis** | LV size and function, aortic root, LA, mitral and aortic valves, pericardial effusion |
| **Parasternal short axis (papillary level)** | Global LV function, wall motion, septal flattening (D-shaped septum in RV pressure overload) |
| **Apical four-chamber** | Chamber sizes (RV:LV ratio), LV and RV function (TAPSE), mitral and tricuspid regurgitation |
| **Subcostal** | Pericardial effusion, RV, **IVC size and collapse** |
| **TOE: mid-oesophageal four-chamber and transgastric mid short-axis** | Repeated LV assessment; the mid short-axis view misses basal/apical disease |

## Systematic assessment

- **1.** **LV:** size, global function (hyperdynamic, normal, poor), regional wall motion.
- **2.** **RV:** size relative to LV, function, septal position.
- **3.** **Filling and tolerance:** integrate chamber size, RV function, venous congestion and lung findings; a small LV/IVC alone does not diagnose fluid need.
- **4.** **Valves:** gross stenosis or regurgitation.
- **5.** **Pericardium:** effusion and tamponade signs.
- **6.** **Dynamic:** VTI change with fluid or leg raise.

## Limits

Windows, operator skill and interpretation; refer for comprehensive study when findings are complex. TOE permits repeated imaging with an indwelling probe but remains operator-dependent and invasive.

## Self-marking checklist

- States aim and the focused nature of a goal-directed study
- Lists standard views and the findings in each
- Covers LV, RV, volume, valves and pericardium
- Mentions IVC and septal flattening
- Describes response to therapy with VTI or volume challenge
- Mentions TOE views and training standards

items.title: 9. Doppler echo: stroke volume, cardiac output and pressures
items.q: Describe how Doppler echocardiography can be used to estimate stroke volume, cardiac output and intracardiac pressures, and the sources of error.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Quantitative Doppler echocardiography" (BJA Educ 2016): the only directly measurable variables are length (2D) and velocity (spectral Doppler); velocity-time integral (VTI) underlies most calculations; beam alignment is critical; pressure gradient is estimated by the simplified Bernoulli equation.

## Principles

- **Pulsed-wave Doppler** measures slower velocities at a chosen depth; **continuous-wave Doppler** measures any velocity along the beam without depth information.
- The area under the velocity-time curve is the **VTI**, the distance a column of blood travels with each beat.

## Calculations

| Quantity | Method |
|---|---|
| **Stroke volume** | VTI at the LVOT x LVOT cross-sectional area (pi x (diameter/2)^2) |
| **Cardiac output** | Stroke volume x heart rate |
| **Pressure gradient** | **P = 4V^2** (simplified Bernoulli) across a stenosis or regurgitant jet |
| **RV systolic pressure** | 4 × (TR velocity)^2 + estimated RA pressure; approximates PASP only without pulmonary/RVOT obstruction |
| **LV filling pressure** | Integrate E/e′ with mitral inflow, e′, LA size/strain, TR/PASP, rhythm, valve and loading conditions; E/e′ alone cannot grade diastolic dysfunction |
| **Fluid responsiveness** | Respiratory variation of LVOT VTI, or its rise after leg raise |

## Sources of error

- **Beam alignment:** the beam must be parallel to flow (angle correction is unreliable); poor alignment underestimates velocity.
- **LVOT diameter measurement error** is squared in the area; it is the greatest source of absolute error for CO, so trend with VTI is more reliable.
- Assumptions: laminar flow, circular LVOT, stable heart rhythm (average several beats in AF), no significant aortic regurgitation or shunt.
- Poor image, high heart rate, respiratory variation and operator experience.

## Self-marking checklist

- Distinguishes pulsed-wave from continuous-wave Doppler
- Defines VTI and uses it for stroke volume and cardiac output
- Quotes the simplified Bernoulli equation
- Gives RV systolic pressure or E/e' estimates
- Notes beam alignment as a key error
- Notes that LVOT diameter error is squared and trending VTI is more reliable

items.title: 10. TTE in the haemodynamically unstable anaesthetised patient
items.q: Evaluate the use of transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in a haemodynamically unstable patient under general anaesthesia.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would answer the exact question: intraoperative TTE in an unstable patient. I would evaluate its value as a rapid mechanism-finding and treatment-response tool, outline a focused scan, then balance this against intraoperative access, image quality, operator/training and time limitations. I would not turn the answer into a generic essay on TOE or preoperative echo.

## 1. Why TTE is useful in acute instability
- Rapidly differentiates major shock phenotypes: LV failure, RV failure/pressure overload, tamponade, gross underfilling/vasodilation and selected major valvular/mechanical causes.
- Can be repeated after fluid, vasopressor, inotrope, pulmonary vasodilator or decompression to determine whether the expected physiological response occurred.
- Provides anatomy and flow information that a pressure number cannot: the same MAP may occur with a small hyperdynamic LV, severe LV dysfunction or a dilated pressure-loaded RV.
- Can be integrated with lung POCUS for pulmonary oedema, pneumothorax or pleural pathology.

## 2. A focused TTE sequence

| Question | Views / findings | Management implication |
|---|---|---|
| LV? | PLAX/PSAX/apical: size and global/regional systolic function. | Low LV output → avoid blind fluid loading; address ischaemia, afterload, rhythm and consider inotropy where appropriate. |
| RV? | Apical/subcostal: RV:LV ratio, function, septal shape. | RV failure/pressure overload → support systemic pressure, reduce pulmonary vascular load, treat PE/ventilation cause, avoid RV overdistension. |
| Pericardium? | Subcostal/PLAX/apical: effusion and chamber interaction. | Tamponade physiology → urgent drainage strategy and careful preservation of venous return. |
| Forward flow / preload response? | LVOT VTI before/after PLR or small challenge. | Supports/argues against fluid only if fluid is clinically needed and tolerated. |
| Alternative major cause? | Valves/aortic root + lung POCUS adjunct. | May reveal acute MR/AR, LVOTO, pulmonary oedema or pneumothorax and redirect treatment. |

## 3. Advantages

TTE is non-invasive, available at the bedside, radiation-free and repeatable. It can provide immediate causal information during instability and can show whether treatment is working rather than relying on delayed laboratory or intermittent pressure data.

## 4. Limitations in the actual intraoperative setting
- Patient factors: obesity, hyperinflation/COPD, chest wall anatomy.
- Surgical factors: drapes, sterile field, positioning, pneumoperitoneum, open surgery and limited access to normal windows.
- Operator/training: a focused study can miss pathology and should not be over-interpreted as a comprehensive examination.
- Equipment/time: obtaining images must not delay treatment of obvious haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax or cardiac arrest.
- Intermittent rather than continuous information; TOE or invasive monitoring may be more suitable when continuous or higher-detail imaging is needed.

## 5. Translate the image into treatment

| Echo phenotype | What I would do next |
|---|---|
| Small/hyperdynamic LV + positive dynamic flow response | Look for true volume loss/vasodilation; give a small measured fluid bolus only if clinically indicated and tolerated, and use vasopressor if vascular tone remains the dominant problem. |
| Severe LV systolic dysfunction / new regional abnormality | Avoid repeated empirical fluid; support coronary perfusion, evaluate ischaemia/afterload/rhythm and consider inotropy or specialist escalation where appropriate. |
| Dilated failing RV / septal flattening | Maintain systemic pressure/RV perfusion, correct hypoxaemia/hypercapnia/acidosis, reduce pulmonary vascular load and treat the cause such as PE; avoid RV overdistension. |
| Tamponade physiology | Prioritise urgent drainage and preserve venous return/contractility until relieved. |
| No clear cardiac mechanism | Reassess haemorrhage, anaesthetic depth, tension pneumothorax, equipment and distributive causes; do not force an echo diagnosis. |

## 6. Overall evaluation

In an unstable anaesthetised patient, TTE is particularly valuable when the cause is uncertain and a rapid distinction between preload, LV, RV, obstructive and vasodilatory physiology will alter therapy. Its usefulness falls when windows/access are poor or when the operator cannot obtain/interpret a focused study reliably.

**Examiner lens:** The 2025.2 report said many candidates lost marks by giving generic uses or discussing TOE/preoperative echo. Strong answers stayed specific to intraoperative TTE, used it to distinguish shock states and assess response to therapy, and explicitly evaluated patient, surgical, training and equipment limitations.

items.title: 11. Point-of-care ultrasound in undifferentiated shock
items.q: Discuss the role of point-of-care ultrasound in the management of a patient with undifferentiated shock in the intensive care unit.
items.a:
> **Recent reading:** Flower et al., Point-of-care ultrasound in shock, BJA Education 2026;26:464–472. Full text directly reviewed through ANZCA ClinicalKey; integrated with current echo/POCUS guidance.

## Role

Shock types: distributive, hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive. Examination alone is unreliable. POCUS is **rapid, non-invasive and repeatable**, needs no transfer or radiation, and bedside echo is a first-line diagnostic tool in shock where expertise is available, with escalation for inadequate or complex studies.

## Findings by shock type

| Type | Ultrasound findings |
|---|---|
| **Hypovolaemic** | Small hyperdynamic LV/variable IVC may support the diagnosis in context; neither is specific; lung findings help assess tolerance |
| **Distributive** | Hyperdynamic LV (or septic cardiomyopathy); variable IVC |
| **Cardiogenic** | Poor LV function and dilated LV; B-lines; plethoric IVC |
| **Obstructive** | Tamponade (effusion, RA or RV collapse); pulmonary embolus (dilated RV, septal flattening, McConnell sign); pneumothorax (absent sliding is nonspecific; lung point supports pneumothorax but may be absent in a large/tension pneumothorax) |

Also assess lungs, abdomen and veins (DVT), directed by the suspected mechanism and source.

- **Lung/source assessment:** consolidation with dynamic air bronchograms supports pneumonia; a complex pleural collection raises concern for empyema. B-lines show an interstitial syndrome, not its cause. Lung sliding or a lung pulse excludes pneumothorax only at that point; absent sliding alone does not diagnose it.
- **Abdominal/source assessment:** free fluid needs clinical interpretation; hydronephrosis in urinary sepsis may indicate obstruction requiring urgent decompression. Ultrasound can support cholecystitis, but ICU gallbladder-wall thickening is nonspecific.
- **Safety:** a small, rapidly accumulating or loculated postoperative pericardial collection can cause tamponade without classic appearances. RV strain supports a differential, not a definitive diagnosis of PE.

## Guiding therapy

Fluid challenge response (measured VTI/SV change), congestion/tolerance and inotrope or vasopressor choice (ventricular function plus haemodynamics; echo does not directly measure SVR), and early intervention: **pericardiocentesis, pleural drainage** and line placement under ultrasound. Serial scans show the response and prompt changes. Document the question, image adequacy, findings, intervention and response; archive images and escalate inadequate or complex studies.

## Limitations

- Operator training and experience; risk of misinterpretation.
- Windows (ventilation, obesity, dressings, subcutaneous emphysema), intermittent nature.
- Overlapping or mixed shock states; static IVC measures are unreliable on positive pressure.
- Not a substitute for clinical assessment; formal echo may be needed.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes the four shock types and the role of POCUS in diagnosing them
- Gives findings in each shock type
- Describes use to guide fluid, vasopressors and inotropes
- Mentions procedural guidance (pericardiocentesis, drainage)
- Includes source-focused lung/abdominal assessment and diagnostic caveats
- Mentions serial reassessment, documentation and image archiving
- States limitations (training, windows, mixed states)

items.title: 12. TOE in non-cardiac surgery: indications, contraindications, complications
items.q: Discuss the indications, contraindications and complications of transoesophageal echocardiography for intraoperative haemodynamic monitoring in non-cardiac surgery.
items.a:
## Indications

- **Unexplained or persistent haemodynamic instability** when TTE fails or surgery blocks windows.
- Intraoperative monitoring in high-risk surgery: liver and lung transplantation, major vascular surgery, thoracoabdominal aneurysm, trauma, patients with known ventricular dysfunction or valve disease.
- Diagnosis of embolism (air, thrombus, fat), tamponade, acute LV or RV failure, ischaemia (new regional wall motion abnormality) and aortic dissection.
- Guiding volume and inotropic or vasopressor therapy; confirming placement of lines, cannulae and devices.

## Advantages

Continuous monitoring, excellent views not limited by the surgical field, quantitative Doppler and 3D, and rapid diagnosis in unstable patients.

## Contraindications

**Major contraindications:** oesophageal perforation or obstructing structural disease and active significant upper-GI bleeding. Diverticulum, recent surgery, varices, coagulopathy, dysphagia, radiotherapy and cervical-spine problems require case-specific risk/benefit assessment and sometimes specialist advice; classification varies between guidance.

## Complications

- **Oesophageal injury** (mucosal damage, haematoma, perforation; rare but serious), dental or lip injury, bleeding.
- Hoarseness, vocal cord and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, throat pain.
- Haemodynamic effects (hypotension, arrhythmia), airway displacement or endotracheal tube dislodgement, and compression of the left atrium or vessels in children.
- Prolonged use: heat injury to the oesophagus; infection control.

## Practical points

Check the swallowing history, gentle insertion under direct view or with a laryngoscope, avoid force, stop image acquisition/leave the probe safely neutral when not imaging, follow manufacturer dwell/temperature precautions and avoid unnecessary manipulation, and use the limited standard views (mid-oesophageal four-chamber, transgastric short-axis, long-axis, bicaval). Training is required (ANZCA PG46 (2025) and PG47 (2025)).

## Self-marking checklist

- Gives indications for intraoperative monitoring and diagnosis
- States advantages over TTE
- Lists absolute and relative contraindications
- Lists complications with oesophageal injury highlighted
- Gives practical safety points
- Mentions training requirement

items.title: 13. TTE versus TOE versus PAC in complex haemodynamic instability
items.q: Compare TTE, TOE and a pulmonary artery catheter for the assessment of complex perioperative haemodynamic instability. Give examples of when you would favour each.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would compare the three by the type of information they provide, invasiveness, continuity, access and operator dependence. They are complementary rather than mutually exclusive: echo is strongest for anatomy and mechanism, while a PAC is strongest for continuous pulmonary pressure/flow/SvO₂ data in selected complex physiology.

## 1. Comparison

| Feature | TTE | TOE | PAC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main information | Ventricular/pericardial/valve anatomy + flow; lung POCUS adjunct. | High-quality cardiac/valve/aortic imaging when TTE access poor. | RA/PA pressures, PAOP, CO/CI, SvO₂ and derived SVR/PVR. |
| Invasiveness | Non-invasive. | Semi-invasive oesophageal probe. | Invasive central/right-heart catheter. |
| Continuity | Intermittent. | Can be repeated/near-continuous intraoperatively. | Continuous pressure and often CO/SvO₂ trend. |
| Major strengths | Rapid shock phenotype; treatment response; no vascular instrumentation. | Excellent intraoperative windows and structural detail. | Serial pulmonary haemodynamics and flow/oxygen-balance data. |
| Limitations | Windows/access/operator dependent. | Oesophageal contraindications/injury, training, anaesthesia dependence. | Serious complications and measurement assumptions; no routine survival benefit. |

## 2. When I would favour TTE
- Initial unexplained hypotension/shock when windows are accessible and I need a rapid mechanism diagnosis.
- Serial bedside reassessment where a non-invasive study can answer the question.
- When lung POCUS and cardiac findings together are useful.

## 3. When I would favour TOE
- Intraoperative instability with poor TTE access due to drapes/position/open surgery.
- Need for detailed valve, aortic or surgical structural assessment in an appropriately trained setting.
- Continuous/repeated cardiac imaging during major cardiac/vascular surgery.

## 4. When I would favour a PAC
- Severe pulmonary hypertension or RV failure where serial PA pressure, PVR, CO and SvO₂ directly guide therapy.
- Selected complex cardiac surgery/mechanical support or refractory mixed shock when continuous invasive data add information that echo cannot provide continuously.

## 5. Overall judgement

I would usually start with the least invasive tool that can answer the clinical question. Echo often comes early because it identifies mechanism. A PAC is justified when its unique continuous pulmonary haemodynamic/flow information is actionable and outweighs procedural risk.

items.title: 16. Applying ANZCA monitoring standards in a remote anaesthetising location
items.q: You are asked to provide general anaesthesia for an interventional radiology procedure in a remote suite. Outline how you would determine whether the location, staffing, equipment and monitoring are adequate, and what monitoring you would apply.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would start with the principle that the standard of patient safety does not fall because the procedure occurs outside theatre. I would assess the patient/procedure risk and the environment against PS55, apply PG18 clinical observation and physiological monitoring, then add case-specific monitoring and ensure rescue/recovery/transfer capability.

## 1. Decide whether this patient/procedure belongs in this location
- Patient factors: airway, comorbidity, haemodynamic/respiratory reserve, obesity/OSA, anticipated blood loss, need for advanced monitoring or postoperative support.
- Procedure factors: duration, position, limited access to the airway/patient, contrast/radiation, bleeding/vascular complications and whether the procedure itself may cause abrupt instability.
- Environment: physical space, lighting, electrical/gas supply, access to the patient, infection control, ability to evacuate/transfer and proximity of emergency support.

## 2. Staffing and rescue capability
- Appropriately trained anaesthetist and assistant; clear roles and communication with procedural staff.
- Immediate access to additional skilled help, resuscitation/defibrillation, difficult-airway equipment and emergency drugs.
- A safe recovery plan with appropriately trained staff, monitoring and transfer pathway to PACU/ICU.

## 3. Monitoring

PG18 places continuous clinical observation and vigilance alongside electronic monitoring. I would use the standard monitoring required for the anaesthetic technique — oxygenation, ventilation/capnography as appropriate, circulation with ECG/pulse and BP, inspired gases/agent where relevant — and make sure alarms are audible and enabled. BP intervals should shorten with instability; I would not accept a remote setup where the patient cannot be observed or alarms cannot be heard.

## 4. Add monitoring for specific risk

| Risk | Additional monitoring / preparation |
|---|---|
| Expected rapid BP change / vasoactive infusion | Arterial catheter; infusion pumps and secure access. |
| Major bleeding | Arterial line, serial Hb/coagulation as indicated, rapid-infusion/warming capability, blood access. |
| Severe cardiac disease | Echo/TOE or advanced haemodynamic monitoring where results will change management. |
| Long procedure / temperature risk | Temperature monitoring and active warming. |

## 5. If the suite cannot support the plan

I would change the anaesthetic technique, bring additional equipment/personnel, or move the procedure to a location that can safely support the patient. “Remote” is not a justification for lowering the standard.

items.title: 17. Choosing monitoring for a high-risk anaesthetic
items.q: A patient with severe pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction requires urgent non-cardiac surgery. Justify the monitoring you would use and explain what each addition would change in your management.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would justify each monitor against a specific threat: acute RV failure, systemic hypotension reducing RV coronary perfusion, arrhythmia, hypoxaemia/hypercapnia and abrupt changes in pulmonary vascular resistance. I would use standard monitoring plus beat-to-beat pressure, direct assessment of RV physiology and selected flow/pulmonary haemodynamic monitoring if it will change therapy.

## 1. Standard monitoring and vigilance

Apply full PG18 monitoring appropriate to GA, including continuous ECG/pulse, SpO₂, capnography/ventilation, BP and inspired gas/agent monitoring where relevant, with temperature and neuromuscular monitoring as indicated. ECG should be configured to detect rhythm/ischaemia because arrhythmia and RV perfusion failure are major hazards.

## 2. Arterial catheter

I would place an arterial line before induction if time permits. Systemic hypotension can rapidly reduce RV coronary perfusion and precipitate a spiral of RV failure; beat-to-beat pressure allows immediate vasopressor titration and repeated blood gases for oxygenation, ventilation and acid–base control.

## 3. Echo

Focused TTE or TOE, depending access and expertise, helps assess RV size/function, septal position, LV filling, pericardium and treatment response. It can distinguish low preload from RV pressure overload and guide whether fluid, vasopressor, inotrope or pulmonary vasodilator is appropriate.

## 4. PAC — selected rather than automatic

For severe pulmonary hypertension with unstable or complex physiology, a PAC may be reasonable if serial PA pressure, CO and SvO₂ will guide pulmonary vasodilator, vasopressor/inotrope and fluid decisions. I would balance this against arrhythmia/insertion risks and whether echo plus less invasive monitoring can answer the same questions.

## 5. What I am trying to prevent
- Avoid systemic hypotension, hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis because each can increase RV strain or reduce RV perfusion.
- Avoid both hypovolaemia and RV overdistension.
- Detect falling CO/RV failure early and treat the cause rather than chasing a CVP target.

items.title: 18. Vascular access in the shocked patient
items.q: Outline your approach to obtaining vascular access in a patient in shock.
items.a:
## Priorities

Rapid, reliable access for **resuscitation, drugs and monitoring**, while treating the cause. Large-bore access takes priority over central lines.

## Approach

- **1.** **Peripheral IV first:** two **large-bore** (14 to 16G) cannulas, antecubital or forearm; use **ultrasound** if veins are not visible. Flow is greatest through short, wide catheters.
- **2.** **Limit attempts:** use an early escalation plan; do not persist with repeated failed attempts during shock. A fixed two-attempt/90-second rule is a local/resuscitation-context rule, not universal.
- **3.** **Intraosseous (IO) access:** proximal humerus, proximal tibia or distal femur; fast, reliable and suitable for fluids, blood and drugs (flow is slower than a large peripheral line; use pressure). Contraindications: fracture of that bone, infection at the site, previous IO in the same bone, and prosthesis.
- **4.** **Central venous access:** use a large-bore introducer or multi-lumen catheter under ultrasound (internal jugular, subclavian or femoral); femoral is quick and compressible in arrest or major haemorrhage with site risk determined by patient, technique and duration. Avoid delay to resuscitation.
- **5.** **Alternatives:** external jugular vein, venous cutdown (saphenous at the ankle), and in children IO early.
- **6.** **Site considerations:** avoid lower limb access with suspected abdominal or pelvic venous injury; avoid the injured limb.

## Practical points

Use pressure infusers and fluid warmers, secure lines, confirm placement, label arterial or IO lines, give drugs through reliable lines, and review emergency lines promptly; replace within the locally recommended timeframe if asepsis was uncertain, rather than replacing every emergency line automatically.

## Complications

Extravasation, compartment syndrome (IO), infection, pneumothorax, arterial puncture, air embolism and delays to resuscitation.

## Monitoring

Add an arterial line when it will not delay care.

## Self-marking checklist

- Prioritises large-bore peripheral access and ultrasound
- Limits the number of attempts before escalating
- Describes IO access with sites and contraindications
- Describes central and alternative access options with site choice
- Includes practical measures (pressure infusers, warmers)
- Lists complications

items.title: 19. Improving cannulation success and minimising discomfort
items.q: Outline measures to increase the rate of successful intravenous cannulation and to minimise patient discomfort.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Ultrasound-guided peripheral venous cannulation" (BJA Educ): ultrasound improves first-attempt success, guides the choice of catheter gauge and length, and the catheter length/diameter should suit vessel depth, therapy and thrombosis/extravasation risk; do not transfer a PICC diameter-ratio rule uncritically to every PIV.

## Improving success

**Planning**
- Identify patients with difficult access (history, obesity, dehydration, chemotherapy, intravenous drug use, oedema, extremes of age).
- Choose the **appropriate site and size**: forearm or antecubital for large cannulas, dorsal hand for small; avoid joints.

**Preparation**
- **Warm** the limb, place it **dependent**, apply a tourniquet and correct genuine dehydration when appropriate; do not give unnecessary fluid or use topical nitrate routinely for cannulation.
- Good lighting, comfortable positioning, and a skilled operator.

**Technique**
- Palpate rather than rely on sight; anchor the vein; correct angle; advance the cannula after flashback.
- **Ultrasound guidance** (dynamic needle-tip positioning), near-infrared vein finders, or an experienced colleague after one or two failed attempts.
- Limit attempts and consider alternatives (IO, central) when urgent.

## Minimising discomfort

- **Explain** and reassure; distraction, music, play specialists for children.
- **Topical local anaesthetic** (EMLA, tetracaine) with product-specific time to work (EMLA on intact skin usually ≥60 minutes), **intradermal lidocaine** (buffered), needle-free jet injection, or vapocoolant spray.
- Small, appropriate cannulas, smooth technique and prompt removal of the tourniquet.
- Anxiolysis or sedation for phobic patients; nitrous oxide for children.
- Pre-warm and avoid repeated attempts.

## Complications to prevent

Haematoma, extravasation, phlebitis, nerve injury and arterial puncture.

## Self-marking checklist

- Lists measures to improve success (site, warming, tourniquet, hydration)
- Describes ultrasound guidance and catheter-to-vein ratio
- Describes limiting attempts and escalation
- Lists topical, intradermal and non-drug comfort measures
- Mentions special groups (children, phobic)
- Names complications

items.title: 20. PICC versus percutaneous CVC for three weeks of therapy
items.q: A patient requires reliable intravenous access for three weeks of antimicrobial therapy. Compare a PICC with a percutaneous central venous catheter and outline how you would minimise the risks of PICC placement and use.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

For three weeks of therapy, I would compare the devices by insertion risk, flow, thrombosis/infection, patient comfort and intended use. A PICC is attractive for prolonged stable therapy but is not automatically safer overall, particularly because thrombosis and occlusion matter. I would then outline risk reduction from device selection through insertion, tip confirmation, maintenance and timely removal.

## 1. Comparison

| Issue | PICC | Percutaneous CVC |
|---|---|---|
| Insertion | Arm insertion avoids insertion-related pneumothorax and major neck/chest arterial injury. | IJ/subclavian/femoral insertion has site-specific mechanical risks. |
| Duration / outpatient care | Well suited to weeks–months and often convenient for mobilisation/outpatient therapy. | Suitable for acute/short-medium term; neck/groin access can be less convenient. |
| Flow | Long/narrow — poor for rapid high-flow resuscitation. | Can provide larger/shorter lumens or introducer access for high-flow therapy. |
| Thrombosis | Upper-extremity thrombosis is an important risk, especially larger/multilumen devices. | Thrombosis risk remains but differs by site/device. |
| Infection | CLABSI risk still requires bundle care. | CLABSI risk also important; site and maintenance matter. |
| Mechanical issues | Malposition, occlusion, migration; no thoracic insertion complication. | Pneumothorax/haemothorax, arterial injury, malposition, bleeding. |

## 2. Minimise PICC risk before insertion
- Confirm that central access is actually required and choose the minimum number of lumens/diameter needed.
- Assess upper-limb veins with ultrasound for patency, size and thrombosis risk; avoid unnecessarily small veins/large catheters.
- Use an appropriate vein/site and full aseptic technique.

## 3. Safe insertion and confirmation

**1. **Use real-time ultrasound-guided venepuncture and a controlled wire/catheter technique.

**2. **Advance to an appropriate central tip position.

**3. **Confirm tip location using the local validated method before using the line for therapies that require central placement.

**4. **Secure and dress the line to reduce migration and contamination.

## 4. Maintenance and removal
- Use an evidence-based central-line infection-prevention bundle and aseptic access technique.
- Monitor for arm swelling/pain, catheter dysfunction, infection and thrombosis.
- Remove the catheter as soon as the indication ends; unnecessary catheter-days create avoidable infection/thrombosis risk.

**Examiner lens:** The historical PICC SAQ expected a balanced comparison rather than “PICC is safer”: lower pneumothorax/major arterial injury risk was offset by thrombosis concerns, and risk reduction needed to include placement confirmation, line-care bundle principles, minimum lumens and removal when no longer required.

items.title: 21. Maximising rapid intravenous fluid/blood delivery and using rapid infusers safely
items.q: Describe the factors that determine the maximum achievable rate of intravenous fluid administration. Outline the issues and hazards associated with rapid infusion devices.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would answer this from fluid mechanics and the complete delivery system: driving pressure, catheter radius/length, fluid viscosity and every resistance in the circuit. I would then discuss rapid-infuser benefits, device/circuit hazards and the physiological consequences of delivering large volumes of cold blood or fluid quickly.

## 1. Determinants of flow

| Factor | Effect on flow / practical meaning |
|---|---|
| Radius / internal diameter | Dominant effect: for laminar flow, flow is proportional to radius⁴. A short large-bore cannula dramatically outperforms a narrow catheter. |
| Length | Flow is inversely proportional to length; long PICCs and standard CVC lumens are poor for rapid resuscitation. |
| Driving pressure | Pressure bags/pumps/rapid infusers increase flow if the circuit can tolerate it. |
| Viscosity | Blood flows more slowly than crystalloid; warming reduces viscosity somewhat and prevents hypothermia. |
| Circuit resistance | Filters, narrow connectors, stopcocks, extension tubing and partially kinked lines reduce flow. |
| Catheter position / vein | Catheter against wall, thrombosis, small vein or extravasation limits effective delivery. |

## 2. Practical setup in major haemorrhage
- Use short large-bore peripheral access or an appropriately large central introducer rather than a long narrow lumen.
- Minimise unnecessary connectors/long extension sets; use compatible blood filters and warming/rapid-infusion circuits.
- Secure lines and check the full circuit before applying high pressure.

## 3. Rapid-infusion device hazards
- Air entrainment/air embolism if the reservoir or tubing is allowed to run dry or air-detection safeguards are bypassed.
- Line/catheter disconnection or rupture with sudden blood/fluid loss into the environment or tissue extravasation.
- Haemolysis risk depends on device, pressure, catheter and product; avoid inappropriate narrow high-resistance circuits.
- Very rapid transfusion increases citrate load/hypocalcaemia, potassium delivery and volume shifts; monitor ionised calcium/electrolytes in major haemorrhage.
