items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
- **OPTIMISE II (2024, BMJ):** [Cardiac output–guided haemodynamic therapy for major gastrointestinal surgery](https://www.bmj.com/content/387/bmj-2024-080439).
  - In 2,498 high-risk elective gastrointestinal surgery patients, a CO-guided fluid protocol plus fixed low-dose inotrope did **not** reduce 30-day infection (23.2% intervention versus 22.7% usual care); early acute cardiac events increased.
  - Do not generalise this result to every use of physiological monitoring.
- **RELIEF (2018, NEJM):** [Restrictive versus liberal fluid therapy for major abdominal surgery](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1801601).
  - A strongly restrictive regimen did not improve disability-free survival and was associated with more AKI than liberal therapy (8.6% versus 5.0%).
  - Avoid treating any fluid as inherently harmful; treat measured need.
- **CLASSIC (2022, NEJM):** [Restriction of intravenous fluid in ICU patients with septic shock](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2202707). Restriction and standard care had similar 90-day mortality after initial resuscitation. Results concern subsequent fluid exposure, not the necessity of early effective shock treatment.
- **CLOVERS (2023, NEJM):** [Early restrictive or liberal fluid management for sepsis-induced hypotension](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36688507/).
  - The trial found no significant 90-day survival difference between early vasopressor-prioritising and fluid-liberal strategies in the enrolled population; manage individual patient physiology.
- **ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (2019, JAMA):** [Peripheral perfusion–targeted resuscitation versus lactate-level–targeted resuscitation](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2019.0071).
  - The primary mortality difference was not statistically significant, but it illustrates why capillary refill and dynamic clinical context should inform resuscitation rather than chasing lactate alone.

items.title: References by subtopic
items.body:
## Evidence audit and scope

This audit uses the **original workbook allocations**, not previous teaching notes or an inherited crosswalk. The source of the allocation is the 10 Monitoring & Haemodynamics sheet in Prioritised LEarning Sets(4).xlsx (30 parent LO rows, 33 explicit components). The chapter references below are specific locations to inspect; a curriculum entry is considered addressed only if the teaching explains indications, measurement technique/assumptions, interpretation, errors, safety, and clinical decisions where these are germane. 'Complete' means the workbook assigns the LO to this set, **not** that reading a document confers procedural competence.

### A.1 Separate curriculum-coverage verdict

Curriculum mapping (27 outcomes assigned for completion): All 27 rows have a corresponding substantive teaching location, with the three shared components distinguished separately. The subsequent independent depth audit found that this crosswalk alone overstated completeness of several 'evaluate' and practical-procedure outcomes. Those gaps have now been integrated at 2.5–2.6, 4.5, 5.8, 6.7, 7.8, 8.7–8.9, 9.5, 10.6 and 11.7. This is evidence-based written learning coverage rather than proof of bedside procedural competence; some device-specific detail and protocols legitimately require local teaching.

**Components only (3/3 rows).** IT_SQ 1.1 covers monitoring/equipment/standards here, with broader professional safety content assigned to Set 36. AR_ME 3.2 covers invasive monitoring/vascular access procedures here, with remaining procedures allocated to Sets 21, 24, and 25. SS_IC 1.29 covers goal-directed therapy here; broader shock management was allocated to Set 1. No claim is made that these parent outcomes are complete in Set 10 alone.

Examiner-depth audit: the 2025.1 question required obesity-specific advantages and disadvantages of BOTH invasive and non-invasive BP monitoring; 2025.2 required evaluation of intraoperative TTE rather than an uncritical catalogue of echo uses; 2026.1 required complete confounders and measurement errors for CVP; and 2015.2 required procedural risk reduction for PICC, not merely a comparison with CVC. These are now taught explicitly alongside access rescue, PAC calculations and fluid-response interpretation. An 'evaluate' outcome requires the reasons a method is useful AND circumstances where its information may be inaccurate or harmful.

### A.2 Evidence accuracy and limitations audit

| **High-risk decision** | **Evidence-checked interpretation and caveat** | **Where integrated** |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum monitoring | PG18 (2025) states monitoring requirements; **10 minutes is a maximum allowable BP interval**, not a recommended usual interval for unstable patients. Frequency must rise with risk. | 2.1–2.2 |
| Dynamic fluid assessment | PPV/SVV depend on controlled ventilation, suitable tidal volumes, sinus rhythm and suitable chest/lung compliance; fluid responsiveness does **not** imply fluid tolerance or benefit. | 4.1–4.6, 12.3 |
| PAC and CO monitors | Values depend on assumptions, transducer and calibration validity, shunts/TR/ventilation, waveform interpretation and operator skill. There is no evidence basis to insert advanced devices routinely in all major operations. | 5–6, 12 |
| Focused echo | POCUS answers bounded bedside questions; it does not replace comprehensive TTE/TOE or an appropriately credentialled operator. PG46 and PG47 define different scopes. | 7.1–7.7 |
| Central venous access | Dynamic site selection requires mechanical injury, thrombosis, bleeding, infection, future dialysis access and expected treatment duration; the 2026 WHO infection recommendations cannot override an immediately safer access route. | 8 |
| Routine GDT for abdominal surgery | OPTIMISE II and POQI 2025 **do not** support routine use of a fixed inotrope plus CO-guided protocol in unselected elective major abdominal patients; this does not disprove selective physiological monitoring in complex cases. | 5.9, 10.3 |
| Septic resuscitation | The 2026 SSC targets and dynamic reassessment guide selected shock care; microcirculatory/perfusion endpoints and prompt source treatment matter more than a prescribed normal CVP or lactate. | 10.4, 11, 12.3 |
| Fluid volume and renal injury | The RELIEF, CLASSIC and CLOVERS findings support avoiding reflexively restrictive or liberal protocols that disregard phase, volume status and fluid tolerance. No single trial establishes one universal fluid quantity. | 9–10 |

**Limits of the audit:** This document is an independently researched educational synthesis with hyperlinks to publicly available guidelines, BJA Education and trials, plus comparison with uploaded ANZCA examination reports. It does not reproduce subscription textbook chapters in full, and it cannot verify the trainee's practical competence. Local hospital policies, drug formularies and the current ANZCA online documents take precedence for clinical decisions.

### A.3 Depth audit: gaps corrected and residual boundaries

Significant corrections integrated: a two-sided obese-patient BP appraisal (2025.1), PG18 axillary-dissection guidance, selection of valid dynamic tests, device accuracy versus trending, PAC zone-3 wedge and PVR/SVR calculations, an explicit TTE-first shock examination (2025.2), procedural PICC and central-access safeguards (2015.2), blood/rapid infusion circuit mechanics, stepwise low-risk fluid prescriptions and more critical appraisal of goal-directed therapy.

High-stakes sources cross-checked: ANZCA PG18 (2025), PG46/PG47 (2025), 2025 Association of Anaesthetists safe vascular access, 2026 WHO central catheter infection guidance, ASE 2025 ultrasound-guided access recommendations, 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign and POQI-11 (2025). The original haemodynamic equations and numeric examples were spot-recalculated; no major mathematical correction was required.

Residual limits: written knowledge and evidence appraisal do not replace supervised ultrasound/vascular access and PAC skills. Absolute flow and pressure thresholds remain device-, loading- and context-dependent. Guideline wording changes over time; current institutional formulary, safety protocols and specialist assistance govern clinical care. The linked supplementary sources below provide the current primary documents, rather than relying on exam-report shorthand.

## Core guidelines, BJA Education and examiner cross-checks

- **ANZCA PG18 (2025):** [Guideline on monitoring during anaesthesia](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/6296ef66-b43b-4dc6-938b-770f94ba7e6e/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/PG18-Anaesthesia-monitoring-2025.pdf?language=en). Minimum intraoperative monitoring, availability, clinical observation, alarms and recording.
- **ANZCA PG46 (2025):** [Guideline on perioperative echocardiography](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getcontentasset/59f8ec2b-8327-4df2-9db3-b247fbb0d649/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/pg46-perioperative-echocardiography-2025.pdf?download=1&language=en). Comprehensive perioperative echo and competence.
- **ANZCA PG47 (2025):** [Guideline on training and practice of perioperative diagnostic point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/8ca3291d-4f5b-4434-8433-78bfcd239b7f/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/PG47-Perioperative-diagnostic-POCUS-2025.pdf?language=en). This guideline sets the training and practice expectations; focused bedside POCUS has a narrower scope than formal TOE/TTE.
- **POQI-11 (2025):** [Goal-directed haemodynamic therapy: evidence-based recommendations](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2025.05.033). Read with OPTIMISE II; not a mandate for all abdominal surgery.
- **POQI (2024):** [Perioperative fluid management consensus](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2024.07.038). Fluid phases, monitoring and personalised balance.
- **Surviving Sepsis Campaign (2026):** [Management of sepsis and septic shock](https://sccm.org/clinical-resources/guidelines/guidelines/surviving-sepsis-campaign-international-guidelines-for-management-of-sepsis-and-septic-shock-2026). MAP goals, vasopressors, fluids and frequent reassessment.
- **WHO (2024):** [Prevention of bloodstream infections associated with peripheral catheters](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240093829). Insertion, maintenance and safe catheter removal.
- **WHO (2026):** [Preventing bloodstream infections associated with central venous catheters](https://www.who.int/india/publications/i/item/9789240121805). Infection-prevention strategies, insertion sites, sterile practice and bundles.
- **CDC:** [Prevention of intravascular catheter-related infection: recommendations](https://www.cdc.gov/infection-control/hcp/intravascular-catheter-related-infections/summary-recommendations.html). Practical aseptic care, dressings, hub care and device minimisation.
- **ASE (2025):** [Ultrasound guidance for vascular cannulation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.echo.2024.12.004). Ultrasound technique and procedural safety.
- **AHA/ACC (2024):** [Guideline for perioperative cardiovascular management in noncardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001285). Patient-centred haemodynamic risk assessment and blood pressure management.
- **German haemodynamic guidance (2024):** [Intraoperative haemodynamic monitoring and management](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10877-024-01132-7). Structured BP/CO selection and individualised monitoring.

2025 Association of Anaesthetists: Safe vascular access—site selection, catheter-to-vein ratio, inadvertent arterial dilation, peripheral noradrenaline and catheter thrombosis.  [Open source](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.16727)

ANZCA PG18 2025 Appendix 1: Intravenous access and BP monitoring after axillary nodal dissection; avoid unsupported blanket prohibitions.  [Open source](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

2025 narrative review: Measurement and interpretation of central venous pressure—waveform, venous congestion and clinical pitfalls.  [Open source](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40457939/)

ASE 2025: Guidelines for Performing Ultrasound-Guided Vascular Cannulation—needle/wire tracking and safety.  [Open source](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39909653/)

Desai and Garry, BJA Education 2018: Dynamic fluid responsiveness using TTE—technical prerequisites and limitations.  [Open source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2018.03.005)

Cheng and Arntfield, BJA Education 2024: Critical care echocardiography—views, clinical use and training.  [Open source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.07.003)

ANZCA Australasian Anaesthesia 2019: Preventing vascular damage during internal jugular catheter insertion—checklist and verification.  [Open source](https://airr.anzca.edu.au/anzcacrisjspui/bitstream/11055/958/1/Australasian%20Anaesthesia%202019.pdf)

WHO 2026: Guidelines for prevention of bloodstream infections associated with central venous catheters.  [Open source](https://www.who.int/india/publications/i/item/9789240121805)

## B.3 BJA Education articles and ANZCA Blue Book

- **Cheng and Arntfield (2024), BJA Education:** [Critical care echocardiography: training, imaging, and indications](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.07.003) — standard views, training, limitation and interpretation in shock.
- **Desai and Garry (2018), BJA Education:** [Assessing dynamic fluid-responsiveness using transthoracic echocardiography in intensive care](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2018.03.005) — physiological assumptions behind dynamic indices and passive leg raise.
- **ANZCA Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) archive:** [Official Blue Book collection](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29). The 2019 vascular-access chapter, Preventing vascular damage during central venous catheter insertion via the internal jugular vein, is especially relevant to chapter 8; apply its prevention principles alongside updated WHO/ASE guidance.

## B.4 ANZCA examiner-report cross-checks

The uploaded 2015.2–2026.1 reports were searched for examination demands and common deficits, notably **2026.1 central venous pressure limitations**, **2025.2 intraoperative TTE**, **2015.2 PICC access**, damping/arterial monitoring, haemodynamic calculations and pulmonary hypertension. Where a past paper tests an old protocol, the modern guidance is taught in the chapter, with historical questions used for examiner expectation, not to override current clinical evidence.
